Crystalline materials are traditionally modeled using anisotropic elasticity theory. In this study, the fracture resistance of these materials is added to the theory. The fracture characteristics are defined by a surface energy density and a fracture strain, which varies depending on the direction relative to the crystal lattice. An extension of the theory of elastic fracture is developed, taking into consideration the factors of direction-dependent fracture strain and surface energy density. Forms of these factors that are consistent with crystallographic structure are explored, particularly those that are consistent with common fracture laws across crystalline materials such as minerals and glass. These forms of fracture characteristics enable the conversion of elastic theory to fracture theory, and enable the determination of fracture resistance through a stable elastic path. An analysis of the fracture resistance characteristics demonstrates that the fracture resistance depends on the direction relative to the crystal lattice. The fracture theory is applied to the study of fracture resistance in amethyst, rock, and glass, revealing the existence of non-trivial fracture resistance characteristics. The fracture theory and fracture resistance characteristics are validated by matching the theoretical and actual acoustic emission signals generated by the materials studied. The proposed theoretical framework and methods provide a basis for the prediction of fracture resistance characteristics in crystalline materials, which are essential for the prevention and management of fractures. The fracture theory and fracture resistance characteristics are suitable not only for the study of minerals and glass but also for any crystalline material, which can be used to develop strategies for the prevention and management of fractures in engineering applications. Furthermore, by employing the tools of nonlinear functional analysis, specifically the compactness-Schauder method, it is proven that there exists a unique solution to the Navier-Stokes equations that satisfies the specified requirements, provided the parameter that governs nonlinearity is sufficiently small. Moreover, through the application of the quantity $M_2(u_0)$, the well-known result that involves the Beale-Khajahanov-Lin type estimates for the quantity $\| \nabla u \|_{L^\infty(0,T;V^2)}$ is achieved. An interesting aspect of this approach lies in the fact that it avoids the use of classical compactness arguments, such as those based on the Lebesgue integration theory, which fail to provide finite values for $M_2(u_0)$. Instead, the developed method seamlessly builds upon the initial conditions and leads to a clear and straightforward proof of the desired result. Finally, the research presents a complete diagram of the problem's well-posedness in the specified functional space setting. The results of the present paper correspond with those obtained in Alves, Bares and Simas (Math. Mod. Anal. (N. A. M. A.) 2020). Nonetheless, the novel method presented here for deriving the finite value of $M_2(u_0)$ is considered original. Moreover, the research was carried out with full funding support. In this pattern-based cell morphology, anomalies can signal health issues, while normal variations render traditional descriptor methods ineffective for representation. To capture cell morphology's rich nuances, we propose utilizing implicit neural representations, an approach successful in creative applications such as generative modeling for 3D objects. To effectively utilize IRRs, we developed a training method involving generators and discriminators, enabling the creation of a cell morphology dataset. Our approach produces a data-driven cell morphology model, allowing for the creation of realistic, unseen cell structures through adversarial training, and demonstrating promising results in both objective measures and qualitative evaluations. Additionally, we explore applications for the created model, including manipulating cell structures for a specific task and generating novel, diversity-rich cells. Our work highlights the potential of creative applications for the creation of implicit neural representations, particularly in domains where domain-specific methods have limitations in capturing pattern-based phenomena. The study of exoplanet atmospheres via low-resolution transit spectroscopy holds significant potential in identifying exoplanets that may resemble Earth and understanding their composition. Nonetheless, the presence of stellar activity can complicate these findings. To gauge the influence of stellar activity, we performed spectroscopic analysis of a synthetic low-resolution data set of a hot Jupiter system, incorporating data from the Kepler space telescope and operating under conditions of variable activity. We discovered that low-resolution data is susceptible to signals of stellar activity, which translates to incorrect atmospheric composition and high uncertainty in interpretation. Conversely, our results demonstrate that high-resolution spectroscopy provides a robust solution for the planetary parameters, even when the data contains signals of stellar activity. This is due to the enhanced ability of high-resolution data to detect and isolate planetary and stellar features. Notably, when operating at high resolution, the effects of stellar activity can be identified and, in some instances, mitigated through analysis. This is achieved by applying specialized methods, such as the "nulling method," which can neutralize stellar activity signals while providing inaccurate atmospheric parameters without these contaminants. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the necessity of accounting for stellar activity when interpreting spectroscopic data of transiting exoplanets, whether utilizing low- or high-resolution spectroscopy. Given the limited understanding of stellar activity patterns, employing techniques that allow for the neutralization of activity signals appears to be the most reliable approach. To further the field, we suggest incorporating "external nulling" methods as a straightforward means to alleviate the influence of stellar activity on exoplanet atmosphere studies. Nonetheless, we recognize that this approach does not address the underlying activity patterns, which require dedicated monitoring observations, such as those provided by Kepler. To overcome this, we propose establishing a new mission dedicated to characterizing stellar activity, which would mark a crucial advancement in exoplanet atmosphere research. This mission would mark a natural progression of the efforts started by Kepler and would provide the necessary insights to standardize stellar activity corrections in exoplanet systems, ultimately paving the way for the accurate identification and characterization of potentially habitable exoplanets. The study ultimately provides an in-depth analysis of the centipede's unique gait, offering new insights to the field of locomotion biology. Several solution methods exist to approximate the dispersion and absorption of tsunami waves generated by an asteroid impact. One set of methods, typically used in tsunami simulations, employs the Riemann problem-based shallow water wave equation with drag factor to account for dispersion, yielding an average first-order approximation of the dispersion relation. However, the inability of this model and its corresponding numerical methods to accurately solve the fully dispersive Bessel equation results in significant errors for long-range asteroid impacts. In contrast, a more advanced model uses a series expansion of Bessel functions combined with a run-length conversion to describe wave propagation in the ocean and atmosphere. Following an asteroid impact on a low-budget computing system, we demonstrate the implementation of both methods using the CLAWPACK software package. Subsequently, a combination of the solution methods is proposed to achieve a multi-scale approach to accurately simulate dispersive tsunami waves over long distances. Initially validated using a simple domain with multiple sources of contamination, we aim to further develop this approach in future work. Our research identifies and analyzes a rare and enigmatic galaxy subset that is brightly visible in the infrared, yet extremely dim in the optical spectrum. A distinctive, extremely faint and highly reddened galaxy, named Z8G4, was previously reported due to its exceptional redshift of $10.3$. Another galaxy, M1000-SG, is a young, luminous galaxy located at $6.2$ ($z=5.3]$) that exhibits a similar optical faintness. Both galaxies can only be observed in infrared light. We propose that a supernova explosion from a massive star forms the core of an optically hidden, heavily dust-obscurated galaxy. We ran simulations for galaxy formation through gas outflows and have compared them with infrared and optical data of nearby galaxies. We estimate a high degree of certainty ($\sim$60%) that the galaxy subset in question corresponds to dust-obscurated young (early) starburst galaxies similar to COSMOS-GR8, whose age is around two hundred million years. We predict the following can be observed in the galaxies such as these in deep optical and infrared imaging taken by JWST: large amounts of dust, heavy heavy elements, extremely young stars and very young supernovae among others. These findings highlight a previously unappreciated phenomenon where early starburst galaxies are cloaked by dust from our view, pointing to dense dust clouds playing a crucial part in the formation of these galaxies. It is also suggested that a method involving deep optical imaging followed by selective applications of spectral analysis could serve as an effective means to discover these galaxies at greater redshifts ($z>6$). Lastly, if the phenomenon remains consistent, it is predicted that a subset of two galaxies per unit of a specific stellar luminosity ($L_{\lambda 1600}$) should exist within the deceleration parameter space for every redshift above $6$. These newly discovered galaxies, in turn, can serve to constrain theoretical models of galaxy development. Our research involved analyzing global patterns of precipitation in relation to different El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation types, which were identified through a canonical correlation analysis between sea surface temperature and precipitation. We utilized three various ENSO types: the traditional Western Pacific and Eastern Pacific patterns as well as a recently discovered conjugate configuration. Following the identification of ENSO types, we computed and compared zonal and meridional precipitation anomalies for each, differentiated by their very low and elevated seasonal variability. Notably, the conjugate configuration exhibited distinctive characteristics in comparison to the traditional Western Pacific and Eastern Pacific patterns. Furthermore, significant disparities were discovered in terms of geographical distribution and intensity of precipitation anomalies. This distinction has implications for understanding various ENSO types and their effects, particularly on regions experiencing severe precipitation and precipitation-related natural disaster risks. Such information may be useful for enhancing ENSO-related prediction accuracy and efficacy. Finally, the findings of this analysis contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of ENSO-type precipitation patterns, which will help inform ENSO-related scientific research and predictive methodologies. We observe ENSO-type precipitation patterns to vary in intensity and spatial extent but share common characteristics such as amplified precipitation in regions receiving atmospheric water via the Western Pacific Subtropical High. Additionally, through a meridional decomposition of annual precipitation, over 60\% of total precipitation variability in Asia, particularly in countries such as China, Indonesia, and the Philippines, was attributed to ENSO types exhibiting conjugate configuration precipitation patterns. Conversely, in South America, regions such as Ecuador and Colombia, more than 60\% of total precipitation variability was attributed to the traditional Western Pacific and Eastern Pacific patterns. We uncover ENSO-type and region-specific pattern diversification through ENSO-type precipitation analysis. Consequently, the conventional model used to predict Western Pacific and Eastern Pacific patterns in countries such as China may prove ineffective for countries in the opposite hemisphere. Conversely, in countries receiving conjugate configuration-dominated precipitation, correspondence with conventional model precipitation patterns may be observed in countries such as Peru and Ecuador. This research reveals the importance of processing local data to accurately predict ENSO-type precipitation patterns. We recommend a double-cross correlation strategy to differentiate conjugate and traditional ENSO types beyond geographical boundaries, promoting convergence between meteorological observations and predictions. This technique may effectively rectify the current ENSO-type prediction accuracy issue. Our research examines the kinetic equation of polymerization-induced surface shrinkage and its associated scattering changes, which create temporal fluctuations in the intensity and correlation of scattered light. A novel factor that emerges in our model accounts for non-affine deformations resulting from localized stress fluctuations. We discovered that the kinetic equation can be reduced to a well-known Smoluchowski-Collins-Melzer (SCM) equation under conditions of small fluctuation amplitude. However, our model diverges from the established theory beyond this threshold. Through experimental validation using silicone oil as a reference, we found that the scattering pattern modification is predominantly influenced by fluctuations in scatterer density. Conversely, when the polymerization agent has a substantial molecular size compared to the scattering medium, the primary factor affecting the pattern shifts to particle position correlation. A comparative analysis between our model's predictions and experimental observations reveals correspondence between the two. Ultimately, our study provides an assessment of the relevance of our model to a wide range of epipolymerization experiments, encompassing both large and monodisperse particles. Our findings support the notion that the kinetic equation is a universal tool for studying surface contraction, applicable in various polymerization contexts. Moreover, our model offers a means of distinguishing between SCM-equivalent and large-amplitude fluctuation behaviors in real-world experiments. Specifically, our approach enables the determination of key parameters such as stress correlation lengths and deformation factors. Additionally, our model can be used to predict a critical threshold above which the SCM equation is invalid, marked by a specific large-amplitude fluctuation amplitude that depends on system parameters. Studies of systems featuring size nonuniformity among particles indicate that the corresponding backscattering intensity should exhibit a non-SCM behavior characterized by a local maximum. A thorough examination of our model is suggested for future research and experimental investigations involving a range of materials and conditions. Specifically, our approach may be effectively applied to observing large-amplitude fluctuations in systems involving monodisperse and bidisperse scatterers or extremely large particles. Moreover, our method could be used for analyzing data from previous experiments with improved precision, leading to a deeper understanding of non-affine deformation behaviors. To support future investigations, a comprehensive dataset is provided, including relevant parameters and experimental results, in addition to related simulation data. The associated Python code is also made available for public access. A deeper discussion of our model's numerical solving process is provided in a separate appendix, along with related implementation details. We examine the properties of hypersequent logic subclasses, particularly those that allow contraction and the contraction-free "alleviation" rule, within the framework of Fitch-style natural deduction systems. Our investigation encompasses the analysis of admissibility, completeness, decidable and undecidable inference, and complexity in these logical systems. The results we obtain show that most "alleviation" logics with regard to standard logical properties are undecidable if they incorporate contraction, whereas those without it often present undetermined cases. Conversely, we find that logics allowing contraction but devoid of another property we studied are usually decidable. Furthermore, we identify instances of logics with unique properties that differ from their contraction-free or fully exponential counterparts. The outcome also indicates that some "alleviation" logics with certain properties can be rendered decidable by adopting a semilinearization method. The study offers an in-depth examination of undecidability cases in hypersequent logics and proposes decidable alternatives for selected logics. Ultimately, we provide reasons for the choice of a particular direction in further research. The main challenge in expanding pre-trained language models for specific downstream tasks lies in adapting the model to new data. By assuming that early layers encode general semantic meanings, we propose HyperExpan: a method that utilizes hyperbolic representation and iterative updates for both feature extraction and classification to address this challenge. By doing so, we can efficiently utilize the benefits of pre-trained language models while reducing the number of required new training steps. Experimental results demonstrate HyperExpan's ability to achieve competitive performance with fewer updates of the pre-trained model's later layers. Furthermore, we found that HyperExpan can be effective even when the number of updates is very low, at 10-20 steps, compared to other methods that require numerous iterations. This ability, along with the code and model benchmarks, makes HyperExpan a suitable option for rapid development and deployment on a wide range of downstream classification tasks. We also show that HyperExpan is applicable not only to language-related tasks, but also to tasks involving the use of tabular data. Importantly, we found that HyperExpan's performance varies inversely with the number of data samples and, importantly, outperforms other methods by a significant margin on data sets containing fewer than 100,000 examples. Finally, we have successfully used HyperExpan to develop a classification model on a large dataset consisting of 68 million examples, thereby showcasing its potential for practical use. The model's performance on the Large Book Dataset is comparable to that of a newly trained model, while requiring significantly fewer updates. This result highlights HyperExpan's ability to leverage the full power of pre-trained models effectively and efficiently. Future manufacturing schedules are being disrupted by the widespread adoption of data-driven methods due to several factors, including unpredictable machine breakdowns and unforeseen supply chain disruptions. A crucial challenge in tackling these uncertainties is the lack of detailed information about the stochastic events affecting schedule flexibility. This study presents a novel approach utilizing determinacy mass functions to measure uncertainty levels in various stochastic events within production systems. Specifically, we examine how operational breakdowns, failures in external deliveries, and worker absences can be modeled using determinacy mass functions and example illustrations are provided. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in leveraging uncertainty information to enhance scheduling flexibility. It has been implemented in an Industry 4.0 demonstration system, showcasing its potential benefits in optimized scheduling outcomes. The key advantages of our approach are its ability to enhance dispatching strategy performance, increase productivity, and enable automatic calculation of confidence intervals for performance metrics. It also enables scheduling without assumptions about stochastic information and allows flexibility in decision-making without influencing the original dispatching settings. The code for our approach is openly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/tu-darmstadt-ifs/DMF4Industry4.0. A corresponding video showcasing our demonstration system can be found at: https://youtu.be/KR4iLOo2y00. Cyber-Physical Systems, such as self-driving cars and surgical robots, rely on Time Interval Logic to ensure their complex behavioral requirements are met. However, traditional time interval approaches face challenges in handling dependencies between time intervals and system state, especially when non-linear equations come into play. Furthermore, time interval logic-based methods struggle to effectively mitigate uncertainties in model error, misspecification, and data errors. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing an advanced formulation of robustness tailored to Cyber-Physical Systems, one that leverages Time Interval Logic and the behavior of cyber-physical systems to bound error propagation. This novel approach is utilized to develop robust design methods for CP systems that incorporate model error, demonstrated through a vehicle longitudinal control example showing its efficacy. The methodology is found to provide designs that are more suitable and closer to optimal compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. The research highlights the potential benefits of using Time Interval Logic to ensure the robustness and safety of Cyber-Physical Systems, especially in the presence of uncertainty and error. The proposed approach is found to offer a viable framework for designing CP systems, providing a useful tool for engineers and designers. The method can be directly applied to a wide range of CP synthesis tools, allowing for efficient and effective exploration of design options. The resulting designs obtained through this approach are superior in quality and more adaptable to various CP system applications when compared to traditional formulations. The analysis of the method also confirms its ability to effectively account for dependencies, non-linear dependencies, model error, and uncertainty which is a significant improvement over existing techniques. The introduction of this framework marks a significant breakthrough in the field of Cyber-Physical Systems design and requires no modifications to existing tools or procedures. The research provides valuable insights into the various formulations of robustness and enables designers to effectively utilize Time Interval Logic and the behavior of cyber-physical systems to bound error propagation. The method can be used in various applications such as vehicle longitudinal control, tracking, systems with multiple inputs and outputs, and systems with multiple model representations, making it a versatile tool for CP system design. The resulting parameterizations obtained through this approach allow for easy validation and analysis of CP system requirements and provide a robust and reliable defense against uncertainty and error. The analysis of the method also confirms its ability to effectively reduce conservativeness which is a significant advantage in Cyber-Physical Systems design. The introduction of this framework marks a significant breakthrough in the field of Cyber-Physical Systems design and provides a valuable contribution to the CP system design community. Identifying the patterns of these obscure signals without a reference remains a difficult challenge. We've discovered that sensors with irregular motion, such as accelerometers in buildings and trees, record the dark signals with remarkable precision. Collecting data from these sources can help create a vast network of nodes that work together to identify the dark signals. A cutting-edge AI system can use this network to pinpoint the origin of these signals, even in large areas. Our experiments show that this approach is remarkably effective in locating dark signals. We've applied this method in a simulated investigation of a murder from the TV show "True Detective" and found the key evidence. Our results show that these sources have distinct properties when compared to sub-microJy ablated sources, detected by the FIRST survey but not in the NVSS catalog. The sources used in our study have a minimum flux density of 100 $\mu$Jy, and we were able to stack their spectra, confirming their dimness. Our findings indicate that they exhibit characteristic high-frequency spectral depression, and their radio sizes follow a one-way relationship with frequency, distinct from other radio sources. We introduce the abstract concealed Markov model (ACMM), a universal description for models that describe the process of hiding information as it interacts with an environment. The ACMM, defined within the category of weakly partial control structures, functions as a denotational model that represents a combination of stochastic and non-deterministic behaviour. It serves as a fundamental framework for analysing the hidden aspects of complex systems, providing a tool for predictive modelling and quantitative analysis. By exploring the properties of ACMMs, we demonstrate their potential for expressing a range of established Markov models. Through practical examples, we showcase the ACMM's capability for encapsulating both symbolic and numerical descriptions of hidden state behaviour. A significant concern with mobile localization systems is the potential for users' locations to be linked to their identities, compromising their privacy. Various methods have been employed to conceal one's location after utilizing a mobile localization system. Prior studies relied on an assumption of uniform distribution in a designated area, yet this assumption doesn't reflect actual posterior probability distributions over locations. Conversely, our proposed method utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian model that enables an uninformative prior distribution to evolve into an accurate posterior distribution with knowledge of additional factors like time of day and day of the week. The inherent assumptions of this model are analogous to prior research methods and can be thought of as minimum requirements for preserving location privacy. The first experimental findings indicate that our proposed model is capable of generating $10^7$ to $10^8$ larger possible locations as compared to current best practice methods, thereby enhancing location privacy by almost two orders of magnitude. The research also demonstrates that reducing the size of possible locations and potential observation areas to two dimensions does not diminish the associated location privacy benefits. The theoretical underpinnings of our proposed model are confirmed by empirical results from a month-long data collection process. The research concludes by considering locations where users' activities do not change and how our proposed model can be adapted for such scenarios. The research's primary contribution lies in the development of a reliable location tracking privacy analysis model, to the best of our knowledge, one that doesn't compromise accuracy in such scenarios. The research also presents our understanding of current methods in standardized format, alongside mathematical representations of each technique, enabling a systematic comparison of methods that didn't exist previously. Additionally, our research demonstrates that some methods are susceptible to a significant degree of location precision loss, albeit still providing some level of privacy. Our proposed model represents a significant improvement over these methods and has been shown to provide near-optimal results, opening up opportunities for further research in optimizing location privacy. The research also aims to promote replication of our research across various possible scenarios. The research's major implications are located towards the end of the abstract. The research was conducted at the University of British Columbia, in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. The research's key results can also be applied to other possible scenarios, such as the use of location data to determine the identity of individuals in surveillance footage. To achieve this, a large amount of data is typically collected and analyzed to establish detailed brain networks, which are then used to support various applications such as clinical evaluations, neurological assessments, and treatments. Notwithstanding the extensive use of multisite fMRI datasets in this context, there's still a pressing need for reliable prediction models that can accurately reflect individual differences in resting-state connectivity. These differences are thought to reflect unique brain functions, benefits from specific therapies, and adaptations to environmental stimuli. By leveraging prediction models that consider regional activity and interregional correlations, researchers can gain deeper insights into the intricate processes underlying brain function and behavior. To address these research goals, we conducted a study using the cross-coherence matrix to model pairwise correlations between brain regions, which was applied to data from 1,148 subjects across 22 sites. Our results demonstrate that models based on cross-coherence significantly outperform those based on seed-based measures or structural connectivity, particularly when trained on a small fraction of available data. Notably, we found that cross-coherence models exhibit minimal discrepancies between sites, which suggests a high degree of consistency in functional brain organization across diverse populations. These findings have significant implications for statistical analysis, such as understanding the reliability of group differences in resting-state connectivity and their potential association with traits and behaviors. Additionally, we found that while cross-coherence models demonstrate exceptional generalization using data from new sites, they can still be further improved by incorporating additional covariates such as age, sex, and assessment delays. The objective is to design protocols that facilitate data exchange between specified source and target nodes with minimal power consumption. To measure success, an optimal protocol is sought that minimizes the number of transmissions while ensuring accurate data replication at the target node. Recent advancements have focused on formulating efficient protocols for determining if a particular node is the sole source of data or for establishing a connection with multiple source nodes and transmitting data to a target node. Previous research has already achieved an efficient protocol for determining if a node is the sole source of data, which uses approximately O(n) transmissions when working with up to n nodes. Meanwhile, a different protocol has been developed for establishing connections between source and target nodes and transmitting data, which uses about O(log^2 log k + log n) transmissions when working with k parallel connections. This paper builds upon these findings by creating a new protocol that addresses two problems simultaneously: determining if a node is the sole source of data and establishing a connection between source and target nodes and transmitting data. The proposed solution uses approximately O(min(log k + log n, n)) transmissions. A more nuanced variation of the first problem was introduced in 2018, which incorporates an additional power-saving feature: allowing nodes in an arbitrary network setup to conserve energy by entering a sleeping state. The modified protocol can accomplish this by ensuring that only the source node is awake to transmit data and the rest of the nodes can be in a sleeping state. This paper generalizes the variation by incorporating multiple source nodes and establishing a connection between source and target nodes and transmitting data. The proposed solution uses approximately O(min(log k + log n, n)) transmissions. Using a combination of quantum transport and density functional theory, we analyzed how helium ion irradiation affects the superconducting properties of hydrogen-rich compounds, specifically H$_3$S at high pressure. We discovered that the response to irradiation is influenced by the presence of van Hove singularity in the density of states, with lower pressure H$_3$S exhibiting two distinct types of isotope effect. A false superconducting gap and continuous superconductivity transition were observed in higher pressure H$_3$S with no isotope effect. The critical temperature of H$_3$S was also determined in relation to pressure and irradiation. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into the underlying mechanism of superconductivity in hydrogen-rich compounds. The calculation showed that at the highest pressure and 5 MeV helium ion irradiation, the critical temperature of H$_3$S can be increased to its critical point, suggesting the possibility of realizing a critical temperature of up to 74 K under these conditions. The outcome of our work sheds light on the debate about the origin of superconductivity in hydrogen-rich compounds. By incorporating the density of states with a van Hove singularity, our theory can account for the entire pressure-synthesis of superconducting properties, including the critical temperature, anisotropy of upper critical field, and isotope effect. Thus, our research indicates that such a singularity plays a significant role in superconducting properties of hydrogen-rich compounds. The possibility of realizing unconventional superconductivity in these compounds is, however, excluded. The critical temperature dependence on pressure can be explained by considering the change in density of states at a van Hove singularity without requiring any other mechanism. The influence of irradiation on the critical temperature was found to be directly related to the change in superconducting gap in momentum space caused by the disruption of DFT-coherent pairs of electrons. The increase in superconducting gap in irradiated compound was observed to be the result of the formation of fragments of Cooper pairs that contribute to higher critical temperature. The outcome of our research indicates that an increase in Tc due to irradiation can be utilized as an experimental indicator of van Hove singularity in DFT and, consequently, in real compounds. The dependence of isotope effect on pressure was found to be distinct due to the presence of two types of isotope effects, which indicates that superconducting mechanism in H$_3$S is distinct from that of conventional materials, which exhibit one type of isotope effect only. A significant challenge in visual-based mobile robot navigation is re-localizing, especially in scenarios where GPS signals are interrupted and weak indoor lighting conditions prevail. The proposed method utilizes a pre-built 3D surfel map as a frame of reference for re-localizing robots in large-scale environments. To enhance geometric invariance when matching 3D surfels, a novel technique is developed to break down sequences of transformations between 3D points into corresponding 2D features, utilizing hierarchical feature descriptors that combine deformable part matching and semantic layering. The results indicated that the proposed algorithm successfully re-located the robot with high accuracy in the test sequences. To verify the method's practicality, a practical demonstration is shown where a mobile robot utilizes the proposed algorithm to re-localize itself within a complex industrial setup. The results of the experiments have demonstrated that the method re-lies on minimal feature extraction and achieves accurate results with minimal computational overhead. The method has been successfully tested on two datasets and shows great potential in tackling the difficult task of re-localizing in changing environments. A specific quadruplet of 4-cocycles in the homology of the simplified prismata of a 2-sphere generates a 3rd-order Vassiliev invariant for oriented knots. This characteristic, when applied to a Reidemeister move of order 4, yields a non-trivial coefficient for the transformation of a link's diagram under this move. Calculations involving the action of the quadruplet on a fundamental tangle show that its value for the unknot is zero. The study also expresses the Vassiliev invariant in terms of a coefficient for the link's bridge number. Furthermore, using the concept of the Fox-Hatcher loop, we establish that the Vassiliev invariant can be represented as a combination of the second and third coefficients in the homology of the simplified prismata of a 2-sphere. Finally, we outline a future approach for finding Vassiliev invariants of order 4 by directly computing the homology of the simplified prismata of a 2-sphere. An online supplement containing the source code of the computation is also available at the provided URL. We specifically examine the static nematic susceptibility of LiFeAs in its superconducting and normal states, utilizing two distinct methods in RPA (Random Phase Approximation), which also enables the calculation of its magnetic counterpart for comparison.  Unlike other close relatives that exhibit nematic instabilities, our results indicate that LiFeAs remains stable throughout, implying its superconducting properties are likely rooted in a different mechanism.  Specifically, its superconducting properties cannot be attributed to ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic fluctuations.  Furthermore, through the analysis of band structures and the effects of an orbital-dependent Hubbard interaction, our research suggests that local nematic fluctuations on Fe sites could potentially drive the instability, but that magnetic and broader nematic channels are absent.  We also demonstrate that a refined effective model, which takes into consideration the effects of Fe $d$-orbital dispersion, is necessary to replicate the experimental observation of high-temperature, isotropic superconducting properties.  Our research indicates that a channel of orbital degrees of freedom is necessary to explain the extrinsic nature of LiFeAs's high-temperature superconductivity.  Or put another way, it's non-magnetic, but not quite paramagnetic.  It's possible that related compounds may exhibit a more refined nematic response if modeled more accurately.  Our research was conducted by using a federal effective model combined with local density approximation as the primary computational method.  Importantly, our results indicate that relativistic effects play a pivotal role in determining LiFeAs's spectral weight.  Specifically, our calculation of total spectral weight within the magnetic channel amounts to approximately 80% of that observed in similar compounds like BaFe$_2$As$_2$, implying its reduction is rooted in the dispersal of magnetic susceptibility.  Consequently, our research suggests that a more focused search for novel compounds with magnetic and nematic ordering is warranted, particularly those with enhanced nematic susceptibility.  Our research was completed by applying the federal effective model to a family of materials, including BaFe$_2$As$_2$- and LiFeAs-classes, resulting in the validation of its robustness and refinement. Constructing well-trained, robust anomalies in chiral gauge theories is made possible due to a particular advantage offered by chiral $SU(N)$ theories: they allow for partial gauge fixing. This freedom enables us to combine unitarity from the chiral part of the action with additional contributions from the Faddeev-Popov determinant. A simple example demonstrates this concept, and it's notable that similar techniques can also be applied to theories featuring gauge condensates. Additionally, we observe that chiral theories provide a certain degree of protection against gauge-fixing-dependent anomalies that arise from the Faddeev-Popov determinant. This protection is reminiscent of a particular phenomenon known as partial Peccei-Quinn symmetry, and it could potentially be exploited to build stable, long-lived domains of uniform axion fields. Assuming an initial state devoid of anomalies, the eventual annihilation of the axion zero mode could then serve as a reliable, universal anomaly signal, and we propose that this phenomenon could provide a solution to the long-standing "Peccei-Quinn puzzle" that arises in certain composite Higgs models. A related idea, the "robust Phases" approach, is also introduced, where well-trained, robust Phases can contribute to the Faddeev-Popov determinant and support a variety of phase transitions within the gauge theory's vacuum. A simple example demonstrates this concept, and it's notable that such phase transitions can be driven both by the chiral anomaly and by non-trivial, non-perturbative instanton effects. Furthermore, we propose a general method for calculating the leading-order instanton contribution to the robust Phases, and this method can be applied not only to chiral $SU(N)$ gauge theories, but also to a broader class of theories featuring gauge-fixing-dependent actions and partial gauge-fixing. An example involving a $SU(2)$ gauge theory that emerges from the dimensional reduction of a $SU(2)$ theory in six dimensions is provided to illustrate this method's effectiveness. Ultimately, the importance of realizing the "robust Phases" and "robust anomaly" concepts in experimentally controllable systems would be valuable areas of future investigation. In federated learning, a local device sends gradients to a central server, which consolidates them to update a shared model. An adversary targeting model privacy can manipulate the server's update process by sending forged gradients, which the server believes come from legitimate sources. Our study focuses on "pragmatic" attacks that incorporate knowledge of the model and gradient optimization technique, allowing the adversary to manipulate the model more effectively. We demonstrate the feasibility of these attacks on several industry-grade models and reveal that locally trained models can disclose sensitive information about the data owner's environment. Furthermore, we show that certain pragmatic attacks can evade detection even when the adversary's data does not match the data on the server by modifying the server's update rule. Notably, the simplest attack we considered significantly outperformed more sophisticated approaches, such as the MafiaForensic attack. The world is witnessing an increase in the development of intelligent cities that incorporate advanced technologies such as smart infrastructure, connected and autonomous vehicles, and unmanned systems. Although these advancements enhance quality of life and efficiency, they also create vulnerabilities that malicious entities can exploit for destructive purposes. These threats include assaults that target multiple levels of the socio-cyber-physical space, causing widespread damage and disruption. To address such threats, we present a defense strategy game that enables city administrators to make informed decisions about resource allocation when faced with cyber and physical attacks. The proposed game model allows for the simulation of resource management during assaults on socio-cyber-physical cities, utilizing a range of resources such as sensors, unmanned systems, and communication equipment. The goal of the defense is to minimize the city's damage and exposure to the assaulting entity, mirroring the objectives of the malicious entity seeking to exploit the city's vulnerabilities. We have developed a comprehensive model to analyze and evaluate this game model, providing crucial insights for city administrators to make strategic decisions about resource management and allocation to protect their cities in the face of these complex, multi-faceted threats. The study, presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Sensing, Intelligence and Dynamics of Cities (SIDC), offered a comprehensive understanding of intelligent city games, while a follow-up study, presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Technology and Intelligent Systems (ICCTIS2021), focused on the critical challenge of resource management in these games. The current paper has integrated the concepts from these studies, presenting a comprehensive model of the intelligent city defense game, where city administrators must make tactical decisions about resource allocation to counter simultaneous socio-cyber-physical assaults that incorporate key components like data, physical structures, and infrastructure systems. The game model has been optimized to mimic real-world situations through the incorporation of constraints such as different types of assault agents, variety in target locations and resources, limited communication and sensory capabilities, and a time constraint limiting the duration of the assault. We have developed two algorithms, Self-Optimizing Intelligent City Defense Algorithm and Reinforcement Learning-based Interdeterministic Algorithm, to play this game effectively and provide crucial insights for city administrators to prepare for assaults that incorporate data, physical structure, and infrastructure system attacks. Despite GNNs' excellent performance, most current methods require extensive, expensive annotated data, significantly limiting their practical use. In this research, we propose a novel, unsupervised multi-task learning framework to address the issue of limited available labels by fully leveraging pseudo-labels generated by GNNs. We developed a task-adaptive mechanism to produce high-quality pseudo-labels for each specific task within the framework. Experimental results on four datasets demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with notable improvements of 4.1-11.7% overall performance and 2.4-20.2% performance on isolated nodes. Our framework's effectiveness also extends to semi-supervised learning scenarios. The source code is available on GitHub. Analyzing our framework's performance, we find that incorporating a task-adaptive mechanism and utilizing multi-task learning are both crucial components. While early enhancements can be achieved with these methods, our framework provides significant enhancements over them. Our framework's integration is demonstrated with current state-of-the-art methods, resulting in substantial performance improvements. Ultimately, the enhanced method outperforms existing methods with even greater margins. Analysis of our framework's performance reveals that (i) multi-task learning is the primary factor driving performance improvements and (ii) task-adaptive pseudo-labeling mechanisms surpass existing methods. Our framework's successful application in semi-supervised graph learning tasks further underscores its efficacy. Moreover, our framework's components are easily interpretable, as explained in the conclusions section. Additionally, we establish that the net's electromagnetic flux through a chosen spectral flow path is equal to the log of the quantum Yang-Yang twist of one of the generating reflections within the spectral network. Consequently, we obtain a generalized version of the Verlinde formula for GNC_3, which describes how the individual components of the net's structure interact with one another. However, determining optimal spacing configurations to minimize time-related objectives such as the sum of the time gaps between vehicle fronts remains an unresolved issue. To address this problem, a new method is proposed based on differential games to establish optimal spacing distributions in vehicle platoons. The approach provides a geometric framework to calculate and organize vehicle positioning in a way that each vehicle minimizes its own spacing with the others and their velocities while maintaining a safe minimum intervehicle distance. The proposed strategy is further validated by its ability to handle unexpected events, such as sudden braking, in a controlled and coordinated manner among vehicles. Moreover, this method allows vehicles to adapt their spacing and arrangement in response to changes in the road and environmental conditions as well as the presence of non-autonomous vehicles. The approach can be implemented using a straightforward linear matrix inequality-based method that can be computed offline, resulting in a control arrangement that allows vehicles to maintain a safe and optimized spacing while rapidly responding to critical situations on the road. The efficacy and safety of this new method of vehicle spacing arrangement are evaluated through simulations and testing. The approach has been successfully demonstrated at the University of Texas at Arlington's driving simulation center. The method achieves a notable performance metric of $\mathcal{L}_\infty$ stability with a level of abstraction of 94%, indicating its potential capacity to outperform other commonly used spacing control methods such as the 'gap' and 'gaps' methods used in vehicle platoons. Research has revealed that users are ultimately constrained in their content creation by time constraints. Presently, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding users' time allocations across different social media activities and how they intend to utilize their available time. Our findings are further illustrated by a case study of 21 participants who tracked their social media activity for a week, providing rich contextual information. In light of our findings, we present a series of design recommendations aimed at mitigating these hurdles and facilitating content creation on multiple social media platforms. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach that combines genetic algorithms to design user-specific sequences for low-latency low-power data transmissions over power-controlled wireless channels. A global optimization algorithm is first utilized to identify a set of channel-norm normalized sequences that can be easily jointly pruned for their high correlation. Subsequently, a localized genetic algorithm is employed to fine-tune sequence length and preambles' spreading factors, maximizing sequence uniqueness. Our approach allows for precomputation and efficient transmission. Simulation results validate our basic premise and reveal that our method surpasses existing sequence design techniques, including an enhanced generic genetic algorithm and a recent optimization algorithm. Our approach also proves to be more power-efficient in terms of overall wireless channel power transfer. Additionally, our bit-error-rate (BER) performance is shown to be superior using bit mapping functions, reducing the need for additional channel encoding. Finally, our method is demonstrated to be scalable for use in diverse situations where mMTC users may be using different types of modulation techniques. As a result, our approach is a promising candidate for low-power, low-latency communications in situations where there is a high density of users. To determine the entanglement of a two-qubit system, we examine the optimal performance of a quantum cloning machine designed to replicate the state of one qubit for the purpose of optimizing the probability of correctly identifying the original qubit's state in a random sample. We find that the optimal probability of state identification is controlled by the von Neumann entropy of the original state and that a specific type of nonlinear cloning called directional optical cloning is particularly effective in this regard. We further demonstrate that the optimal probability of state identification via directional optical cloning is directly proportional to the entanglement of the original two-qubit state and provide examples from a recent experiment that illustrate this relationship. Additionally, we show that the optimal probability of state identification via directional optical cloning offers greater value than the optimal probability of state identification via linear optical cloning, which is known as the SPC (same-state probability of correlation). Specifically, we find that the ratio of the optimal probabilities of state identification via directional and linear optical cloning is greater than or equal to 2/3, with equality occurring when the two qubits are in a maximally entangled state. Consequently, the optimal probability of state identification via directional optical cloning serves as a stronger measure of entanglement than the optimal probability of state identification via linear optical cloning. Moreover, we observe that the optimal probability of state identification via directional optical cloning is insensitive to variations in structural parameters and, in some cases, can achieve values that are greater than 1, indicating that this method offers greater utility than the SPC measure, which is known to be subject to a structural parameter-dependent window of applicability. Ultimately, the findings of this study indicate that the optimal probability of state identification via directional optical cloning is a reliable and effective measure of entanglement that is worthy of investigation in future experimental and theoretical research. Moreover, in accordance with a tenet of quantum mechanics known as Machado's principle, the optimal probability of state identification via directional optical cloning is a reliable measure of entanglement that is consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics, irrespective of whether the two qubits are pure or N\"otte's mixed states. The existence of Palm Tree Modes (PTMs) in magnetic confinement devices such as JET is confirmed through experimental evidence. These unstable edge localized modes reduce the plasma's inner boundary, contributing to increased radiation loss of energy, faster diffusion of particles and seed alphas produced from hydrogen injection/neutral beam injection experiments. PTMs appear almost exclusively in plasma scenarios with internal coils activated and are more frequent with increased edge recycling, narrower separatrix and lower magnetic field strength. They can be classified based on their frequency characteristics except for a gap ranging from 50-150 kHz which remains uncharacterized. PTMs have two possible origins; they can either arise from the resonance of edge plasma currents or result from the persistence of residual edge structures stemming from the quenching of edge modes such as Edge Localized Modes (ELMs). It is observed that PTMs tend to precede ELMs and it is hypothesized that they might be a sign of an edge stabilized marginally unstable plasma state, susceptible to various types of drives such as geodesic mode, Ernie-like mode or a more modern theory known as neoclassical zeta ion mode. These theories are to be studied further in order to understand more about the PTMs observed in JET. The fact that PTMs are more prevalent in experiments that aim to achieve an energy break (the burning plasma limit) suggests that they could be an important feature in this area of study. It is also observed that in certain scenarios, PTMs tend to disappear on their own or can be driven towards a steady state by varying plasma parameters such as the magnetic field strength. However, the desired outcome of PTMs, reduced transport and increased confinement, has yet to be observed. Therefore, it is best to consider PTMs an undesirable feature of plasma behavior and eliminate them. Finally, the observation of PTMs in the edge of the JET call also raises questions about their occurrence in other devices such as AUG and C-Mod and whether they might be an essential feature in stellarators and other type III devices. Further investigation of this matter is recommended. The discussion leads to the conclusion that the challenge of understanding and controlling Palm Tree Modes is an exciting area of study in the field of magnetic confinement. A comprehensive review of the subject is proposed in the form of a review paper or seminar. Further investigation is necessary in order to understand more about the origins of PTMs observed in C-Mod, AUG and other devices such as EAST and the Chinese experimental stellarator, the Compact Stellarator Balloon. As social media continues to grow in influence, its negative effects from hate speech and similar harms are increasingly being highlighted.  A particular challenge in addressing this issue comes from the sheer volume of posts being made on these platforms, making automated hate speech detection a highly sought-after solution.  We recognize the drawbacks of relying solely on automated methods, such as the lack of transparency in models that have been trained using large datasets.  In our work, the primary objectives are two-fold: first, to improve understanding of hate speech detection by investigating the techniques and datasets used; second, to counteract bias in machine learning models through data manipulation techniques.  Our research confirms that utilizing various methods for analyzing hate speech is essential and that incorporating multiple modalities for identification is possible and effective.  Additionally, our findings reveal that manipulating training data to remove biased terms can significantly impact a model's ability to accurately distinguish between hateful and non-hate language, with improvements of up to 20% observed in our experiments.  We hope that our study will contribute to the development of more effective and ethical automated hate speech detection methods.  In the interest of promoting reproducibility and transparency, we are providing open-access to all of the datasets and source code used in our research through the accompanying repository.  We intend for this repository to continue to evolve into an advanced, developable platform for conducting in-depth analyses and exploring various techniques related to hate speech detection.  We invite experts in NLP and related fields to collaborate with us to address the many challenges and mysteries still surrounding this critical issue.  Furthermore, we are committed to addressing the current shortcomings in NLP, such as the lack of open and accurate data annotation, as seen in our recent study on COVID-19. The objective of Automated Program Repair (APR) is to utilize different methods to locate repairs for broken parts of software code, with the goal of fixing defects automatically. APR has achieved success in fixing a considerable number of software defects, with over 90% success rate on a range of existing software systems, but a significant number of previously unknown software bugs still can't be fixed. Many existing APR approaches work well on data that is available upfront but a problem exists with the approach that it doesn't work effectively when no data is available initially. One of the key challenges with the APR approach is that it doesn't use counterfactual information when no data is available initially. We propose an innovative method called antagonistic patch creation to tackle this particular issue. Our approach suggests that by generating an alternative solution, which is likely to fail, we can understand the errors made by the original code more effectively, and utilize this counterfactual information to guide the APR process. We evaluate our approach on a range of existing APR tools and a number of software systems, with the results suggesting that our approach is successful and can fix a range of previously unfixable software bugs using counterfactual information. We also reveal that our approach is in line with the latest insights from the fields of logic and machine learning. Our analysis suggests that our approach is effective and can fix a range of previously unfixable software bugs using counterfactual information. Furthermore, we reveal that our approach is effective in fixing previously unfixable bugs in various domains such as data-to-text, android, and software compliance. We hope our analysis will inspire the development of future APR approaches that utilize counterfactual information to understand the errors made by the original code more effectively. The Generalized Inverse Fractional Cosmic Ray (GIFC) model, a comprehensive statistical model, has the capacity to incorporate diverse types of data, including zero-measured outcomes, by utilizing a mixture model of the fractional form and incorporating Hahn's theorem to facilitate maximum likelihood estimation. This research delves into two critical issues related to the GIFC model. Firstly, it examines two dynamic data spectrum models - type-I and type-II, which respectively represent the fundamental and complex characteristics of data spectra derived from GIFC model-generated zero-measured outcomes. These models comprise a fractional probability model and a zero-measured outcome probability model. The type-I data spectrum model is characterized by a constant fractional parameter, whereas the type-II data spectrum model features varying fractional parameters across different data intervals. A mathematical method for computing these dynamic data spectra is developed, along with an assessment of their efficacy using simulated and empirical data. Secondly, this study investigates the efficacy of GIFC model-based estimation using data spectrum-preprocessed zero-measured outcomes and demonstrates, through simulation and empirical analysis, the optimal approach to parameter configuration and preprocessing depth for maximizing model efficiency. Consequently, this study yields a practical method for estimating GIFC model parameters using data spectrum-preprocessed zero-measured outcomes. The proposed approach is validated via simulation and empirical analysis, showing that data spectrum preprocessing enhances the estimation accuracy and robustness of the GIFC model parameters. Additionally, this study provides model selection criteria for the GIFC model based on a likelihood ratio test and zero-measured outcome probability models. The proposed methods are applicable to a range of applications, including astronomy, cosmic ray research, and ecology. A relevant software package, the GIFC-dataSpect, has been implemented in the R programming language. Its availability will be publicly announced upon publication in a scientific journal. The software can be accessed via the following link: https://yinchao.github.io/GIFC-dataSpect/. A 30-day free trial is also available. The GIFC-dataSpect package comprises four primary functions: GIFCModelSpectrumTypeI(), GIFCModelSpectrumTypeII(), GIFCPreprocess(), and GIFCEstimate(), which respectively compute the type-I and type-II dynamic data spectra, perform GIFC model-based estimations using data spectrum-preprocessed zero-measured outcomes, and offer a range of configuration customization options. Additionally, this software includes supplementary functions for simulating and fitting GIFC model parameters. Achieving convergence in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) at varying learning rates relies on theoretical bounds from online learning that guarantee convergence as long as the step size remains within a certain threshold. In practical applications, adjusting the step size can be impractical due to the need to regularly update based on the estimated optimal step size for the specific task and data. Furthermore, frequent updates may slow processing speed, so combining accelerated SGD, which establishes convergence at larger step sizes than theoretical bounds, is often desired to improve real-world efficiency. Unfortunately, existing implementations of accelerated SGD rely on similar bounds for step size recommendations, which can lead to suboptimal performance when these assumptions are violated. As a result, accurately predicting the efficacy of different step sizes for accelerated SGD remains a crucial open question. Our study explores the relationship between step size and convergence probability in accelerated SGD at the individual and ensemble levels. Our findings demonstrate significant performance gains for both standard and accelerated SGD when adapting step sizes based on the unique characteristics of the data rather than relying on broader assumptions. When applied to challenging dataset classifications, our method significantly outperformed the state-of-the-art approaches, achieving up to a 5-fold improvement in convergence speed. Additionally, our adaptive algorithm behaved optimally under theoretical conditions, yielding comparable convergence results in standard scenarios. This category includes solutions that display chaotic and periodic behavior simultaneously, with the system's parameter-driven chaos triggering its own regeneration and eventual return to periodicity. These systems are marked by "self-excitation" and "self-extinction" and exhibit two separate, intertwined phase spaces. This innovative category of systems is foundational and may be applied to broader concepts, such as their equivalents in classical physics and even complex biological systems. It's also notable for being easily identifiable, due to the distinct and non-interchangeable roles of system and parameter dynamics. Moreover, this category of systems shows a significant, non-linear response to external influences, characterized by a well-defined "tipping point" that occurs long before it reaches criticality, when additional adjustments might restore their original rhythmic behavior. Automatically collecting grasp information can be a time-consuming and costly process, especially when applied to various dexterous robots. As a result, leveraging simulation tools has become a feasible approach to gathering grasp data, although the current methods face limitations such as simulation accuracy and domain-specific applicability. In an effort to overcome these challenges, we developed a comprehensive simulation framework to extensively collect dexterous grasps for diverse robots. Our approach, named DexGraspNet, encompasses three key elements: a precise simulation environment with a physically-based rendering framework, a flexible planning algorithm, and a robust grasp success predictor. Utilizing our simulation, we collected over 547k dexterous grasps for seven dexterous robots, spanning across three formats, across ten diverse environments. Our results, specifically regarding success rate and average grasp force, demonstrate that the grasps learned through simulation exhibit high real-world effectiveness. Moreover, when employed in combination with existing policies, our approach leads to an improvement in success rate by approximately 10%. Given its vast collection of grasps, broad applicability, and high-performing features, we intend to release DexGraspNet for public use. A novel, motion-corrected technique has been developed to enhance the accuracy of conventional turbo spin-echo MRI sequences through the integration of parallel transmit and receive arrays and sophisticated optimization techniques. This development, which utilizes a novel optimization algorithm to minimize effects like diaphragm and ventricle shifting during breathing, accurately predicts and corrects for residual motion without increasing the overall scan time. To achieve this, a series of four-dimensional data are initially collected with motion-induced errors, which are subsequently corrected in a lower-dimensional space using the established four-dimensional data. This innovative approach has successfully demonstrated its ability to provide high-quality, scan-time-synchronized images in patients undergoing liver function evaluation following liver transplantation. Notably, the technique has delivered high-quality, motion-insensitive T2-weighted images with minimal artifacts, while also preserving the original scan time and without the need for gating. This method is suitable for a diverse range of applications, including the assessment of the heart, lungs, liver, stomach, and other abdominal organs. Furthermore, the technique has also successfully illustrated its ability to detect pathologies, such as the presence of liver metastases and liver tumors. This technique is expected to significantly contribute to the study of abdominal organ functions and diseases, as well as play a vital role in the accurate diagnosis of organ-related pathologies. Additionally, the technique's novel approach to using a low-dimensional system to correct high-dimensional data is expected to have far-reaching implications for various applications within the field of MRI technology. Neural network-based models, developed for various applications from disease diagnosis to language translation, have become ubiquitous due to their robust performance. However, traditional large-scale models necessitate significant computational resources and may not be feasible on lesser devices. Compressing these models using dimensionality reduction techniques like quantization and sparsity has been a pressing issue, but often hinders their performance. This problem is particularly challenging when reducing the size of large transformers, whose numerous self-attention computations are difficult to compress. To mitigate this, a new method called InDistill was developed that utilizes another, internally-trained neural network to progressively minimize model size. InDistill effectively compresses large transformers by retaining the original model's data flow, thereby simplifying the compression process. The inner network's weights are learned through a novel form of knowledge distillation that focuses on the original model's intermediate outputs, facilitating compact models with superior performance. This approach is particularly effective for large transformers and can effectively compress smaller models as well. The source code for InDistill is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang90/Indistill. Experiments using the COALA dataset for protein classification and the WuDaFeng dataset for machine translation demonstrate InDistill's efficacy in compressing large transformers while retaining high accuracy. Notably, a compressed model achieved 79.2 mIOU on the COALA dataset, and another achieved 44.8 BLEU on the WuDaFeng dataset. InDistill's superiority was further validated through ablation studies that proved its robustness across various datasets and models, whereas model degradation was observed in all cases. The InDistill method represents an important breakthrough in compressing large transformers by internal learning, facilitating efficient model transfer and deployment on devices ranging from GPUs to lesser devices. The method has extensive applications, and may be adopted in various fields such as natural language processing, computer vision, and program analysis. Moreover, InDistill's internal network may be used to improve data augmentation methods, facilitating neural network training and troubleshooting. The study is available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.4858/00007033. Moreover, InDistill's efficacy was validated through comparisons with top conferences, including NeurIPS and ICLR. InDistill won first place in the Model Compression Track at the NeurIPS 2022 Competition and second place in the Model Compression Track at the ICLR 2022 Competition. The study is available at https://github.com/zwang90

This report presents a stochastic individual-based model to simulate the impact of grazing by the large grazer, the black-buck, on the individual growth dynamics of plants in a dry-land ecosystem. A vast number of plant and black-buck populations are simulated on a two-dimensional grid, with a focus on the effects of non-resident grazing. Plant growth is represented by a state variable that dictates how far from the root a plant can grow in a given time step. In each time step, grazer births, movements, feeding, and births are simulated. A key feature of this model is that black-bucks do not reside in the system but periodically appear and disappear as dictated by a control parameter. Each grazer has an assigned feeding radius and during its presence, it randomly moves and feeds on individual plants within the specified radius. In the model, the concept of plant immunity is incorporated, which serves as a plant defense strategy. Generating concise yet engaging human stories is a challenging task for AI systems.
Most existing story generation methods produce either lengthy or fragmented stories,
leaving a gap in discovering shorter, yet equally engaging narrative paths.
To address this issue, we present an innovative technique that leverages planning
methods, combined with a non-markovian language model, to produce abstractive
condensed stories by extracting key entities and their roles from existing stories
and using them as guides for future stories. The model is trained on stories with
various numbers of entities to accommodate different levels of abstraction.
Notably, our approach demonstrates promising results on the Tales of Tales dataset,
achieving significant improvements in both plot coherence and overall story quality. 
The model's stories are found to be as engaging as human-written stories in
human-led accuracy evaluations. Moreover, the findings indicate that stories
involving fewer entities tend to be less interesting, and that entity prompts can
be utilized to assess story engagement. The developed model is currently
available on https://github.com/allenai/LADPI. The model's performance is
characterized by several key aspects: it generates stories with fewer entities than
exemplary stories, despite maintaining crucial elements, and it outperforms
alternative methods of story condensation that we introduced. The approach
demonstrates its potential for abstractive story condensation, and its
constituents can be applied to other fields, such as question-answering. The
model's ability to utilize fewer entities than the original story still enables
effective engagement, and this capability may be simply adapted for processing
text in other domains. The model's current performance serves as a stepping stone
for story condensation, and its limitations provide valuable insights for
future research. The model's stories are included in supplementary materials. The
plot structure extraction code is accessible at https://github.com/plusk2/
plot-structure-extraction. The model's story quality estimates can be found on
https://story-cmp.github.io/. The model is initially trained on the Tales of
Tales stories, but it can easily be modified for use with other datasets without
significant modifications to the underlying architecture. The model's initial
training process takes approximately 8 hours, and each subsequent iteration
takes roughly 2-3 hours. The model's training requirements can be easily
replicated on a standard AllenNLP installation, and the process of adding
new stories is straightforward from existing stories in the dataset.

A crucial assumption is that each individual component function is differentiable. Based on this premise, it is proven that the differentiability of the component functions is a sufficient condition for differentiability in the multi-dimensional function. A key finding also reveals that these multi-dimensional functions possess a specific property involving the partial derivatives of their partial derivatives. Furthermore, this research yields an additional result that is an enhancement of a previously established theorem. A significant application of these conclusions is achieved through their implementation in the field of optimal control. By leveraging the differentiability properties, it is possible to compute the exact Jacobian of the maximum time function. By doing so, it is possible to demonstrate that specific vector control functions are unique solutions to a particular maximum and minimax problem. A crucial verification procedure is formulated to ensure the validity of the optimality of these vector control functions, thus providing a comprehensive solution to the problem. This research is an advancement of the preceding work, where the first- and second-order maximum problems were addressed, and it specifically tackles third- and higher orders. A unique aspect of this research lies in the computation of the exact Jacobian of the maximum time function, which serves as the foundational element for local stability analysis in the optimal control theory. Employing our proposed framework, we evaluated vocal entrainment among dialoguers in various contexts using data sets of different sizes. The results validate the method's dependence on the context and reveal a distinct pattern of entrainment in conversational exchanges. Specifically, we observe that vocal entrainment is more pronounced in cases where there is mutual communication between interlocutors. Researchers analyzed an intriguing phenomenon, triangular flow, in gold and copper collisions using a sophisticated multiphase transport model. Triangular flow was found to increase significantly in both gold and copper collisions at the highest energy level, although it was found to be faintly visible at lower energy levels. A correlation between this flow and the anisotropic fireball temperature was observed, with the largest triangular flows occurring at the largest fireball temperatures. In copper collisions, triangular flow was found to resemble the behavior of triangular symmetry collisions. This distinction suggests that triangular flow may originate from triangular structure nuclei at the level of proton, with the largest triangular flows occurring at the lowest and highest particle densities. Further investigation found that triangular flows originate not only from isothermal multiphase states but also from nonisothermal states using a temperature-dependent freeze-out procedure. Despite this, the triangular flow residual at the complete freeze-out of the system was found to be negligible. In copper collisions, the largest triangular flows were found to occur at the same system sizes as those of the v1 and v2 flows, suggesting that triangular flow may originate from the same cause as these flows, possibly due to initial state effects, with further investigation needed. Overall, the largest triangular flows occurred at the earliest stages of the collisions at parton level and at the complete hadron level, with the largest flows occurring at medium to high multiplicities. This suggests a complex relationship between initial conditions, partonic and hadronic flows, with the largest triangular flows occurring at the earliest stages of the collisions at the highest multiplicities. Such behavior could indicate a complex transition from parton to hadron states that may differ at different energy levels. Further model development and analysis is required to understand the relationships between initial conditions, parton-to-hadron transitions, and final observables. A description of this process can be found in the author's Ph.D. dissertation.
