A generalized framework for incorporating external geometry data in motion planning has been developed, addressing one of the main obstacles in robotic planning by efficiently utilizing available extra sensors. This approach is accommodated by various sensor types including cameras, lidars, radar, sonar, and GPS. The geometric constraints of the environment are leveraged to narrow down the motion planning search space, thus the computational complexity is independent of the task's complexity and is only determined by the sensor data resolution. The proposed algorithm is applicable to robots operating in 2D and 3D dimensions and has been demonstrated in experiments using a quadbike on uneven terrain. The results show that the proposed method outperforms baseline planning methods across diverse terrain conditions. Furthermore, the proposed method allows for real-time feedback and can be executed in real-time on low-cost hardware. The corresponding code is openly accessible on the repository https://github.com/behzadrasoul/SimGeometric. The quadbike videos are accessible on https://youtube.com/behzadrasoul. The geometric properties of navigation have significant real-world implications in multiple fields such as robotics, computer vision, and engineering, and have recently gained a considerable amount of research interest. Historically, the research in geometric robotics has primarily centered on reconstructing the environment using sensor data and incorporating the resulting 2D map as an input constraint to motion planning processes. Nevertheless, the environment model obtained through this approach often fails to align with the actual world observed through a camera, with the discrepancy being typically 10 to 100 times larger than the sensor resolution. Consequently, the motion planning process based on this model may result in suboptimal performance and may even disregard crucial elements in the environment. The proposed framework overcomes these challenges by directly utilizing the geometric properties of the sensor data in motion planning, thus avoiding the environment reconstruction process and enabling robots to simultaneously take advantage of available extra sensors and geometric data. The approach is based on the assumption that the world's geometric structure can be described using basic elements such as points, lines, and planes. The corresponding sensor data is preprocessed and incorporated into an on-the-fly data structure named SimGeometric Data Structure. This structure enables efficient detection of geometric intersections that the robot may encounter or pass through during motion, including collisions and reachability analysis. The proposed algorithm has been successfully tested in experiments and has been validated against baseline planning methods in diverse conditions. Results show that the proposed method outperforms existing algorithms and maintains optimal performance in various scenarios, and is applicable for robots with different shapes and sizes.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires vast amounts of annotated images. A common technique is to first engage in "pre-training" which involves teaching the network general visual skills. This research introduces a novel class of surfaces, referred to as Euler surfaces. 
These are derived from general, non-regular surfaces. The topology of these 
surfaces is characterized by the integration of Euler characteristic and connective 
components. Specifically, the Euler characteristic serves as a framework for the 
number of components, and their orientation is indicative of the surface's connectivity. 
A key finding is that these surfaces form a distinct group under composition. 
Consequently, the Euler transformation group is generated and comprised of all 
possible Euler transformations. Additionally, this study presents sample applications 
and challenges associated with determining such surface groups in general cases. 
Finally, this research reflects on the connections between these surface groups and 
three-dimensional spatial arrangements. Specifically, the group underlying Euler 
surfaces is discovered to be equivalent to the group governing spatial arrangements, 
and this relationship is confirmed through a three-dimensional spatial demonstration. 
Lastly, this study presents an alternative model based on the surface type found in 
three-dimensional space, known as the Euler torus. The Euler torus model offers yet 
another means of understanding these surface groups in three-dimensional space. 
The consequences of these discoveries are further explored.

A crucial aspect of APS is the efficient full dimensional pivot, which reduces the number of iterations significantly in comparison to the original Jordan algorithm. To achieve this, a new concept of "facial basis" is utilized along with "full dimensional" pivot rules. Many Evolutionary Algorithms are designed to run in parallel, but their performance is often compromised by an uneven distribution of computational resources. This phenomenon, known as evaluation time bias, causes later-evaluating agents to gain a disadvantage in multi-objective problems. One effective approach to counter this bias is to employ a parent selection strategy based on frequency. This method proves its advantages by continuously updating the parent pool with the best-fit agents throughout the search process. To further address the issue, this paper presents an innovative solution where the parent selection mechanism relies on a time-sensitive approach. This approach involves dividing the search space into distinct, equivalently sized segments, and selecting parents based on their performance within each segment. As a result, all agents are given a fair opportunity to excel and be represented in the parent pool. To validate the proposed strategy, four multi-objective optimization problems with diverse characteristics are used, and our approach is compared against a variant of the Continuous Evolutionary Algorithm for Multi-objective optimization known as Non-dominated Sorting Genetic-II. The experiments show that our solution successfully mitigates the effect of evaluation time bias and yields a high-quality approximation of Pareto-optimal solutions with a low spread. This improved strategy holds promise for enhancing the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms and is thus suggested for use in future designs. Radio observations of a region around a massive star formation site, G176.51+00.20, have revealed the presence of multiple HI narrow-line self-absorption (NILSA) components within our line of sight. This phenomenon typically signifies that we are looking at ionized gas that is interacting with its own molecular environment. Upon closer inspection, three distinct spectral features were identified which correspond to large-scale outflows, one of which is likely associated with a 1-million-year-old protostar. This newly discovered NILSA component offers valuable insights into the outflow's velocity and mass, which measures between 15 to 20 $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ per year. To further understand this system, future optical observations are encouraged to reveal more about the protostar's properties and further study these massive star formation sites is recommended. The discovery of these new outflows brings the total number detected at G176.51+00.20 to three, and it suggests that wide-scale outflow detection may be possible in other similar regions. The data is accessible through the CASU CASA Science website. The optical data, however, requires access to the CDS service for the Vizier catalogue. Upon reviewing the current optical data available, it appears that no widespread optical outflows have been observed in this region yet, and it is hoped that deep-scale optical observations in the near future will reveal more about these massive star formation sites. The optical data is encouraged to be taken through broadband filters to reveal the spatial and temporal patterns of the outflows' emission. Many "A Demonstration Without Words"-style illustrations feature rotating objects, which engages the reader's spatial reasoning and visual processing skills. This style of presentation can hinder analysis, as readers may not thoroughly engage with the information and may incorrectly infer methods or purposes. We offer an alternative interpretation of one such diagram: an arrangement of triangles in a two-dimensional triangular lattice. By providing a clear description of the process, we present a companion argument that mirrors the original diagram's structure, demonstrating that this interpretation is indeed viable. Our approach focuses on showing that certain movements can result in the same final arrangement, and it involves a step-by-step process that builds on previous steps, similar to a geometric proof by induction. Ultimately, this analysis reveals that the primary skill required to tackle these types of diagrams is not necessarily geometry or dynamics, but rather the ability to recognize that a change of perspective can often provide a clearer understanding of a situation. Additionally, we propose a series of accompanying illustrations that could help viewers develop this perspective shift, and we explore the various forms of visual and textual cues that could effectively support these diagrams. Such schematics would allow readers to see that their initial assumptions about the information presented (in this case, that the triangles are in a specific arrangement) do not necessarily match the actual arrangement, while also showing that the final state can be achieved through a series of incremental steps (in this case, adding or removing one specific shape). These accompanying illustrations would serve as a means of facilitating a "diagnostic diagram," one that helps viewers identify their own biases and assumptions. In the process of doing so, however, we also identify some potential limitations to this approach: primarily, that some readers may struggle to fully engage with the information, at least initially, and that they may require some form of "anchoring" to get started. Ultimately, in the spirit of the original 'A Demonstration Without Words' style of presentation, we also provide the information without words – leaving the interpretation and companion argument to the reader. While this may not provide a definitive answer, we hope it will spark a more in-depth and interesting one. A companion movie is available at https://youtu.be/3y4i1h0QY4g. Deep learning model explainability, particularly for graph neural networks, is a demanding and largely unresolved issue. The complexity of graph data and GNN models makes them unsuitable for the application of existing explainability methods. To address this challenge, this study introduces the Graph Explanation Interpreter, a generalized tool that can instantly provide explanations for any GNP model, without the need for modifications to the model parameters. The results of our experiments demonstrate the interpreter's high performance in accurately identifying key graph factors for prediction and surpassing the performance of other explainability methods in generating node-level attention distributions and feature importance maps. Notably, our interpreter can explain models within any of the six possible GNN hybrid layers with a time complexity of $O(n\log n)$. Due to its non-iterative nature, the interpreter is well-suited for rapid deployment in production environments, making it an ideal choice for rapid, parameter-free model explanation. A naming game simulation with mobile actors explores language development as a decentralized process. Our proposal for an efficient naming game simulation involves two primary components. First, a localized memory system for agents is implemented to minimize communication requirements between them. Secondly, a migration mechanism is introduced, allowing agents to move and spread languages to newly acquired locations. Using both theoretical analysis and simulation, our results investigate the interplay of language spread and the movement of agents, revealing how language development is influenced by factors such as the number of agents, locations, and their migration pace. Key outcomes include the observation that, under certain conditions, a uniform language can eventually emerge despite continuous migration. Additionally, our simulation demonstrates the emergence of lingustic diversity through the naming game process, albeit only up to a certain limit, beyond which a single consensusual language is inevitably developed. However, this consensus is temporarily halted by the continuous movement and migration of agents and their multiple languages. Ultimately, it is shown that the naming game simulation successfully achieves a final, stable state where a uniform language is developed and spread across all locations. Overall, our simulation demonstrates the capacity of a decentralized system, the naming game, to effectively produce linguistically consistent outcomes. Moreover, our simulation showcases the emergence of a balance between language spread and the movement of agents, revealing how factors such as the number of agents, locations, and their migration pace can affect the development of languages. Consequently, our simulation contributes to our current understanding of the naming game as a tool for studying language development as a decentralized process. Finally, our simulation has significant implications for understanding the dynamics of a decentralized system, which may be applicable to various real-world problems and scenarios.  Our simulation has been successfully implemented using a combination of Python and C coding. Traditional reinforcement learning methods can be problematic due to their incomplete training data, unreliable forecasts, and lack of explainability. In an effort to overcome these challenges, we've developed a combined approach that uses model driven methods with the goal of learning skills at high-level abstract states, rather than raw sensory data, making it easier to interpret the acquired skills as applicable to real-world situations. This technique adheres to a hierarchical framework for skill acquisition and employs Inductive Logic Programming to address the challenges associated with transferring skills from simulated environments to real-world settings through explanation and adaptation. The efficacy of this method was tested using the OpenAI Gym library and the Air Warfare Simulation model, and promising results were achieved in both cases. The results demonstrate the ability of this approach to acquire skills effectively in both simulated and real-world environments, and the accompanying theorem proves the existence of a limited set of skills necessary to accomplish a task at high-level abstract states. The research highlights the advantage of executing reinforcement learning with abstract states and transparent transfer methods as the benchmark for across-environment skill acquisition. The paper offers a comprehensive set of actionable recommendations for other model driven reinforcement learning methods and showcases the practical potential of Inductive Logic Programming in the field of reinforcement learning. This research was conducted within the framework of the EPoS project (European Project for Operational Strategical Levels) led by Leonardo Caldana. The project's goal is to enhance the operational effectiveness of the Belgian and Brazilian armed forces through the integration of strategic planning and operational control systems. The research can be found at the official EPoS project website. The provided Air Warfare model serves as a practical example of applying hierarchical model driven reinforcement learning using Inductive Logic Programming, and serves as a starting point for other research in this domain. A ground-breaking achievement has been made in using lithium-6 as a detector for dark matter interactions, particularly concerning the neutron-proton vertex. By examining the 1.056 MeV gamma-ray production in $^{6}$Li, scientists have been able to set new limits for the Dark Matter-Recoils Interactions, with the current record having a sensitivity of $10^{-5}$ pb at a dark matter mass of 1 TeV. Notably, this discovery holds the record for the softest threshold energy for dark matter detection, with potential implications for future $^{6}$Li-based dark matter searches. Furthermore, this finding highlights the potential of isotopes with the $^{6}$Li nucleus to detect dark matter interactions, especially those involving spins. Importantly, this discovery serves as a reminder that certain nuclear isotopes can serve as effective detectors for dark matter, particularly those with the $^{6}$Li nucleus. We present an effective, yet straightforward model for the blind restoration of images that have been damaged by ill-defined shifts or blurring effects. Our approach centres on the Kernel Mixture Model (KMM), where the intensity of a convolutional kernel that multiplies the input image results in the original undamaged image output. Notably, unlike many existing methods, our KMM framework requires minimal assumptions regarding the nature of these shifting or blurring effects. Utilizing the EM algorithm, we have developed a two-clustering method that efficiently separates noisless image pixels from those that have been damaged. Furthermore, we have established the strong empirical guarantees behind this approach, specifically related to the upper bounds of the KMM's estimation accuracy. Our algorithm has been empirically verified to outperform various state-of-the-art image restoration methods in multiple scenarios. Our associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/kaitoTeng/KMM_image_restoration. As demonstrated by the results of our experiments, the images restored by our KMM method appear more realistic as judged by multiple human evaluators, with the substantial majority agreeing that our method surpasses other comparable techniques. Moreover, when leveraging pre-trained models, our KMM method is capable of achieving superior restoration quality within a fraction of the time required by existing state-of-the-art methods. For instance, it takes our KMM method roughly 40 milliseconds to restore a 512x512 image, whereas existing models like D-Deart and CFCN require 277 and 410 milliseconds, respectively. Ultimately, when judged by quantitative metrics, our KMM method has consistently outperformed other existing models, with the substantial majority of the results we obtained through our extensive experiments generalizable to a broader range of situations and scenarios. This paper introduces a new concept based on the associative Yang-Baxter equation (AYBE), which leads to the definition of a couple of equations known as the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations. These enhanced equations have the AYBE as a specific instance and are shown to be linked to the nonuniform quantum Yang-Baxter equation previously explored. The study derives two subcategories of solutions to the NAYBEs, which are revealed to be equivalent to the T-matrices of quasi-tri-algebras, particularly in quasi-bialgebras of diagonal type. Moreover, the paper illustrates the NAYBEs' relationship with local quantum groups, as well as their potential applications in creating new comodule-superalgebras through a diagonalization process. To validate the concept of nonuniformity, the paper specifies two explicit instances of the NAYBEs' solutions, which are shown to be consistent with the uniformity property. The study also recovers several prominent solution families as specialized cases of the NAYBEs' solutions. Finally, the paper outlines open challenges and potential future research directions in this context. One such direction is the investigation of NAYBE's potential link to homogeneous spaces generalizing the $A_{m,1}$ type. The paper concludes by exploring the potential generalization of the 3-dimensional sphere $S^3$ through a novel quasiperiodic structure arising from the NAYBE's solutions. These equations offer a fresh perspective on quasiperiodic structures, which can be considered an extension of the three-dimensional sphere analogy. The study provides an implementation example of a proposal made by S. Aggarwal and P. E. M. Sottile in their published work. The accompanying animated GIF file illustrates the new quasiperiodic structure on the 2-sphere $S^2$. Formal verification through Hoare calculus is an effective method for ensuring program correctness, but it demands intricate logical formulas as inputs, which are difficult for natural language-based specifications to express. Moreover, the vast number of possible programs makes it necessary for Hoare calculus to focus on a specific program each time. Unfortunately, writing and verifying program specifications become extremely challenging as the program sizes increase. To address these difficulties, we propose a method integration that combines Hoare calculus with linguistic techniques aimed at transforming natural language descriptions into predicate calculus statements, thereby simplifying program specifications and allowing a single, comprehensive verification process for any program. Our proposed method is an advancement of Hoare calculus and is presented through a concrete demonstration of proving a program's termination from a naturally expressed specification in English. Ultimately, this method is an essential step towards validating programs based on linguistic forms of natural language specifications. However, first, we need to develop a framework that can accurately translate linguistic forms into predicate calculus statements. Although some recent works have made significant progress in this area, such as the Paxborough system, fully automated transformations from linguistic forms to predicate calculus statements remain inefficient, especially for detailed descriptions, and often result in an excessively extended logical formula. To overcome these limitations, we outline an alternate framework with improved efficiency and semi-automated features, accompanied by a discussion of its potential future developments to facilitate descriptions of increasingly complex statements. Once this framework is established, we can utilize it to generate predicate calculus statements for Hoare calculus and demonstrate our approach's effectiveness in a concrete verification process. This study marks an innovative step in integrating linguistic techniques with formal verification and presents a promising contribution to the field of formal verification. It also serves as a fundamental work that can shed light on the intersection of natural language processing and formal verification, exploring promising avenues of research. Specifically, our approach aligns with ongoing research in natural language inferencing and formal verification within the NLI-FV research program initiated by Lhamtong et al. In this program, we aim to develop methods for inferring implications between sentences and utilizing these insights to verify the correctness of programs specified in natural language. Our study is an important development in this research program as it establishes essential links between natural language processing and formal verification, and it demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating linguistic techniques with Hoare calculus in a comprehensive verification process. This research also addresses challenges related to the efficiency of sentence interpretation, parallel transformations, and program termination validation. In the final stages of this study, we considered methods for addressing these difficulties, which are presented in the corresponding documentation

Distributed consensus is a fundamental process that enables multiple entities to agree on a common sequence of events within a decentralized system. Our research focuses on the canopus consensus protocol, which demonstrates exceptional performance characteristics. Although canopus is designed for use by processes with identical input parameters, it lacks mechanisms for failure recovery and protection against malicious behaviors. Our proposed solution, RCanopus, addresses these shortcomings by integrating a reliable failure detection mechanism and a system for validating inputs to prevent manipulation by rogue processes. Combining these systems enables RCanopus to maintain canopus's high performance characteristics, even in the face of failure or malicious behavior. Traditional failure detection approaches significantly reduce the canopus network bandwidth and computation speed. Input validation approaches prevent input manipulation but allow the system to continue operating with reduced performance. Our novel failure detection and input validation hybrid, the RCCanopus module, is the first to address both failures and malicious behaviors simultaneously. The RCCanopus integration with canopus results in a robust, trustworthy canopus consensus protocol, which we call RCanopus. Recently, pre-trained deep neural networks have shown remarkable performance in object detection tasks across various industries. Nonetheless, their reliance on unreliable classical methods for uncertainty quantification is a major limitation. To address this issue, this research introduces an innovative method called BayesOD, capitalizing on the low computational requirements and type specification of pre-trained object detectors. By treating the object category distributions as random variables drawn from Dirichlet distributions, BayesOD develops an accurate and efficient estimation method for uncertainty quantification. Building upon the prediction networks, BayesOD enhances uncertainty models with posterior expectations of the object instance variables, including box, semantics, and scores. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of the proposed exact Dirichlet estimation (EDE) approach and its enhanced prototypes, yielding meaningfully lower uncertainty losses compared to existing techniques. Notably, the efficient prototype estimation of BayesOD requires only 0.45-2.17 milliseconds to compute on modern GPUs, making it highly practical for real-world applications. Furthermore, the proposed methods achieve significant improvements in energy-per-surveilled-meter and surveillance effectiveness factors, with average increases ranging from 23% to 81% and 3% to 27% respectively. As such, the outcomes of this research offer critical insights for designing better object detection systems with reliable uncertainty quantification. BayesOD has been successfully deployed on a practical surveillance system known as ODAS. Furthermore, the paper's findings and associated code are freely accessible at https://github.com/apolania/bayesod-uncertainty-od. Lastly, the research is supported by funding from the Data Science and BIoinformatics Training (DSBT) flagship. Specifically, the data science component of the DSBT flagship is instrumental in addressing the dominant role of deep neural networks in data-driven object detection. Moreover, the research is also supported by the Social Sciences and Humanities Small Grant Program, which focuses on the social and humanitarian impacts of the proposed research. Lastly, the research is further informed by the broader context of the Data Science and BIoinformatics Training (DSBT) flagship, which is dedicated to the educational and training aspects of data science and bioinformatics. Nonetheless, the research is not without its own set of critical limitations and potential biases, which are thoroughly discussed in the paper. Notably, the research is conducted under the framework of the data protection and privacy regulations of the University of Montreal, which is listed as a mandatory requirement for academic publishing. Consequently, the research is not presented in a manner that is tailored to a general audience

The overall purpose of a transportation network is to efficiently move people
from one place to another. To achieve this, various entry and exit points must be
used to distribute and collect traffic. During peak hours, a limited number of entry
points become congested as they try to release traffic onto the network simultaneously.
This thesis studies the problem of predicting the required exit roads for a given traffic
amount on a network with multiple entry and exit points, assuming that drivers choose
the quickest route to reach an exit road as quickly as possible. We investigated this
issue using a dataset from Zurich, Switzerland and observed that the most congested entry
points are not always the ones that contribute the most to traffic density. Our analysis
also revealed that traffic density tends to shift towards the end of the network during peak
hours. Based on these insights, we developed a method to identify the roads that are most
likely to be used as exit roads for a given traffic amount on a network with multiple entry
and exit points. We applied this method to make predictions for traffic density at exit roads
in the Zurich network. Our experimental results show that the rankings of the top used exit
roads for a given traffic amount are consistent across different traffic densities. This led us
to observe that low traffic densities are associated with a limited range of the top used exit
roads across different traffic densities. High traffic densities, on the other other hand, are
associated with a broader range of exit roads. Our analysis also reveals that traffic density
can be used to estimate the number of exit roads and the associated traffic amounts. We
developed a method to automatically determine the relevant parameters for low, medium, and
high traffic densities, and our results show a good match between predicted and actual
traffic densities on a log scale. We also found that the predicted traffic density for Zurich
is on average 16% higher than the actual traffic density, and the difference in the traffic
density range is between 10% and 30%. Our study reveals that the most challenging situation
for predicting traffic density occurs when the traffic density is high and there are a large number
of active exit roads. We therefore plan to improve our model in two key areas: first, we will
investigate machine learning models that do not require data on traffic density and can handle
multi-modal networks, and second, we will improve our current model to reduce the discrepancy
between predicted and actual traffic densities. Our goal is to establish a system that can
make traffic density predictions

A novel, non-invasive diagnostic method for epilepsy is presented, demonstrating the potential of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to accurately classify a patient's condition solely based on magnetic resonance imaging data. The paper primarily focuses on studying hippocampus disorders in epilepsy patients from MR images. An experimental study is also conducted to compare the accuracy of CNNs in identifying hippocampus abnormalities in patients with a condition known as malformation of cortical development. Our research reveals that a CNN can recognize this condition with a high degree of accuracy. An innovative contribution of this study is the development of a multiple CNN framework, capable of simultaneously identifying and segmenting the hippocampus, subhippocampal regions, and a specific type of malformation known as focal cortical malformation. The proposed network leverages a dynamically calculated number of feature maps for each convolutional layer, thereby reducing computational complexity. Additionally, an improved image preprocessing technique is presented that utilizes residual enhancement and noise reduction adjustments to optimize performance. The outcomes of this study are supported by experimental data. The proposed method is evaluated on two datasets - a subset of the AutoImager dataset containing MR images of patients with malformation of cortical development, and a subset of the AutoImager dataset containing MR images of patients with idiopathic epilepsy, displaying hippocampal abnormalities. Our method achieved an accuracy of 97.5% in identifying patient conditions and 94.2% in segmenting the hippocampus and subhippocampal regions. Notably, a comprehensive comparison of our method with 51 existing state-of-the-art CNN architectures was conducted, revealing that our proposed network surpassed them in terms of accuracy. The proposed method is successful in identifying malformation of cortical development with an accuracy of 94.67% and 93.85% in segmenting the hippocampus and subhippocampal regions. Unlike previous research, our approach relies on expressing results in terms of transversal modes rather than spatial modes. Due to the inherent decay of coherent states, we measured the pigeonhole principle deviation instead of the expectation value, utilizing the rate of decay as a reference point. Comparing our results for two specific photon number ranges to those obtained in experiments [1, 2], we noticed a significant enhancement in the pigeonhole principle deviation when considering the transversal modes view. Our findings suggest that this method could be applied to other optical scenarios where the pigeonhole principle is examined. Additionally, we observed that utilizing the transversal modes view helps resolve a seeming discrepancy in the photon correlation results obtained in experiments [1, 2]. When analyzing photon statistics in terms of transversal modes, the phase space densities are independent of the missing mirror's position, thereby resolving the discrepancy. Furthermore, based on the transversal modes expression, we derived the modified Thomae's formula, providing the asymptotic probability calculation for the pigeonhole principle deviation as the photon number approaches infinity. Comparing the modified Thomae's formula to the previous research results seems promising. Our study on the pigeonhole phenomenon, analyzed through the transversal modes perspective, may contribute to a deeper comprehension of quantum mechanics, inspiring further research in this field. Understanding that the pigeonhole phenomenon is not a requirement for transversal modes, as evidenced by a first-order perturbation calculation, we examined the first-order correlation function's contribution to the pigeonhole principle deviation. Our analysis showed that this contribution can be beneficial or detrimental, depending on the range of the missing mirror's position. While the pigeonhole principle deviation is generally decreased with the first-order correlation, it can also be increased under specific position conditions. Our study on the generalized first-order correlation's contribution to the pigeonhole principle deviation is still in progress. Cosmic Ray Background radiation originates from sources such as secondary cosmic rays, green lights, and dark matter. A significant but often overlooked source of these secondary rays is the interaction of galactic cosmic rays with atmospheric nuclei on materials such as space craft and satellites. This paper examines the interaction of cosmic rays with the Moon and atmospheric nuclei on low Earth orbit, and considers methods to distinguish particles produced in the atmosphere or Moon, with potential applications in astrophysical particle discrimination methods. Monte Carlo simulations using the FLUKA code are employed to investigate the energy spectra, depth of origin, and nuclear composition of secondary particles. These simulations also quantify the effect of Earth's magnetic field in scattering particles, with particular reference to the detection of neutron-rich particles. The results of these simulations are compared with actual experiments and data on low Earth orbit secondary particles, highlighting the significance of the Cosmic Ray Background in experimental particle physics. Notably, the detection of secondary particles produced in the atmosphere can be distinguished from those produced in the Moon or deep underground through measurements of beta decay rates, neutron lifetimes, and radiogenic neutron levels, with significant implications for the search for neutrinoless double beta decay. Moreover, the data collected during the GERDA experiment on the Muon-induced background shows that the Germanium masses measured during the experiment exhibit variations that correspond with the Earth's magnetic field, with intense localized neutron fluxes detected near aircraft contrails, aircraft, and solar wind activity potentially offering reduced backgrounds, and an observed PMN background rate of $2E-3$/kg/km/h. These findings indicate that the generation of secondary particles deserves greater consideration in current and future particle physics experiments. Moreover, the data collected during the GERDA experiment on the Muon-induced background rate demonstrates that the materials comprising the solar wind, aircraft, and prime numbers may offer reduced backgrounds to experiments such as GERDA and XENON100's XENONnT's up coming searches for the double beta decay of $^{76}Ge$. The prime number criterion has particular significance given that all natural radioactive elements with the exception of prime numbers such as Helium-4, Boron-10, and Beryllium-7 have a half life measured in years. With the search for the double beta decay of $^{76}Ge$ being characterized by an extremely high background sensitivity required to verify or refute theories such as stellar magnetic field penetration, stellar neutrinoless double beta decay, and neutrinoless double beta decay mediated by the exchange of Majorana neutrinos or antineutrinos

Recent improvements in graph deep learning have been accelerated by the development of a new framework called the Graph Deep Learning (GDL) framework. This practical framework offers engineers and researchers a set of design guidelines for tackling graph deep learning challenges. The framework leverages the power of CNN Deep Learning (CDL) lessons learned through image analysis. By applying a global pyramid-like shrinkage framework, the GDL framework addresses problem simplification, from graph downsizing to node feature refinement, enhancing performance at each stage. A local topology link reconfiguration module is also introduced to improve model accuracy. This paper shares the framework's design, key lessons learned, and introduces a new graph deep learning method that solves complex graph challenges. Experimental testing on various benchmarks has yielded promising results, with significant improvements in performance. For example, the method achieved a 3.6% increase in edge prediction accuracy on the Cora dataset and a 0.6% increase on the PubMed-Dataset. Moreover, the approach demonstrated a 3.6% increase in node prediction accuracy on the MuGID dataset and a 0.6% increase on the Facebook100M dataset. The framework's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/mayflyUG/GraphDeepLearning. The development of this GDL framework has helped bridge the gap between computer vision and graph deep learning, offering a practical and effective solution to graph deep learning challenges. A new understanding of graph node and edge interrelations has been achieved, with Interpretable explanations obtained. The GDL framework's success has also highlighted the importance of problem simplification and thorough model tuning in graph deep learning. Additionally, the approach has sparked further research into local graph property modeling. The Facebook100M dataset was used to validate the model's generalizability, with the help of a large-scale online graph database. The GDL framework's design is anticipated to inspire more graph deep learning researchers and engineers to tackle this challenging area. The development of this new framework has also encouraged more innovative graph deep learning challenges to be created and solved. A new GitHub repository has been established at https://github.com/luxiancheng/gdl-challenge to facilitate this process. The GDL framework's success has also led to the inspiration of other graph deep learning challenges at https://github.com/mayflyUG/GraphDeepLearning and https://github.com/luxiancheng/gdl-challenge. Recently, a modified approach based on the Matrix Decomposition of Uncertain Matrices (MODUM) was developed to privately learn the low-rank matrix most similar to a partially observed input matrix with outliers and arbitrarily perturbed values. This iterative algorithm utilizes the Hard Thresholding of Perturbed Matrices (HTPM) process to maintain the privacy of the learned matrix. By applying HTPM repeatedly and incorporating post-processing operations such as rounding and matrix reconstruction, we achieve a statistically valid, differentially private outcome. Additionally, we provide a rigorous examination of the privacy and accuracy guarantees for this process and apply it to a couple of different scenarios. Our results are further illustrated in a functional programming context. This research explores a novel, abstract interpretation-based numerical static analysis, dubbed Decoupling, that uniquely combines a fully-approximate upward analysis with a precise downward analysis. Typically, static analysis has faced the challenge of balancing the precision of lower-bounding numerical values, which becomes inaccurate when the program enters its plateau phase, due to the upward analysis overestimating values. To mitigate this issue, Decoubing achieves accurate lower-bounding of values throughout the program's execution, by tracing the points where the program's output values peak. It subsequently uses this information to refine the upward analysis, enabling a more precise upper-bounding of values. It is noteworthy that Decoubling's combining mechanism differs significantly from existing literature, representing a innovative approach in static program analysis. Pre-trained language models' (PLMs) Interacting Modeling (IM) approaches show promise in improving recommendation accuracy, yet they have been largely met with subpar performance when applied to reviews marked by significant negative sentiment. This study proposes an innovative framework called Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), built on the BERT model, to enhance the interactivity between reviews and items. The proposed Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) addresses a crucial shortfall in pre-trained language models' (PLMs) Interacting Modeling (IM) based approaches by incorporating a sentiment-sensitive mechanism for identifying negative reviews. A sentiment-free model (NoSent) and an IM model (ImBase) are used for comparison, along with an experimental framework that mimics real-world scenarios and datasets. SIFN consistently outperforms the base model across all experiments with notable gains in recommendation accuracy when dealing with extensive negative sentiment in reviews. In-depth analysis of the framework is conducted via ablation studies that validate the reasoning and efficacy behind each component, ultimately demonstrating SIFN's superiority over baseline methods.

Our approach involves generating new CS sentences through lexical substitution, utilizing an existing CS Arabic-English dataset to fine-tune an English language model. We then extended this method to other CS language pairs including English-Latin American Spanish, English-Portuguese, and French-Spanish. Notably, our results show that English-Latin American Spanish NMT models benefit significantly from augmented data, achieving a 2.2% increase in BLEU score. In contrast, our results on English-Portuguese and French-Spanish NMT models were 0.60 and 0.28 BLEU score respectively. While English-Portuguese and French-Spanish NMT models did not benefit as expected, our CS Arabic-English model actually saw its BLEU score increased by 1.88 and 1.65 respectively. We attribute this improvement to a nearly flawless CS Arabic-English data augmentation that produced natural-sounding sentences with correct grammar and vocabulary. Moreover, our CS Arabic-English data augmentation model outperformed other existing approaches in terms of producing valid data augmentation transformations. A low CS lexical substitution rate, defined as replacing one CS lexical unit with another, was found to yield more natural-sounding sentences than a higher lexical substitution rate. We also noticed that generating CS sentences through multiple lexical substitutions failed to add any benefit and may even result in less natural-sounding sentences. We attribute this to the complexity and richness of the CS data, suggesting that CS lexical substitution should be limited to 1. Finally, our CS Arabic-English data augmentation model's effectiveness was validated when used in conjunction with other data augmentation methods such as token-by-token replacement and covered up by CS. We demonstrate that such groups are not topologically compact in their natural topology, which contradicts previous work by Bhattacharya-Bueltel-Kieffer-F Roxburgh, as their action on the Furstenberg measure space fails to be relatively compact. In turn, this relative non-compactness can be characterized by the existence of infinitely many distinct subgroups that each preserve the Furstenberg measure and have infinite index within the original group. Moreover, this result also implies that certain subgroups of surface diffeomorphism groups are not compact in the compact-open topology. In comparative analysis, it was found that lower-entropy groups of surface diffeomorphisms are compact in their natural topology, as they are embedded in a Polish group topologically. In addition, the compact-open topology of monotone diffeomorphism groups is also shown to be compact. Finally, the topological properties of Aslaksen's unitary group of lattices are investigated, revealing that it is not compact in the compact-open topology although it is topologically complete. In fact, this group's automorphism group is an example of a group with the non-Roelcke property, which cannot be topologically complete unless it is compact. Lastly, further work is proposed to extend our findings to broader classes of groups. The provided proofs are constructive, and our work is accompanied by various dynamic examples and illustrations. In total, our study yields four proofs of relative non-compactness, three of which are novel, as well as two proofs of compactness, including one that is novel. The four proofs of relative non-compactness are: the intersection with compact-open topological automorphism groups, following established methods; the failure of the Furstenberg measure space to be relatively compact, as shown for the first time; the algebraic non-compactness within the group's automorphism group; and the compact-open non-compactness of its surface subgroups. The two novel proofs of compactness are that the group is contained in a Polish group topologically and that of Aslaksen's group. The accuracy of spice simulations for complex digital-to-analog converter (DAC) circuits significantly depend on efficient conversion delay models. These models can be classified into two main types: lookup table and analytical models, with the latter offering advantages such as simplified integration with analog circuit simulators and allowing for easy description of non-linear DAC behaviors. However, developing an accurate analytical model can be a complex task, typically requiring time-conversion data obtained through extensive DAC characterization. This paper proposes a new, streamlined approach for deriving conversion delay models utilizing Matlab's curve fitting toolkit in conjunction with basic mathematical functions. Seven pre-defined model types are introduced, accompanied by the corresponding Matlab code and a practical application of this method to DACs employing current steering and pulse coding techniques. The results indicate that using these models in spice simulations can yield high levels of accuracy with minimal computational burden. Moreover, the obtained model equations provide valuable insights into the underlying behavior of the DAC circuit. The research is primarily focused on DACs employing uniform and pseudo-8 bit quantization methods with a nominal output conversion time of 1 ns. The derived model types are capable of describing conversion delays for all output levels, including the critical initial point where the output value transitions from zero to a non-zero voltage level. Several model types feature modulation-free output, which is beneficial for simulations involving modulation schemes. The approach is easily upscalable to DACs with higher bit depths, whether using uniform or noise-shaping modulation techniques. The possibility of extending this method to characterize other analog circuits, such as digital-analog modulators (DAMs), is also explored, with the dependent output level modeled using a linear function for certain types of DACs lacking non-linearity. The application of the approach to DACs employing current steering, with the non-linearity of the output level mitigated by an accompanying feedback loop, resulted in linear output profiles. Similarly, for DACs employing pulse width modulation (PWM), with the non-linearity of the output level mitigated by an accompanying low pass filter, resulted in nearly constant output convergence times. Furthermore, the approach revealed that certain types of DACs lacking modulation could exhibit non-linearity due to variations in the time required for each quantized level to reach a steady output value. Lastly, the approach was used to study the impact of clock frequency on the accuracy of conversion delay models. Our investigation into animacy, the quality that distinguishes living entities, explores its fundamental nature and how it is represented in the human brain. Distinguishing animacy is crucial for comprehending actions and interactions, such as those seen in everyday scenes or wildlife documentaries. To uncover the core characteristics of animacy, we employed a novel, data-driven method combining statistical analysis and dimensionality reduction techniques. Using this approach, we identified distinct animacy classes in a continuous space and found that animals, including humans, are grouped according to visible parts (e.g., whether they have heads or wings). Furthermore, we mapped these animacy classes to specific brain regions using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The resulting map not only explained existing animacy classification results but also highlighted the key features distinguishing different animacy categories. Our work provides novel insights into the animacy classes represented in the human brain and demonstrates the adaptability of our method in investigating neural representations of various visual categories. This study addresses one of the most pressing challenges in visual cognition research: understanding how humans define and differentiate animacy. By applying our method to a broad range of visual stimuli (from body images across the internet), we found that animacy classes are consistently represented in a stable manner. Our findings, however, also reveal that animacy definitions can vary across cultures, influencing perceptions of human-like parts and bodily complexity. Our research aims to facilitate a deeper understanding of the interplay between visual cues and conceptual animacy categories. To achieve this, we investigate the animacy classes learned by a neural network trained on a diverse set of visual data. Our results indicate that while our network accurately identifies animacy classes similar to those represented in the human brain, it may not capture the nuanced distinctions seen in human animacy definitions. Our work aims to promote further inquiry into the visual animacy concept and its associated representations across various domains, such as neuroscience, AI research, and cognitive psychology. An innovative, flexible solution is presented in this paper - the Arrangement-Preserving Filter (APF), which can accommodate various types of simulations and scenarios. Specifically, the paper adapts the convex optimization-based APF to preserve the spatial configuration of the Arrangement-Preserving Filter, even in the presence of irregularly-shaped sub-domains where local computations may be necessary. Lastly, different strategies for handling inhomogeneous material properties in the presence of APF-filtered fields are explored and evaluated. A few potential strategies are probed through actual practice with a simplified model representing a rotating, viscous ring within a static background environment. By employing the semiimplicit time-discrete formulation of the Stokes equations, we simulate the ring's rotation prior to and after an unexpected increase in viscosity (modelled as a sudden, inhomogeneous modification to the relevant degree of freedom values). It is found that stabilization parameters can significantly influence simulation results, with different SPGPM-Stokes strategies yielding a range of effective values within the explored parameter space. Ultimately, the most effective approach proved to be the adaptation of the APF to the Mass Matrix of the Stokes Equations (AMA). A mass-matrix based strategy is, effectively, a generalization of the widely-used Viscousity Parameter Matrix (VPM) used in the context of Vanka iterations. Yet, as opposed to previous implementations of the APF - which are based on the Mass Matrix of the Advection-Diffusion Equation (MMA) - the present realization is capable of preserving intricate simulation arrangements even in the most demanding scenarios. Furthermore, the present implementation is compatible with various local computation techniques, such as Subgrid-Scale Variational Multimodeling (SMS-VMM). Consequently, the proposed abstraction is deemed suitable for the diverse simulations performed using VMM methods. In multi-agent reinforcement learning settings with multiple agents, each agent's policy development is typically evaluated solely based on its individual performance, which can result in agents reacting adversely in situations where their behaviors have a negative impact on others. This undesirable outcome is due to the lack of a mechanism that penalizes an agent for causing negative effects on other agents, leading to social instability among these multiple agents. In order to improve the interaction between agents and prevent social issues, we propose the use of intrinsic motivation based on transfer empowerment as an additional goal for each agent to pursue during policy training, specifically by incentivizing agents to respond to the actions of other agents in a positive manner. This concept of intrinsic motivation is designed to address learning in both decentralized and partial observability settings using variational inequality theory. Empirical outcomes validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, which demonstrates its ability to achieve the goal of empowering other agents through intrinsic motivation while operating in these challenging environments. Furthermore, our framework demonstrates its ability to effectively handle environments with social conflicts for both the large compact dataset and the more complex situations. Finally, through analysis of the results for the latter situation, attributes of both "cooperating" and "defeating" behaviors are distinguished numerically, revealing the respective tendencies of the designed models toward cooperation or competition. According to the analysis results, models with the proposed intrinsic motivation display a strong tendency toward cooperation, whereas those without tend toward competition. This distinction in behavior is, however, difficult to identify numerically through analysis of the models' loss functions. Our proposed framework thus possesses the desirable ability to enhance the performance of other agents, which provides an additional, verifiable explanation for its own behavior. This approach to intrinsic motivation holds potential for application in various multi-agent scenarios, which could lead to the development of a reliable and predictable social framework for its implementation. Moreover, the distinct tendencies toward cooperation or competition observed in the models' behavior without or with intrinsic motivation, respectively, implies the existence of a fundamental, meaningful boundary, which we propose can be effectively defined using loss function values. This boundary holds potential for application in various fields beyond multi-agent learning and could be generally referred to to as the empowerment gap. The empowerment gap can be effectively distinguished using loss function values for both the large compact dataset and the more complex situations. The proposed technique not only simplifies identification but also quantifies uncertainty levels associated with each prediction. The resulting framework combines unsupervised and supervised learning strategies to achieve superior performance on identifying unknown objects across a wide range of categories from a diverse set of viewpoints. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches, both in existing and our benchmark datasets. Our approach, LoFTR, leverages recurrent designs to thoroughly examine context around each point and discovers corresponding areas through a hierarchical process. By employing a parallel-based recurrent model, LoFTR identifies cross-correlation and generates probability maps for optimization, just like feature-based descriptors, without relying on pre-defined keypoints. Experimentation reveals LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques and achieves comparable to superior outcomes alongside leading association and descriptor methods on multiple benchmarks, while also presenting a substantial increase in efficiency. This research proposes a new model of demand-side management through a collective game theory framework that accounts for varied energy consumption planning and real-time load dynamic charging. The key objective of this model is to optimize energy consumption planning and determine the most efficient charging strategy for electric vehicles in order to lower total energy consumption and reduce peak demand. The study first applies an iterative algorithm to determine energy consumption planning that ensures equitable outcomes among participants. Subsequently, a real-time load dynamic charging strategy is developed to achieve a balance between energy consumption and the needs of electric vehicles. The feasibility of this model is validated through simulation tests using a modified IEEE-39 network. The results show that this model effectively reduces total energy consumption and peak demand. Additionally, the output parameters of the iterative algorithm and the convergence properties of the model are analyzed. The study concludes that this model offers a practical solution to demand-side management and can inspire the development of future studies in this field. Deep neural networks can be effectively compressed using various techniques such as dimensionality reduction and quantization. Typically, compression is applied after the network has completed training, but recent studies have explored online compression methods that perform well at various training stages. However, online compression methods often struggle with the loss of key features learned by the model at later training stages. In this research, a new compression strategy involving partial observations is introduced, allowing the model to retain important features by only taking into account a select number of model weights during compression. The method utilizes a special classifier to predict which weights are crucial and at what probability, before eliminating the less likely ones. This approach is supported by theoretical arguments and experimental evidence, showing that it reduces the impact of irrelevant weights to nearly zero, resulting in a notable speed boost with minimal loss in accuracy. The strategy is successfully demonstrated on a range of tasks, including a complex 100-layer convolutional model trained for object recognition in a large dataset. The results show that it achieves near-optimal performance with a very small number of observed weights, just 0.04% of the total model weights, resulting in a speedup of 2.5 times on a high-end GPU without a loss in accuracy. Research into quantum feedback guidance has garnered significant interest due to its implicit restriction on input states. All input states are either guided or rejected. This work examines the necessary conditions for quantum feedback guidance in continuous-variable systems, revealing that state guidance is inherently tied to Wigner negativity. Additionally, we present a practical approach for designing quantum feedback controllers that can accommodate a broader class of input states without rejection. This involves transforming the original system into a new one with an enlarged Hilbert space, allowing for greater flexibility in selecting input states. We demonstrate this method in a coherent linearizer example, enabling it to handle a wider range of states than would be possible with an ordinary quantum feedback controller. Our findings may lead to the development of more general and versatile quantum feedback controllers in the field of quantum engineering. 

Key words: quantum feedback guidance, Wigner negativity, stability, quantum performance criteria, linearization.

A new category of curves, termed the timelike Bertrand curve, is also defined and its characteristics explored. This study demonstrates the existence of a specific geometric field, known as a Lagrangian vector field, associated with the curve, as well as its connection to a new constant, $I$. For a Feller diffusion with its invariant measure being its own martingale density, the work introduces the concept of target combinations and sampling distributions to describe how paths tend towards optimization. It is demonstrated that the maximum likelihood estimator of the target combination achieves the most efficient possible convergence rates, which are the same as those for the basic diffusion process. Additionally, it is shown that the Cram\'er-Rao bound can be calculated and that the sampling distribution consistently estimates the target combination, leading to the identity of their associated combinations. The results are then applied to various scenarios, such as multiple assets, nonlinear models, mixed signals and state-space formulations. A critical interpretation is that the efficient combination can be reached not just by perfectly estimating the model parameters, but also by following the natural natural progression of the underlying dynamic. The work supplements existing findings in the field which focus on the asset-specific and linear aspects of combinations, by removing these restrictions in order to reveal a wider range of applicable scenarios. A practical implementation of the methods is also provided, with relevant Python code available for download from the author's website. In waveguide quantum electrodynamics, a new method is introduced to study the scattering of multi-photon states by utilizing Feynman diagrams. This approach is explained through an in-depth diagrammatic analysis of one-photon and two-photon scattering in the linear cavity model. Furthermore, we optionally employ Feynman diagrams in the case of three-photon scattering. Subsequently, we apply our formalism to investigate Lippmann-Schwinger scattering equations in the context of single- and multi-photonic systems, after which we extend our method to tackle scattering within a multi-cavity system. Finally, we revise and reinterpret the scattering operator in waveguide QED, grounding our understanding in the fundamental concepts of Dirac's self-consistent $v$-representation, particularly the scattering operator. To conclude, we examine the potential applications of our formalism in generating entangled states using multiple photons. The presented method holds the potential to expand our knowledge in waveguide QED, aligning with Dirac's self-consistent $v$-representation and providing valuable insights into the field of quantum information and computation. This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why the alternating series of the power series for 1/(1-x) reverses its direction at x=1. Additionally, it shows that this phenomenon is unique to x=1 among all points in the complex plane. As a consequence, it is deduced that the coefficients of the alternating series are alternately odd and even functions of x, specifically with a 4-periodicity. This 4-periodicity is analogous to the 2-periodicity observed in the original Bernoulli polynomials, which arise from the Bernoulli numbers' odd and even parity properties. Furthermore, the note identifies a relationship between the coefficients of 1/(1-x) and Euler numbers, specifically, they are alternately odd and even. Finally, the note proves that the alternating series of 1/(1-x) can be expressed as a product of (1-x)'s and alternating powers of x, specifically with a 4-periodicity. This expression is a consequence of the reciprocal theorem's two equivalences, which were initially presented in the author's "Miracle Octagon" paper. The present notion of'reciprocal theorem' bears no resemblance to the widely known scenario from algebraic geometry in which a geometric object is transformed into its dual counterpart. Rather, it represents a broader application in which a functional equation is concurrently reflected on both sides of the equation, resulting in multiple, sometimes infinite, correspondences. The present article marks the first occurrence of this concept, in which two, specifically three, correspondences yield a mathematical challenge: finding a function f such that the sum of its derivatives is the negative of its values at x=1 and x=-1. This problem is easily resolved using the Bernoulli numbers, but one could also employ Euler numbers or simply directly the values of 1/(1-x) and 1/(1+ x). The challenge is analogous to the standard one of algebra, in which we seek a function whose derivative equals the function itself, specifically with a variation in the periodicity from 4 to 6. This corresponding transformation was initially presented in the author's "Miracle Tetrahedron" paper. The present article explores four, and possibly six, correspondences that are linked to the 4-periodicity of 1/(1-x) and may be expressed as a product of (1-x)'s and alternating powers of x. The article marks a milestone in the author's "Miracle Series" project by employing the reciprocal theorem

We construct a four-dimensional noncommutative function f(x) representing a nucleon's spatial part using the Isospin 1/2 Dirac spinor. Given that each nucleon contains three quarks, including two up and one down quark, we utilize the SU(3)_k group's generators to define these quarks based on Fiertz Pauli constraints. Subsequently, we express the nucleon's configuration function as a function of four coordinates, accompanied by an exponential RC gauge factor ensuring commutative counterparts' recovery. Additionally, for mathematical purposes, we employ the Matsubara-Minkowski approach and simplify our calculations by assuming that all noncommutative components are purely imaginary. Consequently, we derive an expression for the distribution function rho(x) and calculate the nucleon's momentum and energy radii. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of noncommutativity on these radii and study the energy-momentum correlation function. Comparative calculations are presented to demonstrate the distinct influences of the noncommutative parameters sigma and theta on the momentum and energy radii. Moreover, we have determined the moment distribution d(x,p^2) and computed the nucleon's spin, pressure, and energy density. Relevant numerical data have been obtained for momentum and energy radii with specific parameter values. For instance, with sigma = 1/F^2 and theta = 2*pi*M_*H, the momentum radius is approximately 0.885F, whereas for sigma = 2F^2 and theta = 2*pi*M_*H, the energy radius is roughly 1.264F. These results can be used in experiments on the nucleon's structure. Furthermore, we have obtained the distribution function rho(x) and computed the nucleon's transverse momentum and energy moments. The general expressions for the momentum and energy moments obtained here can be applied to any interchanging particle with internal structure, such as gluons, photons, and noncommutative scalar particles. Moreover, our analysis of the nucleon structure at the QCD scale is consistent with our previous findings. For instance, the nucleon's energy and momentum radii were found to be 1.264F and 0.885F respectively, in close agreement with our other results. These comprehensive study and outcomes can be expanded to any particle with internal structure. Such a study on the nucleon structure at the QCD scale could be carried out with the help of experimental data from experiments such as JLab's 12 GeV program

In typical topological systems, disorder leads to a sharp order parameter decline and a shift from a ordered phase to a phase exhibiting non-local behavior. We observe that many frustrated versions of the Toric code model exhibit an unusual characteristic: a topological edge, which appears as a threshold-like transition when measuring the resilience of the order parameter against external disorder. This threshold transition is more pronounced than typical order parameter declines in non-frustrated systems, remaining robust even under significant external influence. This unusual topological edge phenomenon is attributed to the diverse nature of the ordered phase in the presence of disorder, which exhibits multiple types of topological behavior. The second moment of the order parameter distribution serves as an indicator for the system's topological properties. Furthermore, the threshold transition is accompanied by the emergence of a finite-sized topological anomaly in the entanglement entropy of the system. The data we collected can be reproduced using a semi-classical approximation based on the garden of edge disorder concept. However, this approach was not able to account for the full richness of the phase diagram and the complexity of the order parameter distribution in the disordered region. Consequently, it is only partially successful in predicting the phase diagram, particularly in areas close to the threshold where the system exhibits intermediate characteristics. The results we obtained hint at the existence of topological liquid and spin liquid configurations within the parameter ranges we examined. The behavior we observed might be associated with a similar phase transition in superconducting circuits, which are being actively explored in experimental research. The results we obtained suggest that such a threshold transition could be more robust in systems that exhibit topological properties than those that do not. Consequently, it may be feasible to use such a threshold transition as a reliable indicator for topological behavior, which could be utilized in experiments focused on topological quantum error correction methods. The results we obtained make the case for further investigating the characteristics of system failures in topological systems through both analytical and numerical research methods. The data we collected reveals that failure properties can provide valuable insights into the properties of non-trivial topological states. The research methods we employed could be applied to other theoretical and real-world systems that exhibit failure properties and may lead to significant breakthroughs in the study of quantum phases of matter. Ultimately, investigating failure properties might aid in the development of new methods to stabilize topological quantum phases of matter and the creation of more robust quantum phases of matter. We investigate the statistical characteristics of the eigenvalue spectrum in a class of non-diagonal matrix models, characterized by weak, non-symmetric perturbations and large, symmetric band structures. These matrix models are part of a broader family that includes both random banded matrices and certain types of random symmetric matrices, exploring the interplay between their eigenvalue distributions and the asymptotic behavior of their quadratic forms. By leveraging the solution to the associated sigma-model, which describes the macroscopic eigenvalue behavior of these systems, we investigate how various system parameters influence the statistical properties of their eigenvalues and asymptotic quadratic forms. Specifically, we demonstrate how the sigma-model's action is connected to the sum of the differences between dual eigenvalue pair positions, which in turn enables the computation of key statistical properties, including the eigenvalue density and the correlation between quadratic forms at disparate points. Notably, our findings show that the sigma-model's solutions yield an infinitely broad eigenvalue spectrum in a class of unbounded, non-symmetric matrix models, which complements similar outcomes for random banded and random symmetric matrices. Additionally, our analysis reveals a distinct, non-trivial form of asymptotic correlation between quadratic forms that depends on the chosen parameter and the sizes of the matrix. By verifying the sigma-model's validity in this context, we establish a mathematically rigorous ground for our results, which in turn shed new light on the more complex properties of random banded and random symmetric matrices. Specifically, our findings suggest that the latter are on the verge of undergoing a phase transition in their eigenvalue spectra, which could transition from a finite-rank, narrow eigenvalue distribution to a longer, more extended one, albeit this transition remains theoretically unproven at present. As increasingly complex machine learning algorithms are implemented in various systems, understanding their decision-making processes is crucial, especially when these systems are used in security-sensitive applications. Traditional methods for measuring interpretability have limitations, as they often rely on individual experts' or users' assessments, which can be subject to variation. In our research, a new approach to assess algorithmic interpretability through a measurement system centered on human learning is proposed. This system evaluates complex aspects of explanation, understanding, and procedure by breaking down cognitive and social factors into distinct elements. We call this method the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS). We developed and tested CIS on a range of algorithms that perform encryption tasks based on specific requirements. Our algorithm, which calculates CIS automatically, demonstrated its effectiveness by showing a high correlation with human evaluations through a large-scale survey. This score can be used in various ways, such as for comparing the ease of learning about an algorithm as it evolves or when switching to a different algorithm. Our study found that an automatic CIS has a high level of agreement with human evaluations, offering a practical solution for assessing and improving the understandability of complex machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, our framework and CIS score provide a foundation for promoting algorithmic interpretability through a understanding-centered approach rather than solely relying on explainability methods. In the realm of Ultra-Low Power IoT, compact ML systems with minimal power consumption are highly valued for their ability to efficiently process sensor readings and effectively handle resource-strained scenarios on edge nodes. Among the available predictive models, Isolation Forest as a supervised learning algorithm offers superior performance and compactness; however, this model still requires a significant amount of memory (1716 bytes) that exceeds the processing capabilities of certain constrained systems. In this study, a modified version of Isolation Forest, referred to as TiWS-iForest, is proposed which effectively tackles large data sets and reduces memory consumption while maintaining performance. The proposed model is evaluated on two real-world datasets and compared to other baseline methods such as Standard iForest and Weakly Supervised Forest. The results indicate that TiWS-iForest successfully handles large data sets and achieves comparable performance to iForest while utilizing a significantly reduced amount of memory (100 bytes). Informed by these outcomes, a subsequent investigation into the feasibility of deploying TiWS-iForest on real-world edge devices such as the "always-on" ARM Cortex-M0/3/7/ M4/ M7 and "always-off/always-on" Intel M0 and M0+ architectures is presented, showcasing the potential for devices such as the "USB ARM USB Microcontroller" to effectively execute the model. With the ability to efficiently analyze data and detect anomalies on power consumption of $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-3}$mJ per prediction, TiWS-iForest proves to be a suitable choice for edge devices. The introduced model represents one of the first successful applications of a supervised learning algorithm on very constrained IoT systems, opening up new possibilities for processing unstructured data at the edge of the network in real-time.
