A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process, with the extreme event probabilities being sensitive to a variety of factors, such as temperature and wind speed. While Bayesian inference for this type of process is useful, it can be challenging to obtain accurate predictions and perform model comparisons, given that standard sampling methods can get stuck in local maxima due to the discrete and integer nature of the process. To address these difficulties, a new method is introduced for exploring the space of all Poisson processes, using a smooth, non-integer-valued proxy called the Poisson pseudo-process. This pseudo-process has the same predictive distribution as the original Poisson process, allowing it to be used for modeling extreme events. By treating each pseudo-process time parameter as a parameter with a uniform prior, a Bayesian analysis can be performed efficiently with high parallel processing efficiency, regardless of the amount of data. This method is tested on extreme storm simulations and compared to other approaches. Generally, the results show that the novel method produces smooth, representative maps of extreme event probabilities and outperforms the traditional methods in model selection. Notably, the method's predictive accuracy is at least as good as the best traditional Bayesian approach, with significant improvements often observed. Overall, the new method offers a powerful tool for analyzing extreme events, making it easier to understand the relationships between various factors and extreme event probabilities. This tool is available as an open-source R package called XPEER. A second related method can also be used for analyzing extreme events, particularly in space-time scenarios where the novel method may have limited capacity to capture spatial patterns. This alternative approach involves considering block averages as the proxy for Poisson process time, resulting in a more efficient model that can capture a wide range of extreme event correlations. To enhance stability, a Bayesian analysis is performed with Gaussian priors in the frequency domain. The benefits of this alternative approach include the capacity to produce smooth, representative spatial and temporal extreme event probability maps with at least similar predictive accuracy to the novel method. Furthermore, the model selection abilities of the alternative approach often show significant improvements. The new methods for analyzing extreme events have a wide range of potential applications in various fields such as weather, transportation and infrastructure to name a few. These methods are already being used successfully in climate studies such as the analysis of extreme wind speeds in Australia's Outback. The associated software for these methods is publicly available at https://github.com/philippe-vera-awilliam/XPEER

The broader cognitive knowledge network initiative aims to enhance knowledge representation at a general, human-level by incorporating diverse knowledge sources. Prior studies have explored atomistic representation of natural language and multi-modal data to create general knowledge networks. The higher altitude submillimetre survey (Hi-GAL) is a component of the {\lambda}2MHZ project. It is a systematic 70, 160, 250, 350, and 500 ${\mu}$m survey of the Galactic plane area, covering 113 deg$^2$ in the zone between 240$^{\rm o}$ and 40$^{\rm o}$ from the Sun, employing the ESA's Planck satellite density maximizer scanner to assist selection of the most informative sources. The source selection methodology and a data reduction process, incorporating a flagging and editing procedure of Heelsian maps, are presented. The reduction process includes an image reconstruction technique using a weighted 2:1 average of 1$^{\rm o}$ radius circles centered on each beam to produce final images, as well as flagging and editing based on quality indexes. A set of 335 high quality images is produced, covering the entire 1100 deg$^2$ of the Galactic plane, spanning from 240$^{\rm o}$ from the Sun to 40$^{\rm o}$ from the Sun. The images are used to present flux density levels, noise levels, and systematic errors associated with each pixel of the maps. Additionally, a database containing source properties derived from these final images is made available. The survey is realized with a resolution that spans from 1.5 to 17 arcmin and a median S/N ratio that varies from 2 to 60, for each frequency pair. Therefore sources with a S/N ratio lower than 2 are considered unreliable, while those with a S/N ratio higher than 10 are considered robust. The noise levels in the images are between 0.5 and 3 Jy, except for 70 ${\mu}$m, where the noise levels are much higher. Therefore sources detected at 70 ${\mu}$m are considered unreliable, except for very bright IR sources. The lower noise levels for the higher frequency frequencies ensure that extensive studies of infrared circumstellar nebulae and cometary activity can be carried out, while the high reliability of the 250, 350, and 500 ${\mu}$m images allows one to extend the range of the Galactic plane density surveys based on the Planck HFI camera by 30% in terms of mass, moving the range from 3$\times$10$^{20}$ to 3$\times$10$^{21}$ Hz. Astronomers working in ultraviolet wavelengths face significant interference from Lyman-alpha radiation, making it challenging to conduct precise photometric measurements. Due to the line's prominent strength and broad spectral line shape, specialized correction techniques are necessary to enable scientists to collect valuable data from this region. This project develops a mathematical model referred to as the Lyman-alpha filter model, aiming to estimate and subtract out Lyman-alpha radiation within the 125-170 nanometer spectral range. By assuming that the area under the lyman-alpha line within a camera's response spectrum remains constant, the model calculates a multiplicative correction factor for each camera response profile. This factor is used to remove the lyman-alpha radiation, significantly reducing noise and redshift contamination. By applying the model to existing HST/FGS-1r and JWST/NIRISS dataset clips, the research team demonstrated a 2-8 fold decrease in scatter related to diffuse background signal measurements across various extragalactic sources, including quasars and galaxies. This work has significant implications for upcoming space missions like Euclid, James Webb Space Telescope, and E-ELT, requiring robust handling of lyman-alpha radiation to operate effectively. By automating the subtraction process and providing accessible data and tools, the research team is expected to facilitate a vast range of scientific applications, ultimately facilitating a comprehensive photometric catalog that extends back nearly 13 billion years. This breakthrough could ultimately lead to a more profound understanding of the universe's structure and evolution. Lastly, the research team is expected to enable science that was previously unattainable in multiple areas, including: (1) cosmic density and metallicity evolution, (2) galaxy evolution, (3) quasar cosmology, and (4) star formation history. This research builds upon an earlier study, addressing a longstanding challenge posed by Rabin and Grossman. Our focus falls within the realm of physical keyless authentication schemes, a subclass characterized by shared randomness being uniformly distributed across a predefined set of values. We pose the question of whether it's possible to devise a scheme that remains secure for any large subset of uniform random variables, and demonstrate that such a scheme indeed exists. To this end, we design a novel scheme based on one-way cryptographic functions, which remains secure even when faced with adaptive attacks from part or all of the underlying subset of random variables. Additionally, we investigate various extensions to our main result, including the consideration of diverse distance metrics between distributions and a subset that forms a finite ergodic Markov chain. These extensions notably cover the real-additive and discrete metrics, as well as the subset formed by the ergodic Markov chain corresponding to a binary-input binary-output channel in a Gaussian noise background. Furthermore, we explore an even more powerful and versatile variant of our main result, relying on the assumption that one-way cryptographic functions possess a specific quasi-randomness property, a notion introduced here. Our construction also yields the first known result of this nature, which has been a longstanding open question. This specific momentum is achieved by attaching a magnetic dipole moment to a particle, causing its orbital angular momentum and spin angular momentum to differ non-trivially. Our study demonstrates that the magnetic dipole moment induces a cascade of photon excitations from the vacuum, continuing indefinitely. To describe these processes, we develop equations that incorporate the particle's internal magnetic properties and their connection to the external electromagnetic field. Our analysis shows that the induced photon excitations follow a Rooske-Hohmann distribution characteristic of a non-thermal state, leading to a reevaluation of the Casimir effect in terms of this non-thermal distribution. This reevaluation reveals a set of states characterized by the orbital angular momentum and the presence of photons, described as "unstirred" states. In contrast to the traditional Casimir effect, these unstirred states exhibit a non-zero energy minimum. Additionally, we find that the internal magnetic properties of the particle lead to a series of states that overlap with the unstirred states and fill the quantum vacuum, an effect known as "stirring the quantum void." This phenomenon causes the energy distribution of the vacuum to follow a Lorentzian profile and may be experimentally verified via transitions between overlapping states that release or absorb energy. Such transitions, known as zero-point transitions, are known to be possible due to the proximity in energy of the unstirred and stirred states. Our study contemplates experimental methods for observing the Casimir effect in systems with a non-thermal photon distribution and discusses their potential applications. A widely employed modulation technique in modern imaging systems is the
pulse-position modulation method, which utilizes a distinct encoding approach called
gray coding. However, frequently incorporating new data in gray coding often
results in a significant rise in the number of ones within the transmitted signal.
Consequently, it tends to exacerbate the inter-symbol interference issue when
high-bitwidth pulse sequences are utilized. To address this inter-symbol interference,
researchers have developed a method that utilizes ladderization and decoding, which
involves finding the least expensive combination of ladderization values (L-values)
minimizing the bit error rate while constraining the inter-symbol interference.
However, this approach proves computationally demanding, which has prompted the use
of a simplified model for L-value estimation in practical applications.
Unfortunately, this approximation often fails to meet the precise requirements of
various use cases. To overcome this limitation, a neural network-based estimator
has been proposed in this study to accurately predict L-values in practical
applications, which centers around the key idea that optimal L-values can be
generated from corresponding channel correlation matrices. To this end, a
neural network has been used to derive the optimal L-values from these matrices,
which serves as a more efficient alternative to the previously discussed estimation
methods. By leveraging this approach, L-values can be quickly obtained in scenarios
such as binary M-PPM, which relies on the proposed neural network.
Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach achieves a 34.7x speed-up
when compared to the previously discussed estimation methods. Furthermore, our
analysis reveals that the proposed neural network maintains only a minor difference
with the ground-truth L-values in terms of the hamming distance metric. To the
best of our knowledge, this study presents a novel application of deep learning
estimation for L-value prediction in M-PPM encoding. Ultimately, the proposed

In a private, noisy exchange of information, individuals receive incomplete and unpredictable data points about a shared issue. Despite limited knowledge, they use this incomplete information to make decisions for their mutual benefit. This concept is known as the "contest" theory, with the literature focusing primarily on situations where players have partial information about each other's data. However, this research approach falls short in real-world applications, so we present a new model where each participant receives a comprehensive view of their own and others' data, except for the actual values. We show that this "maximally intertwined" information state can still be utilized to achieve an optimal solution and provide a practical method to achieve it. A widely recognized concern surrounding automated testing is the potential for the test suite to struggle with detecting and diagnosing changes that create new crashes not previously encountered by the tester. Prior research, including a genetic protocol for automated crash replication, was shown to effectively classify and generate original test cases for these previously unseen crashes. This study aims to provide a supplementary evaluation of this genetic protocol, focusing on its ability to replicate crashes that were previously encountered by human testers, demonstrating the protocol's value as a tool that complements human exploration, rather than a fully replacement method. Our investigation compares three distinct search algorithms - Genetic Algorithm, multi-point level guided Genetic Algorithm, and multi-point substance guided Genetic Algorithm - each combined with a variety of exploration strategies to establish the most efficient combination for replication purposes. To achieve this, we perform a comprehensive experiment involving 288 crashes from the Microsoft SQL Server 2008 processor, resulting in successful replication of 207 crashes with our guided Genetic Algorithm approach. To verify the validity of our results, we perform a further two evaluations - a controlled re-evaluation of the same crashes, and an uncontrolled comparison involving a diverse range of crashes not initially explored by human testers, both resulting in successful replication of all previously unseen crashes. Finally, through an in-depth analysis of the strategies employed by each of the search algorithms evaluated, we identify key differences in their problem solving approaches and recommend that future research prioritize the development of a multi-point substance guided search algorithm. Our replication tool, built using the Java language, is publicly available via our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/FakeT tester/AutomatedCrashReplication. Our experimental dataset is also publicly accessible at: https://doi.org/10.6018/2021-LiSA-4-00/0/D01. The management of quasiparticle defects within doped semiconductors is a long-standing enigma of great importance due to its potential links with thermally induced transitions and the emergence of unusual electronic states near the Fermi level. By utilizing scanning tunnelling spectroscopy, the spatial distribution of core electronic states surrounding vibrational gaps in the optimally doped and charge-optimal MgxBa1-xCu3O6-$\delta$ was investigated. The results reveal the existence of two distinct organization patterns of core states: a square grid arrangement in the optimally doped sample and a square arrangement with 90-degree rotations in the charge-optimal sample. These findings provide direct evidence for a transition from a uniform lattice to a rotated grid arrangement. The phenomenon can be explained by the fragmentation of a uniform lattice due to the increase in core state density as well as the disappearance of small circular clusters. Notably, this transition bears similarities with a known first-order transition in NiAl2O4 near its antiferromagnetic critical temperature and may also be related to a previously unidentified transition in La1.85Sr0.15CuO4-$\delta$ that occurs near its structural and magnetic phase transition temperature. If this transition were to occur near the percolation threshold for superconductivity, it may impede the development of high-temperature superconductivity. Moreover, the transition may be a common mechanism for the formation of unusual nonhomogeneous electronic states observed in the presence of antiferromagnetic or structural phase transitions in high-temperature cuprate superconductors. The phenomenon could potentially be used as a diagnostic tool to investigate other transitions in doped semiconductors and related materials that have undergone structural or magnetic transformations. By employing high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy, the research opens up the possibility of using scanning tunnelling microscopy to investigate the fragmentation of quasiparticle condensates and the formation of coherent electronic condensates that form upon doping semiconductors. If this approach were to be broadly applicable to the entire class of high-temperature cuprate superconductors, it may provide significant insights into the role of fragmentation in the development of superconductivity. Moreover, the methodology could be used to investigate the disappearance of small circular clusters in various materials that have undergone structural or magnetic transformations. Notably, the technique could be developed to detect similar phenomena in molecular materials, which may be related to transitions in high-temperature cuprate superconductors that occur near the percolation threshold for superconductivity

Our proposed framework, SWIFTER, is designed for generating a more comprehensive set of questions from a single query, thereby enhancing the discovery of underlying concepts.
We build upon the foundations of the Rapid Questioner a hybrid question generation technique that incorporates both rule-based and natural language processing techniques, as well as a crowdsourced post-hoc evaluation process.
The effectiveness of the revised approach is evaluated through a comparison of the generated questions produced by SWIFTER and Rapid Questioner, based on their performance in a concept discovery experiment.
The results show that SWIFTER produces questions with lower semantic similarity to the original question and higher conceptual similarity to the answers, indicating more effective concept discovery, as evidenced by the higher average accuracy achieved by human annotators using the generated questions compared to the original question.
Additionally, an analysis of the questions from a few, limited number of concepts has revealed promising early indications of the ability of SWIFTER to facilitate the identification of additional concepts through question expansion. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the desirability of utilizing SWIFTER to generate a broader set of questions with enhanced conceptual understanding. Notably, our study produced numerous ideas for general education assessment that could be explored further. Domain adaptation  is the adaptation of a model to a new domain with different characteristics.  We're working on source-free domain adaptation – adapting a model without accessing the original domain's data. Our method for adapting models in this way involves using unlabelled data from the target domain to find similar, source-free domains. This is done by initially clustering the target domain's unlabelled data and then using a model pre-trained on similar domains to fine-tune its performance. Our experimental results across various domain adaptation  scenarios demonstrate that our approach yields high performance while keeping data usage efficient. Moreover, our research reveals that the success of our approach is rooted in a previously unexplored phenomenon where models pre-trained on large datasets can transfer domain-level information effectively. This was confirmed through an analysis of the features of pre-trained models and the characteristics of different domains. Our research reveals that semi-supervised unsupervised learning and clustering techniques can successfully identify similar domains through an efficient and data-efficient process. This domain information is then used to improve model adaptation. Our detailed analysis of the experiment's results sheds light on the factors that influence the success of our method and provides valuable insights that could guide the development of future source-free domain adaptation techniques. A nuclear fireball reactor could offer a compelling alternative to chemical propulsion for deep space missions.  However, widespread adoption is hindered by the complex engineering and nuclear physics involved, as well as concerns over nuclear accidents in space.  Variants of the fireball reactor, such as the gas core reactor, may offer potential solutions to these difficulties.  In contrast to conventional nuclear reactors, the gas core reactor operates primarily through fission product reaction, eliminating the need for fuel rods and coolant.  As a result, it possesses a natural resistance to meltdowns and is simpler to manage during nuclear events. A non-probabilistic approach to statistical analysis is presented, focusing on utilizing statistical moments as the sole data representation. The approach enables analysis and estimation of a wide range of distributions, including those that do not have established probabilistic frameworks or are too complex to be modeled probabilistically. The methodology is broad in applicability and is demonstrated through example cases such as cryogenic gas flow, fluid dynamics within a pump, and ballistic flight modeling. The analysis is simplified because it eschews probability density functions in favor of moment estimation. While this methodology is novel, the underlying methods of estimation are standard. Central to this approach is the application of the Toeplitz matrix inversion formula, also known as Stieltjes transforms or Perron-Frobenius equations, to estimate the statistical moments. The method involves linear combinations of these equations to estimate higher-degree moments and inversely reconstruct the characteristic function. The procedure for calculating moments is non-iterative, making it suitable for rapid estimation during real-time data collection. The methods can handle a virtually unlimited number of moments; however, the signal-to-noise ratio dictates the practical limit. The analysis also explores the use of finite spectral representations, such as partial fraction decomposition and Fourier series, for applications where data is continuous but finite in scope. Moreover, a theorem is postulated to assess uncertainty based on moment estimates in conjunction with the statistical moment method. The presented ideas are evaluated through experiments and real-world data analysis. In this study, we have found a distributed algorithm that constructs a distance-2 controlling set on sparse, large-girth graphs. Specifically, we have developed a protocol that achieves this control set in O(\sqrt{n}) rounds on girth-n graphs, which requires at least n/2r vertices, where n represents the total number of vertices in the graph. This algorithm is applicable to any sparse, large-girth graphs and takes advantage of the round complexity to improve its efficiency, especially for graphs with small girth values and a small ratio of the controlling set to the total number of vertices. We have further extended this result to develop a protocol that constructs a minimum distance-2 controlling set in the same time complexity. Importantly, our results do not rely on any specific distribution of the vertices in the graph. Furthermore, we have shown that round complexity is essentially unavoidable, given that our result matches the current best known result from a centralized approach, which was achieved by Cohen, Katzir, and Vena. All the required information can be broadcasted by the initial round, so the subsequent rounds can be parallelized to reduce the required complexity. The CMS experiment's discoveries of $R_{D(*)}$ and $R_{K(K*)}$ anomalies have sparked intense interest in the past couple of years. These phenomena can be attributed to light $W'$ or $Z'$ bosons with masses exceeding 1 TeV, as well as leptoquarks beyond the Standard Model. This presentation will showcase the latest results from CMS on these observables, thereby delimiting the new physics landscape using multibjet and long-lived particle data. Moreover, the presentation will touch on the status of the LHC Run 2 $R_{D(*)}$ search. Furthermore, the presentation will be accompanied by the theoretical interpretation of the $R_{D(*)}$ anomaly. The latter will be derived using the SOFTQCD-A and FANPY projects' calculations, now integrated within the MadGraph5_fauxtator framework. These tools employ matching and shower simulations to assess the impact of different new physics scenarios on the $R_{D(*)}$ observable. The presentation will also compare the predictions of the $W'$ and $Z'$ bosons with those of the $u$-quark induced contribution, thereby shedding light on the role of the CKM matrix element $|V_c|$. It has been found that $|R_{D(*)}-1| \lesssim 0.06$ can be attributed to the $|V_c/V_u|$ ratio, whereas larger deviations require non-standard interpretations. This result underscores the significance of the $R_{D(*)}$ anomaly in testing the CKM matrix and probing new physics. The theoretical interpretation is expected to be useful not only for $R_{D(*)}$ but also for other lepton flavor violation observables. The presentation will be concluded by discussing CMS's prospects for uncovering the underlying new physics with its current and future observations of multibjet data. Furthermore, the presentation will outline the future research plans of being involved in the P5 experiment, a proposed project for uncovering $\mu$-e collisions. This initiative aims to delimit the leptoquark parameter space with its concept of the muon muon collider. The presentation's results can be reproduced by obtaining the code from the respective projects' GitHub pages at https://github.com/juergen-bortignon/SOFTQCD-A and https://github.com/juergen-bortignon/FanPy. Furthermore, the presentation's results can be visualized using the Recola 2.

Lately, the interest in visualizing data from neural networks has been increasing rapidly. Nevertheless, the process of gaining insight into these complex models poses several difficulties, primarily stemming from their intricate architecture and the scarcity of clear explanations provided by the prediction processes. Our proposal is the Bright Field, a novel method for neural network visualization that centers on a straightforward, intuitive approach to understanding how input data impacts output predictions on a per-channel basis. By leveraging an array of binary masks applied to input data at various channels, the Bright Field enables users to exert fine-grained control over model inputs on a per-channel basis while simultaneously enhancing sample diversity, a primary obstacle in network visualization. Our method stands out from existing techniques, including saliency maps and feature importance, due to its clear, easily interpretable results. Moreover, the Bright Field is adaptable to diverse application domains and readily applicable to models employing convolutional operations. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in enhancing the distinctiveness and interpretability of visualizations. Moreover, the Bright Field has successfully replicated state-of-the-art performance in detection tasks, as evidenced by experiments on image classification, object segmentation, object detection, and generative visual modeling. All the code and visualizations used in our study are freely accessible on the github repository at https://github.com/AlbertineBenini/Bright-Field. (https://doi.org/10.5167/onesis-2021-23)

A sudden increase in the Sun's corona, resulting from a shock wave triggered by a hot, high-speed jet emanating from a source of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) emission, was observed using the LOFAR loop-shaped antenna configuration. The observed enhancement, equivalent to a 25% increase in the corona's electron density, was localized within a 10-by-20 solar radii area at an 0.2°41'30" distance from the observer and a 7.5° angle from the vertical, at approximately 2.5 minutes after a 10-minute flare eruption. The calculated wave speed was 640±100 km/s, indicating that the energy was transferred to the surrounding plasma as a shock wave, with characteristics similar to a jet-driven piston shock. The shock was estimated to occur 2.5 minutes after the initial EUV flare, using a combination of theoretical estimates and observational data. The discovered event marks the first occultation observed with LOFAR, providing an opportunity to study low-frequency radio losses and the low-frequency pump-up of MHD waves, as well as the low-frequency wave-particle interaction driven by the shock. The challenge of accurately determining the exact timing and location of the shock highlights the complexities of using pulse width and shift measurements, especially given potential source shape and orientation alterations. The study indicates that future LOFAR observations should focus on observing the "U"-shaped shock shape, rather than the EUV source, in an attempt to accurately capture the shock's progression and the transition of the jet from the low corona to the outer atmosphere. Given the difficulties in pinpointing the exact timing and location of the shock during this event, future observations should aim to capture the pre-shock condition, ideally 1-2 minutes prior to the shock occurrence. The observed event represents only the second time that the shock has been identified with frequencies below 250 MHz, and the first occurrence of using the LOFAR "arms" configuration, indicating the considerable potential of this antenna configuration in capturing the shock through its low-frequency radio emission. Consequently, it is now feasible to employ LOFAR in observing more intense shocks, as well as recurring piston surges, as long as the jet intensity exceeds 20 R$_\odot$ and the shock occurs within a distance of 40 R$_\odot$. Ultimately, it is the substantial frequency shifts experienced by the post-shock plasma that render these events suitable for observation across a broad frequency range, from meter to angstrom

Recent findings from the Belle and LHCb experiments have highlighted discrepancies with theoretical predictions of flavour-changing neutral currents within the Standard Model, particularly in the $K^0 \to \pi \pi$ decays and in the mass of the muon. This analysis reevaluates whether two Higgs doublet models of a $SU(2)_L$ gauge nature can resolve these discrepancies, considering Irregularities (IRs) in $K^0 \to \pi \pi$ and the Anomalous Magnetic Moment of the Muon (amu). Four Higgs doublet variations were examined, with constraints derived from the decays $b \to s\bar{s}\bar{s}\bar{s}$ and $K^0 \to \pi^0\pi^0$, along with the amu, taking into account existing experimental data. Our results indicate that the $4^{\rm th}$ Higgs doublet variation satisfies all considered constraints with its best fit being in line with the observed $K^0 \to \pi \pi$ discrepancy and the amu. This variation possesses a relatively lower tolerance level for the decays $b \to s\bar{s}\bar{s}\bar{s}$ with a slight conflict present if the decays' current agreements with predictions are maintained. This variation possesses a slight suppression effect on its scalar components but compares well with the Higgs boson variation in the double king decays. Furthermore, predictions for the Hoyle state and ratios in $K \to \pi \pi$ decays are also presented. Recurrent neural networks have proven highly effective at solving complex tasks requiring sequential processing. One key advantage is their ability to temporarily store information in an internal state. Building on this capability, we introduce a new method to analyze RNN performance in partially observable tasks. Belief tracking, initially developed for reinforcement learning agents lacking visual inputs, helps identify how RNNs utilize their internal state to predict task-specific observations. By comparing predicted values to actual observations, we can evaluate RNN beliefs and uncover the internal representations these models use. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in identifying hidden variables and assessing how well RNNs learn to anticipate task-specific observations. Additionally, we recovered the underlying factors that RNNs learn to anticipate in the typical Gaussian Bernstein mixture task, and found that RNNs can learn to anticipate tasks with randomly generated observations, even when none of the observations provide specific information about the hidden variables. However, we did find that in cases where observations offer some degree of insight into the hidden variables, RNNs tend to leverage this potential information more than they should, leading to suboptimal performance. Our research indicates that even in cases of partial observability, it remains possible for an internal state to be used to predict task-specific observations. Our work is the first to successfully apply belief tracking to RNNs, and we hope to see more use of this approach in the future to gain insight into the internal representations that these models use. Our research findings suggest that it remains possible for internal states to be used in partially observable environments, and that RNNs can learn to anticipate both fully and partially observable environments. Training deep neural networks via federated learning poses significant challenges:
ensure model consistency, achieve fast training convergence, prevent data exposure,
and minimize communication overhead. Recent studies have made notable progress in
overcoming these hurdles, but most current approaches are incompatible with one
another, hindering a comprehensive understanding of the field. In our research, we
propose a unified framework for federated learning, aiming to refine existing
techniques and develop new methods. By leveraging the interplay between two
key strategies, hard-coded quantization and robust compression, we develop a
two-phase optimization protocol that boosts model training efficiency while
preserving performance and preventing data exposure. Our approach outperforms the
current state-of-the-art in federated learning, achieving up to a 2.44x faster
convergence speed and up to a 2.4x reduction in communication overhead while
maintaining comparable accuracy with state-of-the-art methods. The source code is
publicly available at https://github.com/NTU-NYPTv2/DP-REC. With our framework, we
achieve superior performance compared to the recently proposed NTU-NYPTv2
algorithm. Specifically, DP-REC exhibits performance consistent with state-of-the-art
methods (Comm-CML, ConsecutveML, FedAvg, and LFA) on different datasets,
such as CIFAR100, FashionMNIST, and TNMNIST, whereas NTU-NYPTv2 exhibits a
significant performance decline of up to 4.0% in the TNMNIST dataset. In addition,
DP-REC exhibits superior communication efficiency compared to the current
state-of-the-art LFA method. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates that the
combination of hard-coded quantization and robust compression principles yields
practical and efficient solutions for federated learning. The research is approved

We define a hierarchy of cognitive abilities needed to play such games perfectly. Firstly, players must have fundamental cognitive capabilities similar to those in incomplete information games. Additionally, each phase of the game may necessitate additional cognitive capabilities. Importantly, these capabilities cannot be transferred from one phase to another. We then apply our results to a two-phase garage service game and find that incorporating our proposed cognitive capabilities yields pure equilibrium strategies. Moreover, our study shows that in many situations, the most basic cognitive capabilities among the levels we analyzed are sufficient to induce pure equilibrium strategies in finite games, but we demonstrate that in infinitely repeated games, all the defined cognitive capabilities are essential. To address the indeterminacy inherent in incomplete information games, we establish that our cognitive capability approach can assign probabilities to players' actions, thereby providing a more detailed description of the game. We propose a method for transforming spin-up spin-down pairs into spin-up spin-up or spin-down spin-down pairs through three-body recombination driven by lasers. Building on the coherent preparation of spin-up spin-up pairs using two photons, we utilize inelastic scattering of a photon with a spin-up spin-down pair to produce a spin-up spin-up spin atom and a molecule made up of spin-up spin. The remaining excess momentum is eliminated via a final optical trapping step. Similarly, we outline a protocol for generating a spin-down molecule and a spin-down spin. Our plan incorporates optical trapping to remove excess momentum from the system, achieving a final state with zero relative momentum between the atom and molecule. The process involves a series of quantum gates that operate on the total spin, utilizing spin-dependent light-matter interactions. Using robots to enable remote control via the internet and provide a sense of presences for individuals in various settings has been a pressing issue. This paper focuses on the remote control of telepresence robots and examines the impact of network losses on users' perceived quality. Through a controlled laboratory study involving 30 participants, we evaluated the QoE resulting from different levels of network loss and discovered that users could adapt to moderate network loss by adjusting their control methods. Conversely, severe network loss would result in significantly lower QoE. The investigation further revealed that users could estimate the remote control delay with remarkable accuracy and that this delay had a profound influence on their QoE. Lastly, we found that people tend to undervalue their experienced QoE, especially when network loss is significant. The results from this study offer insights into how network loss affects human perception in remote control scenarios and provide guidelines for designers to create more effective usability designs for telepresence systems, particularly to enhance users' ability to anticipate and prepare for potential delays. The study also serves as a basis for evaluating the QoE resulting from using telepresence robots, employing a method that combines perceived control and estimated delay and their interaction. Theoretical foundations for understanding the impact of network loss on users' perceived quality have been laid, providing a starting point for future research in this area. The data collected in this study have been made publicly available to facilitate replication and foster additional research in this field. In particular, the accompanying code, the experiment data, and the study's findings have been shared on the link provided. Mixed product experts establish independence between dimensions of a input vector by combining multiple expert models in a mixture-of-experts framework. This framework has seen significant use in various neural networks applications such as training conditional convolutional models and constructing flexible functions through piecewise regression. Yet, a major limitation of this model is that its training often becomes stuck in a deadlock, which results in poor performance. The reason behind this lies in how MOE tends to specialize each expert on a subset of its input dimensions, necessitating efficient optimization techniques to circumvent this issue. Our research presents a novel, easy-to-implement algorithm called CEMO that achieves this goal. Our algorithm relies on a symmetric convex optimization technique in each expert training phase, which enhances the rate of convergence. Our theoretical analysis confirms that this optimization approach outperforms the conventional method by reducing the deadlock's threshold. Additionally, we have devised a strategy that dynamically allocates data to experts in order to prevent the resources from becoming imbalanced. Our theoretical analysis confirms that this strategy outperforms the conventional method by lowering the deadlock's threshold. CEMO has been combined with a variety of potential expert models as well as CNNs. Our experimental results demonstrate that our solution surpasses the current best results, bringing MOE-based training one step closer to being scalable for hundreds of dimensions. Our code for CEMO can be accessed at the repository https://github.com/fengler1/CEMO. A piecewise regression-based neural network utilizing CEMO has also been successfully applied to the IEEE-CVF Challenge 2022 "Action Recognition" competition, ultimately ranking top 4 out of 218 participants. D. Meyer's token games on graphs have shown remarkable versatility, with many theoretical applications across various disciplines. His 2010 paper introduced vertex firing games to enable the study of ideals connected to simplicial complexes, primarily focused on graph theory. Subsequent research, also by D. Meyer and others, explored additional applications in algebra and geometry. A key concept, the Jacobian of a token game, represents a combinatorial analogue of an algebraic curve's canonical class. Furthermore, token games are useful for simulating polynomial systems on algebraic curves, further establishing their geometric connection. Building upon this foundation, the authors propose a novel token game on a topological graph, which corresponds to a Jacobian ideal related to a cover of curves. They demonstrate that certain token games on toric curves correspond to Prym varieties, underscoring the algebraic curve's intrinsic connection to Jacobian and Prym varieties. The paper then examines how the newly introduced token game on a toric curve's Jacobian relates to its Prym variety, providing a comprehensive theoretical framework for its algebraic curve-based interpretation. The study also includes computational examples demonstrating the practical utility of the proposed token game. The work aims to further the understanding and implementation of token games, with potential future applications in algebraic curve theory. The accompanying software package provides an implementation of the token game, with documentation available at https://dx.doscheke.gitlab.io/jacobbymp/. Moreover, the provided JavaScript interactive3d demo showcases the curve and Jacobian Prym examples, with user interaction enabled. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the belief that certain deep neural networks are more adaptable to overfitting than others. Many studies have investigated this notion, but a thorough examination of potential factors that might influence transferability has not been conducted. In this paper, an in-depth analysis of factors affecting transferability is provided. Specifically, we question two widely accepted agreements within the deep learning community: one claiming that convolutional neural networks are generally more transferable than others, and another suggesting that models of varying capacities should exhibit transferability patterns similar to their corresponding training losses. Our investigation reveals that these agreements may not hold universally. For instance, certain non-convolutional neural networks can be more transferable than convolutional ones, and surprisingly, our results show that their transferability patterns do not mirror their training losses. These findings are based on a diverse range of benchmark tasks and datasets. To deepen the understanding of transferability, we also introduce a method for assessing the influence of individual training samples on the final model accuracy using our proposed Sample Nearest Neighbor (SNN) classifier. The sample-level analysis conducted in this paper provides significant insights into how transferability works, offering significant potential for future improvements. The source code of our paper is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whwu37/snn-utility. With the help of our proposed SNN classifier, future research can be conducted to identify specific design elements that contribute to improved transferability. The research presented in this paper could potentially be expanded to other machine learning fields, offering a valuable lesson that understanding data properties is of the utmost importance during the design process. Our work ultimately opens the door for more general methods that could support the creation of models tailor-made for various applications and datasets. As such, the main contributions of our paper can be summarized as follows. A comprehensive study of factors influencing transferability in deep learning is conducted, and two widely held beliefs within the deep learning community are disputed. Our proposed method, the SNN classifier, utilizes a nearest neighbor search approach that does not depend on the underlying distribution of the data. The effectiveness of our design elements is supported by experiments conducted across a wide range of benchmark tasks and datasets. Research has thoroughly documented the phenomenon that heavily overparameterized deep neural networks achieve excellent performance even when their underlying architectures remain unsophisticated. Although this phenomenon has sparked significant controversy across the scientific community, the underlying cause remains unclear. This study presents evidence suggesting that poor performance of sparse networks during an initial phase of training is a major contributing factor to their success when overparameterized. To support this theory, we investigate two potential explanations for this phenomenon: one theory posits that limited computational resources (specifically, the tensor-core architecture) hinder the effectiveness of gradient pruning, while another theory suggests that bandwidth constraints (specifically, the 32-bit float half precision) affect the success of fat pruning. To study these theories, we employ a straightforward approach: examining the impact of data precision during training. Our experiments reveal that fat pruning leads to significant performance gains when utilizing half precision float computations, but gradients become impractical to manipulate at this precision level due to overflows. This discovery motivates a simple modification to the SGD optimizer to address this issue, which in turn allows us to successfully apply fat pruning of the network. To our knowledge, this adaptation leads to the first successful implementation of fat pruning of convolutional networks. Our findings demonstrate that the success of overparameterized neural networks can be attributed to overcoming computational limitations, rather than solely attributing it to the phenomenon of "stochastic depth" commonly observed in overparameterized recurrent neural networks. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of data precision as a critical factor influencing the behavior of neural networks. The modifications to the tensor tensor implementation proposed in this study have been successfully applied in various competitions where the constraint of the 32-bit float half precision was enforced. To demonstrate the robustness of the approach, we also apply the fat pruning method to the Luong attention algorithm, which was previously thought to be resistant to pruning due to the complexity of its underlying components. Our empirical findings verify that fat pruning leads to significant one-shot improvements in both the Luong and Standard attention algorithms. This study paves the way for further research on the impact of data precision on the behavior of neural networks and their potential for successful deployment with reduced computational requirements. Such findings could have significant practical implications if successfully applying the fat pruning method to other areas, such as decreasing the computational requirements for the Standard attention algorithm. To facilitate this goal, a comprehensive guide has been created to help researchers replicate the approach and implement fat pruning in their own research settings. The companion code has been released under a custom open-source license to accommodate diverse research environments

The Dial-a-Ride Problem is a challenging task assignment problem with a distinct setting, constraints, and objectives. We propose a Branch-and-Trim algorithm designed to solve the metropolitan Dial-a-Ride Problem, accommodating a large number of requests, vehicle limitations, and various solution quality indicators. Our algorithm utilizes a trimmed search space divided into smaller branches, analyzing each branch sequentially, and we demonstrate its efficacy by comparing it with a standard branch-and-bound method on a set of synthetic instances. We also provide further instances designed to highlight the algorithm's benefits. Our experimental results show that the Branch-and-Trim algorithm significantly outperforms the branch-and-bound method, requiring a much lower number of operations to find high-quality solutions within specified time limits. Moreover, the algorithm is shown to accurately predict solution quality using a linear model without additional computational overhead. We also analyze the impact of request variability, vehicle limitations, and algorithm parameters on solution quality and identify key factors affecting this quality. Finally, we discuss how the Dial-a-Ride Problem's characteristics make this algorithm a promising approach for other vehicle routing problems. Our work is accompanied by open-access instance generators, a detailed description of the instances, and a video illustration of the algorithm's progress in visualizing its operations. This study explores the application of knowledge-aware large-scale pre-training models to enhance e-commerce product description generation using multi-modal data. Considering that incorporating knowledge from product categories, hypernyms, and attributes can benefit description generation, we incorporate an embedding module to capture the meaning of categories and hypernyms from WordNet, and an associative calculator to extract features from attributes databases. To accommodate varying knowledge amounts and degrees of certainty, we design a novel recognition module with a confidence estimator that filters and ranks knowledge entries, ensuring a feasible number of considerations for complex scenarios. This knowledge-aware module is integrated into a multi-modal pre-training framework, which is refined by leveraging three product-related modalities: visual, textual, and structural. Experimental evaluations on three tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, showcasing improved results on textual and structural domains. Notably, our model demonstrates a 5.0% relative gain in F1 score over the best baseline on structural tasks. The accompanying code and model can be found on the repository at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/KnowledgeAware-MLP. Our pre-trained models, hosted on Alibaba's Model Hub, can be accessed at https://alibaba-modelhub.onmachine.com/. Overall, our work showcases the value of combining multi-modal data, category information, and hypernyms for enhancing e-commerce product description generation models. The presented findings indicate that our proposed approach is suitable for handling complex scenarios with varying degrees of knowledge certainty. Moreover, our model's ability to effectively utilize multi-modal data positions it as a strong baseline for related multi-modal and knowledge-aware tasks. Our Model Hub, hosting pre-trained models, can be accessed at https://alibaba-modelhub.onmachine.com/. Our knowledge-aware pre-training framework, modeled after the structural knowledge framework of Lei et al. This study investigates the utilization of the Deep InfoMax self-supervised learning technique to pre-process medical images of the brain, with the goal of detecting early-stage Alzheimer's disease. A Bilinear Convolutional Neural Network (BCNN) model is employed for image analysis and loss function optimization is handled by the InfoMax mechanism, which maximizes correlation between representations of different samples within different domains with negative entropy for uncorrelated pairs. To mimic the correlation found in medical imaging datasets, the model is trained with a dual architecture that combines two domains, and the BCNN loss function is complemented by a combined version of cross-entropy and deep info max losses. As an additional step, the model is integrated with a 218-dimensional bag-of-word word-embedding table, known as BioBERT, to replace the traditional fully connected layers at the top of the BCNN. Experimental evaluations were conducted using the 121-way Pathology-BERT dataset, which is comprised of 12,000 218-dimensional word-embeddings corresponding to BCNN outputs. It is found that the proposed technique achieves a high overall accuracy of 88% and supports advancement detection with 97% F1-score, demonstrating the effectiveness of Deep InfoMax to extract valuable spatial information from pre-processed medical images for early-stage Alzheimer's disease detection. Furthermore, the model's ability to automatically learn feature representations without relying on labeled data makes it well-suited for various medical image processing tasks. For applying the Feshbach-Villars formalism to study pseudoscalar heavy-heavy mesons, a calculation is carried out, resulting in a density of states for mesons with varying masses, ages, and isospin states. The density of states shows certain characteristics that can be associated with experimentally observable low-energy spectral functions. With the help of a scale similar to the kaon, we translate the calculated density of states into a dimension that can be compared with experimental values. Our calculation shows that heavy-heavy mesons have a finite probability of existing within a certain energy range, ranging from a few MeV to over 1 GeV. The probability peaks at around 400-500 MeV and decreases slowly with increasing energy. This finding can be validated by ultrarelativistic collisions between heavy ions. Our calculated density of states, when combined with experimental values from DFs, reveals that heavy-heavy mesons make up a significant percentage of the total meson production, accounting for 30-40% of the total and decreasing with increasing energy. This study provides a fundamental understanding of the density of states for heavy-heavy mesons and pions across a wide energy range, showing a higher density of states for pions but similar percentages of contribution to the total meson production at an energy of around 400-500 MeV. Our calculation also demonstrates that the probability of formation of certain isospin states is not uniform, with a higher Mesarhmic probability observed for isospin 0 states and decreasing with higher isospin values. Our study further shows that the age of the mesons plays a significant role, with a higher density of states observed for younger mesons and decreasing with increasing age. This work provides valuable insights into the understanding of the spectral properties of heavy-heavy mesons and serves as a useful tool for further investigations into the subject. Our study also demonstrates that the Feshbach-Villars formalism is a powerful tool for studying heavy-heavy mesons, allowing for a deeper understanding of their underlying quantum statistics. Our calculation reveals that the quantum statistical model of Feshbach-Villars is compatible with the experimental results, providing evidence for the existence of a large number of heavy-heavy mesons in an energy range of a few MeV. Our study provides an essential contribution to the understanding of QCD at low energies and moderate densities, particularly in ultrarelativistic collisions between heavy ions. Our work also provides an important connection between the study of heavy-ion collisions and the underlying physics of QCD

The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest at intermediate redshifts is the brightest example of the ultraviolet radiation from distant galaxies and their intrinsic absorptions. Its spatial patterns are complex and contain valuable information about the matter distribution, cosmological parameters, and the physics of gas cooling and reionization. To extract these parameters accurately, a novel statistical approach is presented that focuses on the fine structure of the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation function, specifically its third and fourth moments. This methodology has several key advantages over the existing methods: it refrains from utilizing artificial hydrodynamic simulations, does not involve simulated templates, and abstains from making simplifying assumptions about the large-scale structure as linear. Furthermore, it is based on a simplified model of a Lyman-$\alpha$ fog that does not require a perfectly neutral intergalactic medium. Our analysis of the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation function at $z=2.3$ with a $20\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ interval suggests that the squared thermal broadening is less than $10^{3}\,{\rm m{s}^{-1}}$. By comparing our measured growth rate to simulations, we found that the growth rate at $z=2.3$ is $70\pm8\%$ of the expected rate using the best-fit Planck cosmology. Our measured mean bias is $1.44\pm0.04$, which matches our simulation results. We observed that the Ly$\alpha$ fog has a mean transmission of $0.82\pm0.02$ and a mean thickness of $y_{\alpha}=2.4\pm0.1$ ($10^{-15})$. This thickness corresponds to an ionized volume fraction of approximately $3\%$ at $z=2.3$ and indicates that reionization was already $90\%$ complete at $z\approx5.5$. Our analysis further reveals that the Ly$\alpha$ fog has a mean velocity dispersion of $39\pm2\,{\rm km/s}$. This value, combined with a measured skewness of $-0.43\pm0.01$, suggests that the matter at these redshifts is $-0.43$ skewed and that the mean velocity dispersion is primarily driven by rare, highly dense regions. Our analysis, specifically our measured growth rate and mean transmission, is the first to directly observe cosmological parameters from three-dimensional data. Researchers have successfully observed for the first time the transfer of transverse and longitudinal beam emittances between two beams at the Jefferson Lab's Free-Electron Laser. The experiment involved directing a narrow bunch of electrons at a thin target, which then collided with a second untargeted bunch, producing a highly energetic electron beam and a laser light signal. The resulting beam emittances were measured in detail for both the initial and final beams, revealing clear signs of emittance transfer when the two beams interacted. The data showed a notable reduction in the initial beam's transverse and longitudinal emittances and a corresponding increase in the final beam's emittances, which aligned with the expected results of a mutual three-body interaction between the two beams and the target. The outcome marks a new milestone in this field, which may lead to the development of more efficient particle accelerators in the future. The researchers' findings have been published in an article titled "Emittance manipulation using a thin target in a free electron laser" in the journal Physical Review Special Topics. Future motion prediction, an essential component of multi-agent systems, necessitates the incorporation of a predicted future social structure to accurately forecast trajectories. The quality of the forecast is directly dependent on how well the social structure is anticipated. The existing methods primarily rely on a fixed social network to guide their predictions, which is insufficient because social connections are dynamic and the network needs to be continuously updated and reflected through predictions. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages sequence-to-sequence models and dynamic attention to accurately forecast social structures and agent movements, while demonstrating the efficacy of sequential updates in predicting social networks and agent trajectories in diverse scenarios. The approach, known as Sliding Sequential Collaborative Prediction (SSCA), iteratively updates the social network and agent trajectories through categorical variational autoencoders (CVAE), utilizing one step after another to allow the model to adapt to the evolution of the social structure. The SSCA model comprises three core components: Sequential Generation (predicting the current social structure and agent movements based on the previous steps), Sliding Attention (assigning importance to multiple steps in the history), and Rearranging Rethinking (updating the model distribution to accommodate the changing social structure and agent motions). The SSCA framework outperforms other methods in quantitative and qualitative evaluations on established datasets such as SocialBenchmark and TrajectoryChallenge. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the significance of sequential updates in predicting social structures and agent motions. Furthermore, SSCA exhibits superior generalizability on real-world datasets such as HumanTraffics, demonstrating the value of sequential prediction in the context of real-world applications. The implemented code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharafian/SSCA.git. The video demonstration of our approach can be found at https://youtu.be/ds1kxkxu2O0. A fundamental debate exists over the optimal approach to measure system complexity. On one hand, information theoretic measures seem most suitable as they're grounded in fundamental principles of complexity as disorder. On the other hand, measures like diversity that focus on uniqueness can provide valuable insights into complexity. This study investigates the relationship between several information theoretic measures of complexity (entropy, mutual information, conditional mutual information, monotonically increasing measures of complexity) in a bipedal walking Boltzmann machine. The results demonstrate that static system complexity, as gauged by entropy, increases with input density, but interestingly, measures of conditional mutual information reach a maximum at intermediate levels of input density, suggesting optimal information exchange within a middle ground. These findings highlight the necessity of using multiple measures of complexity to fully grasp system complexity. It's also revealed that measures of conditional mutual information can signal critical transitions in system behavior, in this case, between normal and irregular walking patterns. Ultimately, these insights can guide the development of systems that efficiently utilize information, whether in artificial systems or living creatures. This work also discusses how the proposed approaches can be used to uncover the underlying rules of brain function and develop advanced artificial intelligence systems. As such, it has significant implications for technologies like robotics and computational neuroscience. This research is an essential step towards understanding the intricate relationships between information, order, and system behavior, and as such, has far-reaching non-conventional applications in the fields of artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience. This paper showcases an innovative system that facilitates interaction between a group of robots and a person through using their hand movements. By employing a advanced algorithm to analyze sequences of hand positions, the system is able to determine when the person is providing a signal to the robots. These signals, which can be transmitted via a computer or displayed on a screen, allow the robots to adjust their path and maintain a safe distance. Data collected from various participants indicates that the system is able to accurately interpret hand movements in the majority of cases, with an accuracy rate of about 84 percent. Based on these findings, the system's authors propose a model that allows the person and the robots to consistently exchange information, which is examined through simulation experiments. Not only does the proposed system show a high level of stability, but it also enables the person and the robots to seamlessly interact with one another. A fundamental resource in quantum steering, known as secret correlation, exhibits intriguing behavior in many-body quantum systems. Here, we propose a method to manipulate secret correlations through a sudden, discrete change in a Hamiltonian. This approach is particularly versatile as it can be implemented using conventional laboratory techniques via a sequence of optical pulses. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that secret correlations play a crucial role in assembling molecules from fragmented atoms. Furthermore, we show that in a spin-degenerate system, secret correlations emerge at a natural timescale, contrasting with their usual rapid decay. This research offers new avenues in the study of quantum information and demonstrates the potential for secret correlations in driving quantum many-body changes. It also highlights their utility in facilitating quantum chemistry changes in complex systems. The results in this work may lead to a new understanding of secret correlations in many-body systems and their practical applications. The methods presented here could be adapted to modulate secret correlations in systems lacking parity symmetry, such as the Hubbard model's extended version. However, in systems with such symmetry, we have observed that secret correlations typically exhibit instability, preventing their steady growth. This research has significant implications for the creation of secret correlations in assemblies, stressing the importance of their stable emergence. The approach of assembling atoms using secret correlations is likely to facilitate ground-state changes in many-body systems, and may lead to new techniques for generating quantum states. If implemented in a circuit, our method demonstrates that secret correlations can be used for gradient-based steering in systems lacking a quantum controller. In theory, secret correlations could be employed for counterdiabatic steering in many-body systems via a quantum pulse sequence, and this idea may be applied to driving atoms into entangled states in assemblies. The proposed method is general, and can be applied to systems lacking symmetries, such as the Hubbard model's extension, the Hubbard model with spin-orbit coupling, or the extended Hubbard model with an extrinsic magnetic field. In these systems, our approach is effective due to its ability to drive the system along a specific pathway that does not introduce dissipation of secret correlations. Notably, the steering rate is contingent on the specific trajectory, and fastest in regions containing secret correlations. In cases lacking a quantum controller, our method demonstrates that secret correlations can be used for gradient-based steering, and may lead to a new understanding of the role of secret correlations in facilitating quantum chemistry changes in complex systems. Empirically-derived color temperature decline profiles for various atmospheric scenarios are generated through a machine learning-based process utilizing a vast dataset of images captured in high-CO2 and high-SO2 atmospheric environments. These temperature decline patterns are then applied to a widely-used reference image and combined with a reference image brightness map, resulting in a comprehensive dataset suitable for tone mapping purposes. This newly-developed method is extensively evaluated against existing image brightness transfer techniques across a range of atmospheric conditions, with results demonstrated through both subjective and objective performance assessments. Moreover, the simplicity and generality of this proposed approach are highlighted through its simultaneous consideration of both chromaticity and brightness information in color space. Lastly, the effectiveness of this technique is further illustrated by its successful application to a 3D printing simulation scenario. Overall, this research aims to contribute to the development of more accurate and efficient image brightness adjustment methods. This discovery leads to a surprising result that allows the exponential function to be approximated with remarkable accuracy, equaling its true value at the end of two iterations of Taylor series expansion, providing a high degree of precision for relatively small values of x. Conversely, the error margin can be expressed as a function of x, showing that the error remains small, yet grows as x approaches one, culminating in an approximation of e^x that is confined within a range of two elements. While this method may not be suited for calculating e^x for x values close to one, it is highly efficient for calculating exponential values of variables representing relatively small subsets of real numbers. This method of Taylor series expansion can be applied in various contexts such as random walks, as well as statistical mechanics and the Black-Scholes equation, where rapid computation of g(x) is frequently required for x values ranging from 10^-3 to 10^-6. In situations like these, the following formula can be used to approximate e^x while providing a high degree of precision: e^x ≈ 1 + x + (x^2)/2. A cutting-edge scheme for controlled photon-photon interactions has been developed using advanced laser technology and plasma-based tools. The innovative method employs an EUV laser-plasma source that produces coherent, high-energy XUV beams coherently coupled with intense near-infrared light. This wave-matter-wave interaction is leveraged to achieve groundbreaking nonlinear processes such as the coherent production of charged and neutral particles, as well as the creation of entangled electron pairs, and to study quantum optics in a controlled environment. The experimental program is centered on NLO (nonlinear optics) processes enabled by the XUV and EUV regimes, backed by comprehensive particle and radiation beam simulations. This pioneering research paves the way for a new generation of laser-plasma based tools for photon-photon interactions, with far-reaching applications in quantum computing, quantum communication, and fundamental physics research. The study offers a potential solution to the current crisis of monochromatic, high-energy X-ray sources being insufficient to meet increasing demand. Additionally, it highlights the capability of laser-plasma sources to play a prominent role in a broader research network focused on the pursuit of quantum phenomena. The thesis outlines a suite of experiments designed to converge toward quantum computation, and these experiments are positioned to take advantage of the unique properties of wave-matter-wave interactions enabled by the XUV regime. Lastly, it highlights the recent advancements in European quantum research and proposes future collaboration between the new generation of laser-plasma and magnetic-field based research tools and existing state-of-the-art experiments, with a view to combining their capabilities and leveraging each other's expertise towards groundbreaking discoveries in quantum science. The potential outcomes include an integration of the laser-plasma option with existing experiments, such as the construction of a coherent photon source at a synchrotron radiation facility, and the exploration of quantum phenomena using existing and future free-electron laser facilities. Furthermore, it highlights the and future opportunities and collaborations between the laser-plasma and magnetic-field based research tools and suggests that they could be utilized to explore similar phenomena, with the long-term goal of converging toward a unified quantum picture. The study's scope spans a wide range of research from fundamental physics to applications and is tailored to optimize its impact on quantum research and applications. The research program is positioned to leverage the unique properties of laser-plasma sources to push the boundaries of quantum science and engineering, and the technical and scientific outcomes will be disseminated through prestigious scientific publications and conferences. The study's and research's outcomes will be evaluated through presentations at conferences including the LASER AIP-Conf

A relatively unexplored approach is presented to detect the Higgs boson's mixing angle, 
specifically by examining the$c \bar c H$ production process at the LHC via vector boson fusion.
Unlike traditional searches for the Higgs boson, this proposed method leverages its role in producing $c$-quarks and energy density through a process driven by high-energy particles colliding head-on.
Given the Standard Model's prediction that the Higgs boson primarily decays into $b$-quarks, this approach effectively bypasses a significant portion of the LHC's sensitivity, while also capitalizing on its capacity for producing $c$-quarks at the $b$-quark factory.
By concentrating on $\phi$-like states with relatively low masses and using decays into $c$-quarks, this new search method can effectively explore Higgs mixing regions that are currently left unaccounted for by other LHC experiments.
By considering four key variables: the pseudoobservables $t_8$ and $t_7$, the transverse momentum of $c\bar{c}$, and the pseudo rapidity separation between the two $c$-quarks, $|\eta_1 - \eta_2|$ -- which capture crucial Higgs-related information in $c$-quark events at the LHC -- a dedicated experimental analysis is able to differentiate the Higgs signal from the dominant background consisting of standard two Higgs doublet model ($t \bar t$) and relativistic Jungbluth process ($c \bar c$) events.
Utilizing approximately one hundred times more data collected by the LHC during Run II, this new search method is expected to achieve a level of sensitivity that is two times higher than other LHC-based experiments focused on Higgs mixing, specifically those involving the $b$-quark.

The accuracy of automated speech recognition systems has improved substantially, but
the systems developed in the last few years are primarily tailored for English
speakers. People who communicate in other languages are left to find their own
individual solutions. We intend to change this by creating a open-source speech
to text system tailored for German. We fine-tuned the widely used WIT is speech
engine, which runs on TensorFlow, with a large, extensively annotated dataset.
This new engine, which we've made freely available on GitHub, exhibits a 4.5%
enhancement in word recognition accuracy compared to the non-adjusted version
and surpasses the accuracy of a commercially available, closed-source system.
Despite being relatively new, our engine is already being used by several
organisations. We believe that leveraging publicly accessible, automated
machine learning tools like ours will accelerate their development. We also hope
that as more native German users contribute to our project, the accuracy of
our engine will continue to improve. We are committed to ensuring that our
engine remains open-source and accessible to a broad audience. We have also
established a community where users can share their knowledge and collaborate to
make the tool even more useful. We plan to continue working on several key
aspects that will enhance our engine's capabilities. These improvements will
primarily be developed in the browser, which will give users even more freedom
and flexibility. We also aim to integrate our engine with a open-source
transcriber. We are proud to be a part of a larger movement that advocates for
free access to speech technology. We are committed to making the tool
incorporated into our system to create a cycle of improvement and feedback. 
This paper offers a detailed analysis of the technical aspects of our
project contribution and provides essential background information for those
wanting to understand the underlying technology and our approach to
implementation and testing. Additionally, our engine is completely free for
use for both local and commercial applications and is backed by an active
community. We strongly welcome the support and participation of more users. 
Our engine is currently the leading open-source tool of its kind for German
speech within the community and is widely regarded as one of the top three
systems available. We are proud to be a part of this community which shares
our commitment to keeping the technology open-source. We are excited at the
potential for more users to contribute to our project which could lead to a
crossover into other languages spoken by the community.

To overcome this obstacle, we implemented a data augmentation approach that trains a transformer model to normalize input sentences by using consecutive pairs of sentences as input. Experimental results from two benchmark datasets reveal that our method surpasses the existing best-performing techniques. Notably, the model's ability to learn generalized normalization patterns, even with short sequences, makes it highly adaptable and efficient. Moreover, we found that the model's internal embeddings lack semantic coherence, which indicates that it primarily learns a task-specific language specific to the task of text standardization. Consequently, we advocate for further research in this area to achieve more robust and versatile normalization models. This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when applied with a Robin boundary condition to a bounded, classical domain. The inequality is tied to the volume of the domain and is shown to be sharp. Furthermore, investigating the equality case reveals information about the location of the first Dirichlet eigenfunction. Additionally, related inequalities for the second eigenvalue are also explored. The results obtained are considered novel.
