In real-time operating systems, the scheduling function is the primary control mechanism for managing tasks and is typically supervised by the kernel. Alternatively, the root entity in a hypervisor-managed system is the hypervisor, which oversees the scheduling function. Most modern operating systems rely on the scheduling function to implement real-time properties such as predictability and fairness. The scheduling function possesses unparalleled control and insight into the system, making it a breached security asset that can be exploited by attackers. The scheduling function's breach can lead to a universal security vulnerability, which may threaten the entire system's reliability and security integrity. In this research, we examine the scheduling function's breach vulnerability within the context of embedded real-time systems and introduce T-Visor as a hypervisor solution to protect the scheduling function from unauthorized access. T-Visor is a hypervisor designed to manage and oversee the scheduling function through an intermediate hardware layer, thus isolating the function from external attacks and malicious manipulation. By implementing T-Visor, the scheduling function's breach vulnerability is eliminated, ensuring the reliability and integrity of the embedded real-time system. T-Visor is compatible with the Linux operating system and operates on x86-64 architecture. The proposed solution is verified by developing and presenting a universal backdoor attack on the Linux scheduling function, as well as experimenting with T-Visor to demonstrate its efficacy in protecting the scheduling function from unauthorized access and malicious exploitation. T-Visor's integration incurs a mere 6.8% overhead in terms of platform overhead, as the platform efficiency is maintained within this range, thereby ensuring its efficacy in protecting the scheduling function from unauthorized access and ensuring the reliability and integrity of the embedded real-time system. Current techniques rely on least-squares estimation to reconstruct a 360-degree scene, but this approach is often inaccurate due to the possibility of having multiple optimal solutions with similar error rates. The lack of consideration for rotational symmetry in these methods results in unnecessary simplifications of the problem, such as centering the image and eliminating rotation options, which is time-consuming and reduces the chances of accurately aligning the images. We introduce a novel adaptive rotation matrix that is based on the concept of gravity and demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying accurate image connections with minimal information about the scene. The technique is straightforward to use, can be applied to any wide-field imaging algorithm with a single line of code substitution, and bypasses the complexities associated with finding the best possible solution among a multitude of options. We thoroughly tested our method with various indoor and outdoor datasets and found that it consistently produces high-quality results in a wide variety of scenarios, such as using a single camera or using cameras located at a considerable distance from the scene. Additionally, we applied our method to the task of wide-field object detection and found that it consistently performs at a high level of accuracy, surpassing current state-of-the-art performance. The full source code for our method is available for free at https://github.com/hendrykoziu/Gravity_Panoramic_Imaging. The gravitational approach that our method is based on naturally enables the automation of other important tasks such as adjusting the camera's point of view and eliminating unnecessary data. Therefore, we have also released a separate project at https://github.com/specificgravity/automosaic that showcases these advanced features. Furthermore, we have released a separate project at https://github.com/specificgravity/automosaic, which demonstrates the integration of our technique with automatic object detection. We hope that these resources will inspire a new generation of advanced computer vision technologies that are highly versatile and efficient. To address this vulnerability, we propose using probabilistic model checking to generate a layer of protection around the model. This protection defines the extent to which model-based controllers can deviate from the planned trajectory before the system becomes unsafe. In turn, the controller can utilize this protection to anticipate and prepare for potential disruptions by simulating the worst-case scenarios allowed by the model. We demonstrate this concept in a toy car experiment, where the controller utilizes model checking to anticipate and adapt to different types of cyber attacks. To implement this approach, we developed a tool called PROPLIANT that utilizes fragments of probabilistic model checkers to rapidly generate meaningful scenarios related to the system's robustness. These scenarios can serve as a foundation for policy-based learning methods, which we tested through policy search methods. The results show the importance of considering the influence of model fragilities on the learning process, which we found to significantly impact the controller's robustness, with a suboptimal controller being more susceptible to off-trajectory positions and resulting in lower protection bounds compared to an optimal controller. Quantum tunneling is a fundamental phenomenon that has been extensively studied due to its distinctive characteristics. Researchers typically measure tunneling by the change in a beam's density as it passes through a barrier, with the time of transmission often assumed to be the tunneling duration. However, this method is flawed as it only accounts for particles that have successfully traversed the barrier. Alternatively, a Larmor clock has been proposed to measure the phase shift resulting from tunneling, offering an indirect approach. Recent studies have demonstrated that this indirect method is capable of yielding a more accurate tunneling duration than the traditional approach. Notably, a Larmor clock can measure the duration spent by a quantum particle as it tunnels through a barrier, even when only a minority of particles undergo tunneling. Our research has been revised to focus on measuring the phase shift resulting from spin disturbances, not just the beam's density, in conjunction with Larmor clock. Utilizing the spin-dependent Schrödinger equation, we have computed the phase shift resulting from spin disturbances for the three models: the square potential well, the Morse potential, and the Logarithmic potential. Our results, when measured by a Larmor clock, have shown that the tunneling duration can be derived from the phase shift, contrary to what is assumed in conventional models. Notably, a Larmor clock can measure the duration spent by a quantum particle as it tunnels through a barrier, even when only a minority of particles undergo tunneling. Our research has also revealed that the tunneling duration is a function of momentum (p) that is inversely proportional to the barrier's height (V). Moreover, the relationship between the tunneling duration and the barrier's height (V) is directly proportional to the square root ($\sqrt{V}$) of the free-space mass (m)). This study shows that the tunneling duration can be accurately measured by the Larmor clock, even in scenarios not previously considered feasible. Notably, a Larmor clock provides a unique approach for studying quantum phenomena that necessitates a major revision in quantum mechanics. This revised understanding of tunneling has the potential to expand our understanding of quantum phenomena into previously unexplored domains. One such domain is the measurement of particles that have successfully traversed the barrier, now made possible through the Larmor clock. Our research allows for the calculation of the tunneling duration for a broader range of quantum systems than was previously possible. This algebra includes the three dimensions of Lorentz algebra, two dimensions of translation algebra, an N-dimensional algebra (where N is the color charge of Yang-Mills), and specific terms involving N and two cross-terms. Unlike a similar construction for general relativity in four dimensions, the Yang-Mills case necessitates a framing field, which introduces a gauge field into the effective theory. Although the deformation of the algebra is relatively small, it is large enough to preclude the possibility of writing the theory in a manifestly BMS gauge. Next, we broaden our construction to include the case of spinor-boson interactions, which results in an even more substantial deformation of the algebra. Crucially, this more substantial deformation allows us to utilize the Adler-Friedan-Quinn method to establish the existence of the BMS gauge. Lastly, we speculate on the potential for similar approaches to be applied to other theories, including supergravity and super Yang-Mills. Achieving both online learning and ongoing learning poses a significant challenge, as existing algorithms typically need to know the data distribution in advance to select the optimal subset of examples. To address this issue, we present the Neural Structure for Online Ensemble ongoing learning approach, which involves three key components: 1) Online Ensemble: continuously updating an ensemble of individual models by adding newly-formed clusters of related examples; 2) Unified Explorer-Exploiter: an algorithm that balances exploring unexplored regions of the data and exploiting each subset for most accurate learning; 3) Neural structure learning: a method where we embed a conditional random field within a neural network to learn the optimal subset structure. The novelty of our approach lies in its capacity for online learning of subsets on ongoing streams of data, driven by an adaptive exploration-exploitation strategy. The performance of our method is substantiated by both synthetic and real-world experiments, which demonstrate its capacity for ongoing learning. A major health concern caused by WASH issues is thought to be influenced by intestinal parasites, which can spread rapidly due to poor sanitation practices and the mobility of certain worms, carried by water and vectors. These worms cause discomfort, illness, and in some cases, can even lead to chronic conditions. A simple method to detect these worms during bowel checks could greatly benefit public health in Morocco, also aiding similar countries and regions in understanding and mitigating the impact of intestinal parasites. A competition was held, using a dataset of human intestinal parasites, to test various models, with the winner being the Deep Belief Network model. A key outcome of this research is a scalable approach to classify parasites, potentially leading to a significant improvement in public health in Morocco, as well as other countries and regions, suffering from intestinal parasites issues. A crucial next step could be integrating this model with mobile applications, allowing users to easily upload images for expert analysis, accelerating parasite detection and classification. This study aims to contribute to a more precise understanding of intestinal parasites, their prevalence, and distribution, which can inform public health, medical, and related research. The primary concern in flight simulation remains the challenge of achieving steady, straight flight. To address this issue, researchers have developed the Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) method, which employs a Stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm (SDSA) in conjunction with a Genetic Filter (GF) to optimize control settings. By utilizing the PIDA strategy, aircraft can successfully navigate through diverse wind and gravity conditions as well as unpredictable turbulence, allowing for a more realistic and immersive gaming experience. The implementation of the PIDA method is illustrated through a c++/qt based flight simulator called Flight4Sim. According to the simulation results, the proposed PIDA method effectively regulates the aircraft's dynamic behavior across all six degrees of freedom, demonstrating substantial improvements in flight stability compared to the traditional Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) method. Additionally, Fligh4Sim offers a comprehensive user interface and simulated environment, accurately replicating real-world aircraft behavior in terms of responsiveness and controllability. The flight simulations demonstrate that the PIDA method possesses superior capabilities for steady and fluent flight, making it well-suited for a wide range of aerospace and research applications. The corresponding flight simulator Fligh4Sim can be utilized for various purposes such as flight training, testing and evaluation, and multi-agent simulation, offering a significant advantage in these domains. The source code of the Flight4Sim simulator is publicly accessible and extensively documented to facilitate its use and modification by the community. The implementation of the PIDA method in Flight4Sim serves as a practical example of the algorithm's potential in real-world applications and its theoretical implications in flight simulation and optimization. The flight simulations presented in this study reveal that the proposed PIDA algorithm possesses superior steady-state characteristics over its progenitor, Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID), while significantly outperforming its peer, Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Filtering (PIDF), in model dynamic behavior. In the field of complex-valued deep learning, weight sharing is a commonly used technique that has not been fully understood from a theoretical perspective. Researchers have recently discovered that this technique can be seen as applying the same function to the real and imaginary components of the input, much like the way feature maps are shared across different channels in the classical real-valued deep learning framework. However, this equivalent functionality of weight sharing was found to hold true only when considering the domain and range of functions, but not necessarily when considering the intermediate representations generated within complex-valued deep learning models. Thus, it is necessary to revise the underlying framework to permit weight sharing, and it is found that doing so does not compromise the unique characteristics of complex-valued deep learning. The implications of this revision are further explored through an analysis of expressibility and generalizability. While weight sharing was found to have minimal impact on the expressibility of complex-valued deep learning models, it was surprisingly found to lead to improved generalizability with respect to training on complex data. The results of extensive experiments conducted using MRI image classification datasets also validate the effectiveness of weight sharing in practice. The corresponding code for these experiments has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/strlmo/co-domain. The findings of this study are expected to provide new insights for researchers working in the area of complex-valued deep learning. Moreover, the proposed co-domain framework is anticipated to expand the range of applicable techniques in this field. A growing number of studies has discovered significant dispersion in the formation ages and chemical compositions of stars within metal-poor globular clusters in the galaxy's halo. Rather than attributing these differences to the stars' birth from varying initial populations, our research suggests that these differences are primarily the result of an equal probability distribution of being the first to occupy a given location in the galaxy's history. These findings rely on an analytical model and data from clusters such as M5, M22, and NGC 5286, using the probability distributions of both formation locations and star formation times to explain the observed dispersion in birth radii. Not only can this model fit the data but it also predicts that approximately one in five stars in the galaxy's halo were "cosmological relics," existing before the galaxy's formation and being equally likely to be found in any given location. These early-formed stars serve as key indicators for the galaxy's early history and can be identified through their radial distribution rather than traditional methods such as metallicity analysis. Using this approach, our model places tighter constraints on the galaxy's formation time of approximately 13 billion years and a decoupled event that separated the galaxy's disk and halo from approximately 10 billion years old. Finally, our model shows that these early-formed stars, although numerous and easily detectable with modern technology, were unable to significantly influence the galaxy's chemical compositions, explaining why the current data do not yet reveal their presence. These groundbreaking findings highlight an entirely novel perspective on the galaxy's chemical evolution and emphasize the need for a more in-depth study into the galaxy's ancient formation patterns and the characteristics of these unique "cosmological relics." Furthermore, these findings offer implications for the study of supernovae evolution at low metallicity and provide an area for future research, specifically the investigation into the potential connection between "blue hook" supernovae and their role in the galaxy's chemical evolution. Ultimately, these findings offer a significant shift in the perspective on the galaxy's chemical evolution and the characteristics of these unique "cosmological relics," specifically the discovery of their widespread presence and easily detectability with modern technology. Deep Quantum Neural Networks hold significant potential as a quantum analogue to traditional deep neural networks, allowing them to be trained and applied independently. Recently, several QNN models have been introduced, including the quantum circuit deep neural network (QCNN), which combines quantum circuit units to form a deep layer. Unlike other models, the QCNN enables end-to-end training using parameterized quantum gates. Nevertheless, training a QCNN remains a daunting task due to its noisy nature. To overcome this challenge, we've developed Squid, a method to mitigate noise during QCNN training. Squid achieves this through an iterative approach where it constructs a classical shadow model of the QCNN, applying gradient descent to optimize the quantum circuit parameters. By doing so, Squid outperforms other shadow methods by introducing an innovative technique that accelerates the convergence of the shadow model. To demonstrate this improvement, we've tested Squid on various real-world classification datasets, resulting in successful implementations on both simulated and actual photonic quantum processors. Notably, our experiments show that Squid exhibits enhanced noise robustness and accelerated training times compared to traditional gradient descent techniques. As such, Squid represents a crucial step towards the widespread use of quantum machines in machine learning applications. Researchers are developing a experimental project called PALEOCCENE to explore extremely low rates of kinetic energy, down to the 100 fKeV range, using a PArallelized analysis of Xerogel-based EUV-sensitive CENTers.  The method relies on large numbers of doping-free Al atoms trapped in a SiO2 xerogel,  with each atom represented by a single EXACT excitation site.  The project will examine Xerogel-based scintillators with various dopants for their potential in particle astrophysics and cosmology, with PALEOCCENE serving as a prototype for such scintillators.  The concept of utilizing many atoms to detect nuclear recoil excitation is called a "macro-ensemble" detector and could lead to the discovery of solar neutrino interactions with ^{40}Ar if rates remain below 1 count per year or be used in studies of coherent neutrino-nucleus interactions with dark matter.  The PALEOCCENE experiment will be performed using a 30 kg sample, offering a possibility for exploring inactive materials as a option for dark matter detection.  The project may also reveal aspects of neutron background, radioactivity, and other environmental factors that could influence such detectors in the future.  The present paper outlines PALEOCCENE, with early results from a pilot demonstrating the feasibility of the concept and a future appearing promising with high counts.  The project's results may expand existing scientific opportunities in the field of particle astrophysics and cosmology with potential for theoretical implications.  PALEOCCENE's future advancements could lead to Ramsey-like improvements in understanding Coherent Neutrino-Nucleus Alternating Current signals, an essential aspect of neutrinoless double-beta decay with neutrinos. The method is based on a continuous geometric model that represents nodes in a two-dimensional space, with probabilities linked by great circle distances. A diffusion process is then used on this continuous space, followed by a transformation of the resulting distribution into a network format. Additionally, a more efficient algorithm is introduced for identifying clusters in large networks, particularly those with many interconnected components. Clustering on networks is a common problem found in numerous applications, and we present a reference implementation in Python for demonstrating the effectiveness of this geometric method. Furthermore, we evaluate the geometric method against established algorithms in a simulated outbreak scenario and compare the outcomes. Notably, the geometric method exhibits similar efficiency and accuracy but requires significantly less parameter tuning, considering only the network's connectivity structure (with no need to specify the number of clusters, like many other network clustering methods). Finally, an example is provided of how the geometric method can be used to model real-world outbreaks. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to robustly identify clusters in networks characterized by irregular and asymmetric patterns of connectivity. A fundamental challenge in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning involves specifying task objectives through natural language, which often leads to conflicting outcomes due to the open-ended nature of natural language.  This paper focuses on the reference ambiguity challenge in goal-conditioned learning and proposes a new algorithm, called the Natural Language Proxy NL-PC from a suite of advanced algorithms developed to overcome referential ambiguity, titled Advanced Natural Language Policies ANLP.  The NL-PC algorithm develops a strategy to reduce reference ambiguity by leveraging word embeddings from a training dataset using the Word Embedding Learning NEML to determine the objective of a given natural language command.  This objective is compared with a library of pre-defined embeddings stored in a Proxy Cache to select an appropriate sub-objective, thus eliminating reference ambiguity.  To facilitate Word Embedding Learning, a training dataset called the Natural Language Proxy Dataset NLProxy was developed to track changes in word embeddings over time.  Experimental results for robotic pushing and robotic block-stacking tasks show that NL-PC achieves superior performance with limited data and in zero-shot settings when compared to other advanced algorithms.  Moreover, NL-PC exhibits robustness to word embedding degradation over time.  Specifically, whereas PC from the ANLP suite fails with outdated word embeddings, NL-PC continues to perform effectively.  Importantly, NL-PC outperforms previous work including inverse reinforcement learning, inverse reinforcement learning from demonstrations as well as a goal-reduced version of PC from the ANLP suite.  The proposed dataset NLProxy and Word Embedding Learning NEML allow for the independent evaluation of each algorithm from the ANLP suite.  This independent evaluation shows that neither Word Embedding Learning from supervised methods nor online learning from RL results in satisfactory outcomes.  Nonetheless, experiments show that combining both RL and supervised methods in Word Embedding Learning from a combination of each other using online learning from RL in a feedback loop leads to significant gains in performance.  The concept of Proxy Caching is revealed to be the key factor responsible for the improvements.  Ultimately, the most effective approach involves the creation of both a cache of Word Embedding from a dataset such as NLProxy and a cache of objectives stored in a Proxy Cache to reduce reference ambiguity.  Words in the natural language command that correspond to actions or goals are matched with objectives in the cache to minimize reference ambiguity. Quantum channel tomography is a crucial process for fully understanding the characteristics of an arbitrary quantum channel. Although it's possible to accurately reconstruct most quantum channels, there's a notable exception involving the so-called "shadows" of quantum states, which cannot be accurately reconstructed without additional constraints. However, we propose a novel method - shadow procedure tomography - that allows for the precise reconstruction of a quantum channel's shadow, even with the minimal requirement of only inverting an infinite number of equations. This method is practically applicable because it's connected to an existing, efficient approach to fully reconstructing a quantum channel. Consequently, it's feasible to precisely reconstruct the shadow of an arbitrary quantum channel using the same resources. Furthermore, this method has a range of useful implications, such as the enhanced ability to privately release and privately compare random quantum data. Finally, we outline potential experimental approaches to apply shadow channel tomography in realistic scenarios. By combining practical quantum hardware and the advanced techniques of quantum computing, the potential advantages are significant. For instance, shadow channel tomography may enable the verification of quantum supremacy by privately generating random quantum data and comparing it against theoretical expectations. Moreover, it may facilitate quantum advantage by privately generating and mixing random quantum states in line with a given mixture distribution. Ultimately, the possibility of precisely reconstructing the shadow of a full mix of unitary transformations using an NISQ device could serve as a quantum advantage benchmark, much in the same way the quantum volume serves as a classical advantage benchmark. In the context of a shape $\Omega$, we explore the relationship between its area, 
the first moment of its area distribution function, and its Cheeger constant, with 
a focus on inherent inequalities between these quantities, particularly with 
positive lower bounds for the Cheeger constant in relation to the first moment 
of its area distribution function. Additionally, we examine how these inequalities 
can be used to derive sharper upper bounds for the first moment of its area 
distribution function. Notably, similar inequalities have previously been seen in 
the study of convex polygons, whereas our results are extended to general 
convex shapes in the plane and also have applications in estimating the Dirichlet 
energy of functions defined on these shapes, specifically functions in the Sobolev 
space $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$. In particular, a Cheeger problem is introduced in this context. 

Our findings are finalized with the demonstration of a counterexample that shows the 
inequalities we have proposed are close to being sharp. Specifically, this counterexample 
shows that the lower bound we have proposed for the Cheeger constant is essentially attained. 

It's noteworthy that the results we have proposed, although derived in a geometric context, 
are considered novel within this context and are considered classic within the study of 
functional analysis, particularly in the work of Friedlander and McIntosh who first introduced 
the concept of the Cheeger constant as a morphological analogue to the isoperimetric inequality 
in the 1990s. 

Moreover, the results we have proposed, although being first-order, are considered 
progressions of prior results of the second order that have been obtained by several of our 
co-authors and also by Braga Júnior, Brondsted, and Mel'nyik who have previously studied 
theoretical models of the area distribution function. 

Lastly, the results we have proposed, although being analytical in nature, are considered 
progressions of prior results of a geometric order that have been obtained by several of our 
co-authors and also by Barthe, Campi, and Cauchois who have previously studied the 
geometric properties of convex polygons.

Network centrality metrics, which measure node importance with various perspectives, have several applications across various domains. This paper proposes a new metric called Gromov centrality, which quantifies node importance in weighted networks by calculating a node's potential to shortest path routes using a triangle inequality surplus. This metric offers unique properties such as mathematically-verified variations, multi-scale calculations, and the ability to rank nodes consistently in directed networks. Gromov centrality's performance was tested in network ranking tasks on various data sets and the results demonstrate its effectiveness. In addition, Gromov centrality's properties are further discussed and its potential applications and future developments are explored. This metric can be used for network analysis and the development of community structures, particularly in the multi-scale range, and its uniqueness lies in its node centrality calculation method that considers the overall network structure. This study also introduces an efficient algorithm for calculating Gromov centrality and assessing its variations. This algorithm can be used as a base to develop various Gromov centrality variations that capture distinct network characteristics. The proposed Gromov centrality has several benefits such as robustness to scale-free transformations and the ability to assess community structures based on centrality distributions. This metric's performance was evaluated in network ranking tasks and it outperformed various established metrics in multiple network data sets. Therefore, Gromov centrality's unique properties make it a suitable tool for network analysis and the measurement of node importance in the most efficient way possible. This study's outcomes are innovative and comprehensive as they: (a) offer a new way to assess node importance in the most general network case, (b) provide a multi-scale perspective on network centrality, (b) offer a mathematical-based variation development method, and (c) guarantee consistency in the ranking of sparse and dense network components. This study's results can be extended by developing variations of Gromov centrality that capture specific network characteristic patterns. For instance, Gromov centrality's performance on small world networks can be further studied to develop variations that highlight network properties such as strong and weak ties. Similarly, Gromov centrality's performance on scale free networks can be explored to develop variations that assess and measure hub and periphery structures. Ultimately, Gromov centrality's outcomes offer a comprehensive analysis of node importance in the most general network case with the use of triangle inequality surplus. The parameters $m_0$ and $\kappa_0$ are fundamental constants with units of inverse length and inverse mass, respectively, and both play a significant role in the gravitational field. The Schrödinger equation is employed to demonstrate the quantum mechanical origin of the gravitational potential, and the asymptotic expansion is used to compute the potential at large distances. Furthermore, examples are provided to demonstrate the new ASP$\mathbf{A}$ model's capabilities. Specifically, the relationships between the masses of a planet and the sun are calculated for various planets in the solar system. Additionally, the sub-potential $\epsilon$ and the distance at which the solar system's backscatter occurs are determined for the sun and the earth. Lastly, the ASP$\mathbf{A}$ model is used to re-examine the light beam tunneling problem, and the corresponding values of the light constant $h$ and the reduced Planck constant $h_{\textrm{P}}$ are calculated. Moreover, the theoretical foundations for solar panels are laid, and the theoretical maximum currents are calculated. Lastly, the ASP$\mathbf{A}$ model is used to provide an explanation for the reasonable absence of gravitational waves from the sun, and the theoretical maximum speed of gravitational waves near the sun are calculated. The theoretical findings are supported by a large amount of numerical data, and all calculations are based on the second edition of "Dark matter and dark energy: The most up-to-date concepts of cosmology" with some minor changes. The adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (AVQE) family, a group of algorithms that efficiently utilize near-term quantum processors for chemical simulation, is built on a parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) framework. However, the current constraints of quantum hardware significantly hinder the scalability of these algorithms, specifically due to the costly process of qubit excitation during the iterative update of the PQC parameters. We introduce a modification to the standard AVQE, a Qubit-excitation-driven AVQE (QXAVQE) variant designed to optimize the practical applicability of quantum chemistry on near-term quantum computers. By reducing the costly multi-qubit excitation in the quantum circuit, QXAVQE achieves improved efficiency while remaining effective within chemical simulations. We evaluate QXAVQE's performance on a range of molecules within the H$_2$, H$_4$, H$_6$, water, and adenine systems and compare its results to the original AVQE method. We also study the impact of the circuit depth on the performance of both QXAVQE and AVQE and explore the potential for expanding QXAVQE to tackle more complex systems. Using an IBM quantum computer, we successfully converge QXAVQE to the ground state of a adenine molecule in only eight consecutive iterations. We believe that this improved QXAVQE variant, utilizing an efficient qubit-excitation strategy, represents a significant step towards enhancing the scalability of quantum chemistry on near-term quantum computers. Additionally, we provide additional supporting data for our study, including results of QXAVQE's performance on the H$_6$ system, an analysis of circuit convergence, and a document outlining our implementation of the quantum circuits using qiskit. A crucial aspect in understanding how deep neural networks function is the inner workings of an internal representation. Investigating this is challenging because it typically involves intricate architectures and large-scale training on vast datasets. We propose replacing the conventional generative model approach with the 'profound generative decoder', a framework that assumes a trained neural network can be seen as a generative model mapping representations to data. By positing a maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimate for the representation given the data, we create a system where representing the network as a decoder in a Bayesian framework allows us to scrutinize the intermediates at each stage of a trained network with ease. Notably, our method yields results comparable to those from full Bayesian analysis but with a significant reduction in computational requirements. Furthermore, our method has been demonstrated to be useful in analyzing the functioning of a newly trained CNN on the CIFAR-10 dataset, as well as a CNN that has undergone training on the ImageNet dataset. We have also implemented an enhanced version of our method to facilitate the analysis of large-scale networks by approximating the intermediates with samples from a normal distribution derived from the network's loss function and applying a clustering approach to identify the representations associated with each data element. We verify the accuracy of our method by comparing the outputs with the network's trained outputs. Our method has also been successfully applied to analyzing the functioning of a ResNet model on the ImageNet dataset. We also demonstrate how our method can be utilized as an effective tool in finding the most effective layers for model pruning and representational SHAKE to decrease computational requirements while maintaining performance. Lastly, our method has also been successfully applied in analyzing the functioning of a Neural Transformer on the English-to-English translation task within the machine translation domain by discovering a well-known translation bias. The source code for our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/UKHomeAssistant/Profound-Generative-Decoder. Although significant advancements have been made in producing highly realistic text-generated speech, the process remains expensive and time-consuming in terms of computational resources. To address this issue, we recommend exploring alternative approaches that are simpler and more efficient. Our research focuses on an unsupervised speech generation model that requires only speech data for training, without the need for transcripts or labels, making it a more feasible solution. By utilizing the same automatic speech recognition system for data pre-processing, we combined a text encoder with a latent space and a text-to-speech model to produce speech samples from casual listening transcripts. Our model, which utilizes an standard TTS model, generates speech samples at relatively low computational costs and our listener has positively received the results, indicating good speech quality and naturalness. We also compare our method's performance with a supervised speech generation model, yielding comparable results in terms of mean opinion scores for speech quality and naturalness. Our project's source code can be found at https://github.com/Baikyj/unsupervised-speech-generation. Our model's demo can be found at https://speakercafe.github.com/. We have also conducted user studies and obtained user feedback, with plans to make the results available. Our model demonstrates the promise of producing speech samples from casual listening transcripts using only readily available speech data and a standard TTS model, without the need for expensive and time-consuming computational resources. Our work sheds light on the dynamics between human listening experiences and speech, providing insights that are valuable in their own right and paving the way for the development of speech generation models that can produce high-quality speech samples from unstructured text for language model fine-tuning and other related applications. Our model produces speech samples at relatively low computational costs, but the generated audio samples may sometimes deviate from actual speech due to differences in pronunciation, intonation and other speech characteristics. Our listener has reported instances of speech generation failures, with the majority of cases being attributed to incorrect sentence break detection and A/B syllable combinations. Our research has found that the latently encoded text data contains various forms of noise, comprising instances of repeated words and syllable combinations. Our model's performance in the user study reveals a mean opinion score of 3.35 for speech quality and 3.25 for naturalness. Our model has demonstrated the potential for unsupervised speech generation, with the need for further research in addressing speech generation failures and refining the quality of latently encoded text data. Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear problems (MOMINLPs) appear in numerous fields and activities and represent a difficult class of combinatorial optimization tasks. This paper presents an original multi-criteria algorithm (m-CGSA) that expands the concepts of genotype and general variation strategies typically used in evolutionary computations for addressing MOMINLPs. The proposed approach is comparable to a modified NSGA-II method operating within a exploration-exploitation optimization framework. The m-CGSA algorithm converges towards local optima through exploration-exploitation optimization phases, which enhance its search capacity for better precision. The performance of the m-CSA method is evaluated using 12 test cases derived from the PLANT and MULTI-DEP benchmark suites. These test cases involve multi-objective formulations of well-known optimization problems such as the Hateo-Altitude vehicle routing problem and the Multi-Depot vehicle routing problem. Computational results obtained on a 2.53 GHz Intel Core i7 laptop indicate that the m-CGSA algorithm generates high-quality approximations for MOMINLPs, outperforming several competitive methods such as COPASI's multi-objective evolutionary search. This comparative analysis further demonstrates the m-CGSA's robustness against multi-criteria optimization perturbations and its capacity for efficient convergence, thus making it a valuable tool for real-world MOMINLPs and evolutionary computation comparisons. The source code of the m-CGSA algorithm is available at https://github.com/yassine-aboussadi/MCGSA/tree/master/m-CGSA. Our interactive demonstration will emphasize the user-centric and flexible design of the ARKivista gateway's data exchange services, as well as showcase its extensive toolset and analysis capabilities. Our presentation will particularly focus on the importance of safe and efficient data transfer methods such as snapshotting and compression, as well as the value of data analysis logging and reproducibility. Our goal is to engage the audience in a discussion on the importance of data exchange services and cyberinfrastructure gateways for the biomedical research community, with the hope of identifying areas for improvement and collaborating to advance future developments. Furthermore, we plan to provide means for audience members to contribute to a knowledge base of best practices for using the ARKivista gateway's features, as well as to contribute their own stories and experiences with data exchange and analysis. Our presentation represents a part of a larger educational initiative aimed at promoting the understanding and use of cyberinfrastructure gateways and data exchange services among researchers. This research delves into the problems of enhancing secure communication in a multi-user network, aided by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface, despite receivers having imperfect amplifiers. These imperfect amplifiers lead to interference in the other users through the reflection of the incoming signal, which we refer to as residual self-interference. To address this issue, we first establish a practical framework for achieving secure communication at the physical level. Specifically, we develop a novel problem for maximizing the minimum of the interference experienced by individual receivers and the interference received at the intended recipient, under consideration of the effects of RIS phase shift, channel state information, and amplifier characteristics. This problem is then further divided into two sub-problems for solving, which we approach using a combination of iterative optimization and bargaining algorithm methods. Extensive simulation results validate the efficacy of our proposed solution, while highlighting its advantages over existing solutions. Furthermore, the outcomes demonstrate that our approach remains robust across a range of parameters, including varying numbers of RIS units, users, and imperfect amplifier characteristics. The results also illustrate the trade-offs inherent in the design of these systems, as well as the importance of accurately modeling amplifier characteristics. To support our findings, complementary analytical results are presented. The outcome of this research provides a practical method for the design of RIS-aided secure communication networks, which addresses a significant drawback associated with existing approaches, namely the lack of tolerance to amplifier characteristics. The Unruh effect suggests that an inertial observer in a vacuum will perceive a thermal environment from a accelerating observer in the same vacuum. The "timelike Unruh effect" proposes that timelike trajectories will also yield this thermal environment. However, verifying this effect proves challenging due to the lengthy timescales involved. A novel approach to identifying the timelike Unruh effect is presented, utilizing geometric analysis on a three-dimensional Rindler space. The effect is quantified through an path-dependent Berry phase that encodes entanglement between the future and past light cones. The research indicates that when an excitation occurs late and decays early, the sign of the phase is positive; in contrast, when an excitation occurs early and decays late, the phase's sign is negative. Furthermore, the phase's magnitude is found to be dependent on the acceleration $a$ and the decay rate $\Gamma$, with the potential for a significant, observable effect when $a$ is sufficiently high and $\Gamma$ is much larger than $a$. An proposed experimental setup using a quantum system with distinct decay rates could potentially demonstrate the timelike Unruh effect. The effect is found to be equivalent to the phenomenon of quantum interference in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, where the period of rotation mirrors the duration of an accelerated trajectory and the optical path length mirrors the time elapsed. The research also explores the quantum coherence times necessary for an experimental observation and considers the potential impact of classical fluctuations on the phase. When considering these perturbations, the phase's deviation from its on-average value at its minimum point is found to be roughly twice the expression for coherence loss per unit acceleration. The research concludes by discussing the considerable implications of this effect, including its potential to reconcile the fundamental disparities between the inertial and accelerating universes and the universal nature of timelike trajectories. The effect may also provide a means of identifying the existence of gravitons through a gravitational influence on the phase's sign. An proposed experimental strategy to verify the timelike Unruh effect is outlined, involving a simultaneous measurement of the phase's sign and magnitude in a setup with carefully engineered acceleration and decay rate conditions. Potential future research directions inspired by this effect and the phase are also discussed. The associated code for simulating the phase can be found at https://github.com/eric52417/timelike-unruh. A related demonstration is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K-rEa8sR0qY. With the ability to conduct large-scale Multilingual Event Extraction studies using this dataset, we are one step closer to developing a general solution for all languages, thereby bridging the linguistic and cultural divide. The research has also paved the way for the development of a universal model capable of executing tasks in any language. By combining the MEE dataset with other datasets like MED and SARS-CoV-2, researchers may uncover novel avenues of investigation that could lead to the development of models capable of performing not only Multilingual Event Extraction but also named entity recognition and case filling and related topics. The research has also opened the door for the development of a dataset that contains knowledge about specific individuals and groups. By extending our model to medline (a database of publications on various topics including COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, ZIKA, etc.) in collaboration with other researchers who are working on the development of a dataset, we are one step closer to developing a highly accurate model that can make predictions for a wide range of events. In distance labeling, each vertex is assigned a set of labels that allows any two vertices' distances to be calculated in constant time, regardless of their connection. A problem in graph theory, known for offering the most efficient possible solution in some cases, it has been fully solved for planar graphs over the last decade. However, the issue remains unsolved for more general classes of graphs. In line with recent trends in approximate fault-tolerance, we look at the fault-tolerance aspect of distance labeling. Specifically, we provide a way to add small extra numbers to the vertices of a graph, so that even after some vertices are removed, the remaining vertices' distances can still be calculated precisely. For a set of n vertices, we create labels containing a certain number of integers, using a certain number of extra numbers, such that any subset of t vertices can be accurately paired with a constant number of extra numbers, resulting in constant calculation time for distances between vertices in that subset. We provide a solution for the full class of planar graphs, using up to $O(\log^{2/3} t)$ extra numbers, as well as an efficient method for making the required extra numbers as small as possible. Additionally, in the case of embedded planar graphs, we provide a solution using up to $O(\log t / \log \log t)$ extra numbers. We provide similar solutions for a class of semi-bipartite graphs that include the famous mesh and grid graphs. The concepts of 'distance to distance' and 'independent distance sets' are used in our solutions. An independent distance set of a graph is one where any two vertices' labels do not overlap, allowing their distances to other vertices to be calculated in constant time. We provide a solution for the full class of planar graphs, using up to $O(\log^{2/3} t)$ independent distance sets, as well as an efficient method for making the required sets as few as possible. These concepts are related to the well-known 'distance covering' problem in graph theory, however our solutions do not require it. Identifying out-of-distribution data is essential for most machine learning tasks to prevent potential misclassification. This study demonstrates how a specific neural network architecture designed for normal process conditions can effectively detect out-of-distribution data for a variety of datasets. The key to this method lies in the distribution of input data along the normal process's latent variable. A statistical approach is developed to estimate this distributional dimension using a minimal set of parameters, enabling a simple yet robust classification normality test. The benefits of this architecture are illustrated through successful out-of-distribution detection on image recognition tasks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and MiniIMDB, as well as on language processing tasks with the IMDB dataset. Furthermore, the research expands on the use of this architecture for representation learning, applying it to a categorical variable, and demonstrates that normal process characteristics can be valuable for downstream tasks. The source code is available at https://github.com/sterian/dnp. When tested on the PCAM dataset from OpenBenchmarking.org, the DNP-based model exhibited superior robustness and efficiency compared to established methods like Ensemble DOP and Normalizing Flows, requiring significantly fewer parameters and being up to 3.6 times faster. Specifically, the research shows that DNP models score well on various benchmarks, including CIFAR10/100, CIFAR100/MNIST, MiniIMDB, and Higgs, and outperforms competing methods in terms of robustness, efficiency, and parameter usage. The DNP architecture offers a versatile and adaptable solution for out-of-distribution detection, representation learning, and even the development of more robust downstream models. It particularly excels in low-data scenarios and is suited for applications where a minimal set of distributional parameters can effectively capture normal process conditions. Validation is demonstrated on the Google Dataset Toolkit. Additionally, the research is recognized through a benchmark submission on OpenBenchmarking.org. Quantum systems driven far from equilibrium exhibit diverse, Scarn-like stationary states, however the underlying theory for these systems is still under development. By using a simple yet robust many-body model, we demonstrate that a driven optical-lattice system, confined in one dimension, displays a Scarn-like state that arises due to a unique mixture of heating and cooling effects at low temperatures. Unlike typical heat mechanisms, the system's drive actually reduces thermal motion and fosters correlations, ultimately leading to a robust Bose condensate in a robust Scarn state. This unique behavior is distinct from other one-dimensional systems that exhibit nonlinear bandgap mappings. By analyzing the system's relaxation and using Floquet-Bloch equations, we gain deeper understanding of the Scarn state, confirming its resilience in the presence of decoherence. Given that $u\in C^{0}(K)$ solves the Monge--Amp\`ere equation, where $K$ is a compact convex domain in $n$-dimensional space (with $n\geq2$), and that the equation has a nonnegative right-hand side with an exponent less than $1/n$, then $u$ must satisfy a uniform H\"older estimate. This result expands upon an earlier finding by V. Capriati and A. Pratelli. A key component of the proof is a enhanced form of the Alexandrov maximum principle, which we use to establish the H\"older estimate through a suitable rearrangement inequality. Additionally, the proof relies on the Deep Rearrangement Inequality, which we derived in a prior study (along with J. Wang and Y. Zhang). The current result can be applied to establish a strict minimum principle for nonnegative solutions of a certain semilinear elliptic equation without spatial dependence, which is consistent with a related result by P. E. Mironescu, M. Morandini, and M. Shaposhnikova. Furthermore, the result is used to establish a significant convergence theorem for a class of semilinear elliptic equations without spatial dependence, which is consistent with a related result by S. Blitzinger and L. A. Caffarelli, as well as a related result by G. Talbot. An alternative proof of the result is also provided, one which solely relies on the classical Rearrangement Inequality. This approach is presented in the spirit of a classic paper (although an error is identified and corrected). The current result is also connected to a result from nonsmooth analysis that is presented by J. J. Jendrej, L. Lamadé, and R. Zein. A detailed comparison with that result is provided in the text. The discovery of optical clocks outside the realm of fractional laser therapy has led to innovative applications in fields like biomedical imaging and vortex-based devices. Research on these non-repeating clocks is scarce, with existing studies mostly focusing on their unique properties rather than their overall dynamics. To fully understand non-repeating optical clocks, we must analyze the complete temporal behavior and extract relevant physical characteristics. In this study, we utilize a statistical approach to describe non-repeating optical clocks based on the spatial structure of their underlying mathematical models. Our findings indicate that the temporal behavior of these clocks can be fully characterized by two key spatial properties, which allow for a straightforward probabilistic interpretation of their dynamics. We have demonstrated this method with two specific instances, a coherent 1D dark-soliton clock and a quantum-chaos-based clock. Our approach may serve as a starting point for investigating other rare optical phenomena. Furthermore, the principles outlined in this study could be applied to other systems exhibiting complex and random behaviors, such as those seen in biological systems. The importance of accurately modeling optical systems cannot be overemphasized, with potential applications spanning biomedical research and device development. To showcase the potential applications of our framework, we have successfully applied it to developing a novel biomedical sensor using a non-repeating optical clock. The sensor operates on the principle of detecting subtle changes in biological samples' structural or functional properties rather than their overall density. By combining the ability to analyze various sample features and our ability to visualize and extract features that may go undetected by conventional methods, we have established a new path forward. Similarly, the features extracted from our model could be used to determine the number of cells in a sample, such as a blood sample, with potential applications spanning various fields. Moreover, the characteristics obtained from our model of a chiral fiber can be used to develop a practical method for measuring the strength of chiral materials, which could further our understanding of these materials. The work focuses on optimizing SFC delivery through Fog nodes while achieving real-time control via SDN. The key challenges identified are resource allocation, fault prevention, and failure recovery within the integrated Fog-SDN framework. The research proposes an adaptive control mechanism that achieves efficient distributed control over SFCs in both SDN and Fog components. The key goal is to achieve optimal control outcomes that meet various optimization objectives, including minimizing average response time, implementing QoS guarantees, and reducing energy consumption. The study conducts extensive simulations using a large dataset to evaluate the performance of the introduced algorithm in real-world scenarios and compares it with other existing approaches. The results demonstrate that the introduced algorithm significantly outperforms the alternatives in achieving optimal control outcomes under distinct optimization objectives. Recent breakthroughs in self-supervised learning and its applications are creating significant impacts in semi-supervised image classification, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data and vast amounts of unlabeled images. A crucial component of self-supervised learning is the choice of loss function, with minimal understanding of the strengths and limitations of existing methods. This study develops a decision tree to analyze the implications of three primary loss functions - including contrastive learning, multi-criteria learning, and backpropagation learning. Through decision tree analysis, the study uncovers the underlying conditions that distinguish these loss functions, leading to the discovery of novel learning strategies with enhanced performance. Experimental results demonstrate that these new strategies outperform traditional approaches, resulting in better outcomes across multiple scenarios and datasets. For instance, when using the STL-10 dataset, approaches based on decision tree-suggested rules achieve accurate rates of 34.81\% or more, surpassing the 33.26\% achieved by contrastive learning, 34.89% achieved by multi-criteria learning, and 34.94% achieved by backpropagation learning. This study makes a significant contribution to the self-supervised learning field by providing theoretical evidence of the distinctions between different loss functions and offering empirical evidence to support the effectiveness of the resulting learning strategies. The study further demonstrates the versatility of decision tree analysis through its successful application in other learning scenarios and datasets. For example, when using the CIFAR-10 dataset, approaches based on decision tree-suggested rules achieve accurate rates of 80.61% or more, outperforming the 79.09% achieved by contrastive learning, 80.80% achieved by multi-criteria learning, and 80.84% achieved by backpropagation learning. The study's findings are expected to pave the way for future research in the self-supervised learning domain. We create these systems by modifying a well-known tensor theory, the scale-invariant MERA, through a simple and intuitive method. We establish the significant correlations within these systems using a concept called 'power-rule,' demonstrating their significant potential in quantum tasks. We utilized ALMA observations of molecular clouds in the galaxy's central region to examine the properties of filaments. Previous studies of these clouds found similar properties for individual filaments, including those that are dense and rich in gas. These filamentous structures are likely influenced by the formation of stars, although global galaxy patterns suggest that they could also result from complex processes like turbulence and magnetic fields. To further understand these processes, we analyzed a sample of 30 filaments from a nearby galaxy region, observing a average distance between neighboring filaments of approximately 14 to 17 times the diameter of these filaments. This distance between filaments is consistent with our theory that they reside within flat, two-dimensional sheets. These findings align with the view that filament formation occurs within these sheets due to instability mechanisms, particularly the phenomenon of gravitational collapse. Our study of the distance between these filaments adds an additional element in understanding their intricate structure. Notably, their separation suggests that they might not be grouped into larger, cohesive networks, although we do observe some larger gatherings. These findings support our notion that filament formation results from sheet instability and imply that their star-forming potential could be influenced by optimizing their density, whether through aggregation within these two-dimensional sheets or through other scaling factors. To further inform these findings, our study populates a matrix with the properties of over 80 molecular clouds from a galaxy's central region, providing a wealth of data on its filamentary network that can be accessed at www.s3.amazonaws.com/galacticfilaments/data/index.html. These data mark a crucial step in understanding the characteristics of these filamentous structures, informing models of galaxy development, and clarifying the mechanisms driving their complex morphology. An accompanying graphic illustration of these filament networks, which can be viewed at www.s3.amazonaws.com/galacticfilaments/data/FilamentsNetwork.html, visually showcases their two-dimensional spread and facilitates easy navigation. These filamentous structures' characteristics suggest they could serve as ideal test subjects for studying the dynamics of two-dimensional patterns within the galaxy's central region. By analyzing the properties of these filamentous structures across various scales, we have contributed new knowledge of their intricate structure which can be accessed through the website www.s3.amazonaws.com/galacticfilaments/data/index.html. These results inform a broader range of related studies, one of which is detailed in a companion paper, where we offer a theoretical framework for the star-forming potential of these filamentous structures by proposing a general equation that relates their properties to their distance from the galaxy's central region.

This study addresses a scenario in which an energy storage system with a large capacity is used to reduce losses in an urban area's power grid by distributing voltage. A PS-DV model is developed to quantify demand response, and an iterative, decentralized method is designed for coordinating distributed energy storage systems to minimize network losses. A network-wide optimization approach is also presented, using linear relaxation and a novel formulation of the Hessian matrix to effectively model interaction constraints. Computational results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods and reveal their distinct performance profiles, with the decentralized method exhibiting the most significant loss reductions of 3.22% and voltage reductions of 2.16%. Furthermore, the optimization approach showed the greatest success in minimizing network losses, reducing them by 3.41% and the voltage distributions by 2.30%. Additionally, the optimization approach was found to outperform the decentralized method in a multi-agent game setting. However, all methods showed relatively minor voltage reductions, suggesting that other constraints may limit their performance. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the optimization approach poses a challenge to its practical application. A comparison of the two optimization methods for small-scale and large-scale networks, as well as a general evaluation of their performance across various problem settings, remains a future research objective.  Additionally, the computational complexity of the optimization approach, which has potential to hinder its practical application, is another area for further investigation. A comprehensive study across diverse problem settings to compare the two optimization methods and to identify key factors that may impact the performance of the decentralized method and the PS-DV model is also recommended. Within the realm of delayed bandits, we investigate a scenario where agents exhibit delay behavior that's contingent on specific parameters rather than randomness. The standard Koml\'{o}s and Schalkoff (2020) analysis for such cases assumes no prior knowledge of parameter dependencies, instead relying on data-driven estimations of key parameters. In this study, we generate instances where experts provide precise estimates of their parameters after a while; yet, some specialists experience a delayed start or an extended period of suboptimal performance. By reexamining the basic $K$-armed bandit issue using these conditions, we come up with innovative strategies that significantly improve the performance label cost in comparison to non-parametric approaches with similar delay behavior. In addition, we address a simplified version of this problem with simplified features and prove that our approach leads to an exponential reduction of the sample complexity for a given confidence level. Finally, the same techniques apply to the more complex linear bandit issue, resulting in substantial improvements over standard approaches with delayed data. The experiments validate our hypotheses and show that these methods are practical and effective in real-world environments. Human-written stories often seamlessly transition between scripted dialogue and free-form descriptions of the surrounding environment, yet current generative models struggle to replicate this structure, leading to discontinuous and unrealistic depictions of narrative scenarios. To address this limitation, we're developing a generative model that produces text in the context of a structured narrative framework, where each event incorporates both a dialogue and a descriptive component, organized by themes defined by human experts. By utilizing a hybrid threat training technique and incorporating a consistency reward, we're aiming to enhance the coherence and naturalness of our generated text, with promising initial results from a limited dialogue corpus. Furthermore, we're preparing a substantial, publicly available dataset containing 36,000 scenes, 12,000 characters, and 180 themes, carefully created to mimic real-world conditions through its extensive size, variety, and complexity. This dataset, named HATCH, is intended to foster the development of more accurate and detailed generative models of text. Ultimately, we're working to build a model that not only produces text that's indistinguishable from that written by humans but also, through its integration with a planning module, is capable of organizing the narrative into a logical sequence. We're close to releasing our model-based system, which has already demonstrated promising performance in a controlled experiment. Specifically, our system has outperformed existing models in incorporating environmental details in a CoQA-like scenario, with results available on our website. We're also set to release our model and accompanying dataset through controlled experiments at two prominent conferences, MAML at ICML 2021 and DRL at NeurIPS 2022. Further research will focus on an extensive evaluation not only of our model but of the HATCH dataset as well, with plans to publish our findings at EMNLP 2022. The dataset can be accessed at github.com/facebookresearch/LEATHER. Additionally, our model can be accessed through the following repository: github.com/facebookresearch/LEATHER-model. The initial research overview will cover key findings in lattice QCD relating to hadron physics, thermodynamics, CP violation, heavy mesons, nucleon structure, and dark matter, highlighting recent achievements and ongoing challenges. In hadron physics, researchers have made significant progress in understanding decay widths and property corrections of significant mesons. An in-depth analysis of baryon masses has led to new insights in lattice QCD, utilizing various probe methods. To predict the dynamic loads acting on a specific offshore wind turbine design, a statistical model was developed using a combination of Gaussian processes. This model, constructed with sequential pairs of Gaussian processes, simulates the conditional statistics of a target random field given various input parameters. Utilizing the widely available Gaussian process regression technique, the proposed approach enables efficient computation of posterior distributions for wind-turbine loads given arbitrary geometric configurations and environmental conditions. A key innovation was resolving the issue of non-negative surface stresses, which are crucial in determining the loads acting on the turbine's surface. The statistical model was then validated by comparing its predictions with actual loads from detailed computational models of the wind turbine. Specifically, a study examined the stress patterns on the turbine's blades resulting from varying angles of attack and pitch. The results demonstrated that the model could accurately capture the effects of design changes on local stress patterns while also effectively modeling the effects of geometric variations on loads. However, the approach's limitations were also identified, particularly in simulating the load patterns consistent with the physical laws governing stress patterns. Nonetheless, the proposed method is suitable for use in rapid, low-cost design optimizations for offshore wind turbines. Furthermore, an open-source software package was developed to facilitate the use of this model, as well as another Gaussian process-based method, for informing the optimization process with sequential sampling strategies. A potential area for further research was also identified in creating more advanced models that integrate multiple Gaussian processes to tackle specific challenges associated with the simulation of wind-field realism and root-causing of load anomalies. Specifically, incorporating the spatial distribution of wind-speed patterns and identifying the causes of rare, extreme load events would be essential in further refining the models for practical applications in design optimizations. In the future, the proposed method could also be enhanced by replacing its underlying Gaussian process regression with a more recent technological advancement. In particular, transformations like Fourier features or normalizing flows could be adapted to create more realistic models of random fields with explicit separation of their underlying causal factors. In that context, the proposed approach could be reimagined as a data-efficient causal modeling technique, effectively handling the selection bias associated with the data generated during the training process. In a more general context, the method could be applied to various applications such as the modeling of the condition of bridges, the simulation of the traffic patterns, the fitting of medical images to new geometric shapes, the forecasting of the solar power generation, the emulation of the interactions between materials, the ranking of speech for the detection of similar speakers, the simulation of the dynamics of the systems in motion

A positive result is achieved for the $R_\infty$-character of nilpotent quotients in the general case of infinitely generated abelian groups that fit certain criteria, building on previous work by Bult which covered the case of freely generated groups of finite rank. This result is utilized to categorize all generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups that possess an infinite $R_\infty$-character. Specifically, it is established that the group $\Gamma_2(n)$ has an $R_\infty$-character of $n^2$ for all $n \geq 1$, and the character is finite for a specific subset of these groups, defined by $\Gamma_1(m, k)$. All solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups that possess an infinite $R_\infty$-character are consequently identified, and the characteristic values for these groups are either finite (with a value of $|k|^{-2}$) or infinitely large. The work by Bult is thus significantly broadened by the removal of the requirement of a freely generated group with a finite rank. Behavioral data in driving simulates real scenarios, yet there isn't an abundance of datasets that accurately replicate genuine driving conditions. Recognizing driving situations is crucial for drivers and self-driving vehicles alike, and thus we designed a large, 14-category dataset of driving scenarios. Comprising 52 unique situations and nearly 68,000 labeled entries, this dataset is extensively detailed, outperforming currently available naturalistic driving datasets. Comprising multiple data types, including driving scenarios, vehicle and pedestrian data, and camera footage, this dataset is versatile, suited for a variety of research tasks. Utilizing this dataset, researchers can investigate topics such as driving behavior, the implementation of advanced driver assistance systems, the assessment of scenarios involving automated vehicles and pedestrians, as well as modeling driving scenarios. Additionally, a web-based tool allows for interactive data analysis. Furthermore, we developed several metrics to assess situation recognition accuracy and applied these to evaluate the performance of four distinct deep learning models using our dataset: convolutional neural networks, recurrent convolutional energy networks, convolutional neural networks with global average pooling, and residual networks. Notably, we achieved a remarkable 73.7% accuracy in situation identification with the convolutional neural network model. Finally, we applied results from a prior self-driving vehicle behavior dataset to compare and align the situation recognition and behavior data within our new dataset. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of automatically identifying driving scenarios using vision-based deep learning methods. What's more, we've made our dataset available for download, as well as the accompanying analysis code. This research has been made possible through a dataset of over 1,000 driving video recordings, totaling nearly 300 hours of driving footage. Subsequently, we extracted still images from these videos and annotated them according to their respective driving scenarios. Ultimately, we used these images to train our deep learning models. Our research is presented in a formal academic publication. The driving scenario dataset that we've developed has been expanded to include additional features such as lane marking detection, dismount events, and vehicle and pedestrian tracking. Moreover, we've established a web-based data analysis platform that enables researchers to create detailed plots and tables based on data distribution, situation recognition, and other relevant metrics. The analysis platform is available at https://scenndd.azurewebsites.net. The dataset is freely available for download at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo/4973328. We demonstrate through conformal field theory techniques that the underlying assumption of the "c-theorem" in the reflected entropy case is not necessarily valid. A counterexample can be established in the context of the Lie conformal algebra $\mathfrak{sp}_6$. Additionally, for both the Potts model and the Lie conformal model, the assumed "c-theorem" in the reflected entropy scenario leads to a negative or zero value, which contradicts the expected positive value characterizing the entropy from a system with a large number of degrees of freedom. We utilize the refined holographic proposal as a tool for validation, showing that the assumed "c-function" in the reflected entropy case satisfies certain conditions that mirror the properties of the c-theorem. These conditions include non-decreasing behavior and bounded above by the log of the central charge. We also computed the reflected entropy in the respective models using the refined holographic proposal and found that its growth at small central charge is consistent with the assumption made in the proposal. The global COVID-19 pandemic has led to the adoption of contact tracing technology in numerous countries. These services, which utilize mobile device data to identify and alert users who have been near someone who has been infected, have been heavily relied upon by government authorities to combat the spread of the virus. As the widespread use of this technology has raised serious concerns regarding user data privacy and anonymity, it became essential to investigate the potential risks and confidentiality breaches associated with these contact tracing systems. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of several contact tracing apps, including those used in Brazil, Germany, and Mexico, by examining the process of locating users and creating user profiles based on Bluetooth data. A susceptibility study was then developed to simulate and calculate the probability of user re-identification from these profiles, applying both basic and advanced machine learning techniques. In addition to these findings, recommendations are provided to designers of contact tracing systems to prevent the disclosure of user locations. This research is timely and crucial, not only during the current COVID-19 pandemic but also in preparing for potential future public health crises. Moreover, its findings have significant implications that extend beyond the specific context of contact tracing technology, touching on broader issues of user data privacy and anonymity. Ultimately, it is hoped that this research can contribute to the development of contact tracing systems that balance their essential purpose with the protection of user confidentiality. Moreover, a tool called Coronav\'irus-SUS that mimics the functionality of contact tracing apps and allows for the simulation of user location data is made available to researchers and practitioners. This tool serves not only to support the research presented in this paper but also to aid in the simulation of contact tracing systems in general and could potentially be used in future research.
