In modern quantum computing, reducing errors caused by the environment is a critical goal.  Quantum error correction, a crucial aspect of achieving this goal, has seen significant progress since its introduction nearly two decades ago.  Today, a diverse range of correction methods exist, with different mechanisms such as classical, noise-reducing, and resource-based approaches being explored.  A novel, previously theoretical method known as the Raulin-Yanez-Lopartos scheme was introduced in 2020.  This method employs an all-devolution basis to reconstruct the encoding process.  Another proposed approach, the concealed inverses protocol, was conceived in 2021.  This protocol utilizes a different all-devolution basis compared to the Raulin-Yanez-Lopartos scheme.  Both protocols have been shown to efficiently correct quantum errors.  Recently, a research team applied both the Raulin-Yanez-Lopartos scheme and the concealed inverses protocol to superconducting quantum circuits to verify their feasibility in real-world applications.  This study successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of these protocols under various physical constraints.  Furthermore, numerical calculations showed that the concealed inverses protocol exhibits superior performance over the Raulin-Yanez-Lopartos scheme.  The results of this research have been published in The Journal of Superconductivity and Nanoscale Physics.  This work is part of a larger thesis that has been successfully defended at the University of San Juan, Argentina. In a category $\mathbb C$, a subobject $\sigma$ of an object $X$ can be visualized as an indexation of subsets of $X$ that are totally ordered, provided that $\mathbb C$ is regular and has biproducts, enabling a straightforward description of $\sigma$ through its corresponding ordered sets. This results in a two-layered representation of the subobject, with the ordered sets corresponding to $\sigma$ itself. Such a representation is called cartesian. Conversely, a cocartesian depiction of a subobject $\tau$ in $\mathbb C$ involves indexing classes of pairs from $X \times X$ that form $\tau$, with the condition that their first components are unique. This paper explores occurrences of this type of depiction in various categories. It is demonstrated that in general, cocartesian representations do not exist uniquely, nor necessarily for all subobjects in $\mathbb C$. However, in certain specific categories, such unique depictions are possible and often utilized. Moreover, it's shown that in a particular construction method for categories, called free generation, a subcategory of $\mathbb C$ plays a crucial role in determining potential depictions in $\mathbb C$. Finally, it is examined under which conditions such unique depictions are guaranteed in a category, with a focus on regular categories in particular. Results indicate that in a certain type of generation involving equivalence relations, biproducts, and equivalence relations themselves, unique depictions necessarily exist. However, this is not the case with another type of generation involving only equivalence relations. Moreover, it is shown that if $\mathbb C$ has a certain type of generation involving biproducts and equivalence relations, and is well-powered, then unique depictions exist in $\mathbb C$. due to their potential for a range of vision and language tasks, and have shown promising
results in vision-language multitasking and cross-modal learning. Nevertheless, their 
performance in understanding short text snippets and their applications in tasks like 
localizing objects within images still needs to be improved. In order to enhance their 
visual capabilities, we have developed a advanced fine-tuning technique for end-to-end 
training of these models, which integrates three visual input sources: (i) self-supervised 
image pre-training, (ii) image-caption pairs, and (iii) detailed image annotations. Our 
method, known as VT-CLIP, yields better results on challenging vision-language benchmarks, 
such as VL-ADNet and VL-GRAND, demonstrating its potential for efficient learning and 
improved visual capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/whwu VT-CLIP.

The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital pathology is a rapidly
evolving field with significant potential. Current standard procedures for
harvesting and presenting image-based diagnostic data of cancer tissues are not
fully exploited by existing AI tools. Furthermore, the results produced by AI
models are often difficult to understand for practicing pathologists. In our
paper, we introduce a set of standardized data encoding and sharing tools,
known as Highdicom, designed to optimize the processing of image-based data and
AI outputs in pathology. By leveraging our developed tools, the image-based
data and AI outputs can be annotated with precise spatial information, and
transferred into widely supported image file formats. Our analysis shows that
Highdicom's data processing is 3-6 times faster when compared to other popular
libraries. In our demonstration of Highdicom, we employed a well-trained AI
model to process a digital cancer tissue image derived from a slide of HPV-related
adenocarcinoma. The resulting output, presented in a HTML5 interactive report,
clearly shows the AI's decision-making process at each step, enabling the model's
outputs to be seamlessly understood by both pathologists and AI researchers. Our
evaluation results confirm that Highdicom's standardized data encoding and
presenting tools can effectively bridge the gap between AI models and human
interpreters. The source code of our Highdicom Python toolkit is publicly available
at the repository https://github.com/Highdicom/Highdicom under the terms of the
permissive Apache 2.0 license. Additionally, the related demo application is
hosted at the website with a standard URL
https://standardization.ighd.org/2021/11/07/highdicom-visibility-htm5/." The
visually enhanced HTML5 interface enhances user understanding by providing
interactive features, as well as precise spatial highlighting and layering of
annotated data and AI outputs. Our study's findings have significant implications
for the development of new AI tools and existing models, encouraging the use of
Highdicom's data processing tools. Furthermore, the deployment of our demo
application serves as a positive example for effectively presenting AI outputs to
practicing pathologists. The proposed Highdicom standard, in particular its
encoding of AI outputs, may potentially gain international recognition given its
clear presentation on the website. In fact, the relevant proposal, submitted by
the German company, has already been formally submitted to the IHE

The electronic properties of low-dimensional vanadium oxide surfaces are shrouded in uncertainty due to insufficient characterization by surface science techniques. Our investigation reveals the precise nature of the electronic transition in ultrathin V$_{2}$O$_{3$(0001)} layers upon reduction, a phenomenon believed to arise from different reductions. When top-layer atoms are reduced, a metal-insulator transition occurs but the same transition happens with smaller gaps between layers when the reduction occurs internally. Moreover, varying amounts of oxygen exposure on different layers leads to differing work functions, which may account for discrepancies in previous experimental results. Our data also suggests a shift in the metal-insulator transition temperature from the bulk value of 165 K to the low temperature of 50 K, contingent on the surface termination. These findings are further supported by computational modeling using a slab model and validated through comparison with other research. Our investigation significantly contributes to the understanding of the electronic behavior of reduced low-dimensional metal-insulators. Additionally, the dynamic nature of the reduction is not influenced by the surface termination and primarily controlled by the movement of electrons between the metal and insulator states. A critical factor for researchers to consider when interpreting data from various studies on these types of systems is the impossibility of precisely replicating the same film conditions, leading to a variety of results and conflicting reports in the literature. Our data also shows significant potential for controlling the electronic properties of these systems through the manipulation of the surface termination and may lead to the development of new materials with desired insulating or metallic properties, enhancing their potential in an array of applications including spintronics, electronics, and chemistry. Our investigation into the surface-dependent metal-insulator transition offers an opportunity for a new generation of materials design and further investigation into the intricate surface chemistry and physics of these systems. A complementary technique of spatially resolving the work function through kelvin probe microscopy can be applied to further understand the metal-insulator behavior in these systems, providing two-dimensional data that can be compared with our computational models and the results from scanning tunneling microscopy. Our investigation into the insulating layers reveals the precise nature of the electronic transition in ultrathin V$_{2}$O$_{3}$ layers upon reduction, a phenomenon that does not occur in the bulk material and is primarily controlled by the surface termination and dynamic behavior. A plausible mechanism for the electronic transition involves the formation of V$^{4+}$ and V$^{3+}$ states and is influenced by the thickness of the insulating layer, leading to a variety of results and conflicting reports

Unlike previous studies, the measurement accurately accounts for how the top quark's interaction with electrons, photons, and other top quarks affects its detection. The measurement yields precise top quark mass values at various interaction scales, spanning a range of 160-266 GeV, in terms of the pole mass, with an uncertainty of 1.75 GeV. This measurement serves as a robust benchmark against which theoretical calculations of top quark production and decay processes can be compared to further refine our understanding of these processes. Furthermore, the measurement provides insight into how the top quark's interaction with electrons, photons, and other top quarks is related to their respective mass measurements. The findings are consistent with a straightforward interpretation of the data but also, when considered in conjunction with the uncertainty, reveal a considerable range of possible contributions from these interactions, corresponding to a range of possible mass differences of 20-90 GeV when comparing to the mass measurement of a free top quark. This range of possible mass differences could potentially impact the search for new physics, particularly in processes involving rare top quark interactions. Finally, the measurement's high level of precision suggests that it could be used to constrain the uncertainty of QCD calculations, providing additional opportunities to refine our understanding of these calculations. These tasks involve designating a fractional edge coloring for the graphs such that the color of each edge with endpoints i and j has a fractional value less than α times the sum of the colors of the edges incident on i and j. A key research question is to create an algorithm that produces a partial coloring of edges with the minimum possible fractional value, and a crucial aspect of this process is determining the sequence of vertices. We present a novel approach to deriving quantum field theories for particles in curved spacetimes, relying on the concept of $S$-matrices that remain unchanged under general coordinate transformations. This method reveals the underlying symmetry of the derivations of $S$-matrices, consisting of unitary transformations followed by differential operators with coefficients drawn from observables. Utilizing the Keldysh formalism, we derive $S$-matrices for a variety of scenarios, including particles in curved spacetimes, gravitational waves, and cosmological spacetimes. Notably, the derivations are universal and free from assumptions about high-energy behavior. This method is versatile, enabling the extension of the derivations to theories beyond general relativity, including systems with electromagnetic and gravitational fields. Specifically, we derive $S$-matrices for interactions between charged particles and gravitational fields in the test-field limit, as well as for interacting gravitational fields with small spatial gradients. Furthermore, we derive $S$-matrices for a simple model of primordial stochastic gravity and calculate the corresponding observables. This method is widely applicable to various theoretical frameworks and experimental scenarios involving quantum field theories in curved spacetimes. The clarity and trustworthiness of recommendation system explanations are crucial to their user base. A widely used approach to enhance explanations is to limit the number of items shown, however research shows that users still struggle with assessing model reliability on multi-item recommendations. A proposed solution is LIME-RS, a post-hoc method that generates straightforward, interpretable explanations for ranked recommendation scenarios. A new study examines the combination of a fixed number of items with an explicit confidence level of each item, aiming to improve the coherence and psychological validity of such explanations. A large-scale evaluation on real datasets demonstrated the benefits of LIME-RS with variable confidence levels versus a fixed one, revealing that reduced item lists and clearer reasoning are highly correlated with user perceptions. Moreover, user-generated labels indicate that LIME-RS explanations are more stable when the model is subjected to minor changes, in line with psychological principles. These principles also reveal that LIME-RS explanations, optimized for L1-norm, tend to be more consistent with human expectations than alternative optimization methods such as L2-norm or gradient-based methods. Ultimately, the combination of item list length and confidence level, rather than a fixed approach, is found to significantly impact the consistency and psychological validity of such explanations. A newly proposed metric measures the psychological validity of such explanations, found to be closely related to straightforwardness and trustworthiness. A comparison with other post-hoc optimization methods, such as L2-norm and gradient-based techniques, also yields LIME-RS to be the most effective and trustworthy option in the context of ranked recommendation systems. The study concludes by highlighting the need for future research to investigate the psychological validity of such explanations, particularly in the context of multi-item recommendations, and to develop various forms of narrative explanations that increase trustworthiness among users. The surface quantum capacity of existing solid-state quantum processors may be limited by the tendency of photoexcited carriers to pile up at the surface due to reduced surface confinement energy. In order to explore the potential of near-surface quantum wells, comprising a thin InAs layer interposed between GaAs layers, for use as spin-based quantum bits, the electronic characteristics of these structures were examined through X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. These investigations revealed that modifying the chemical composition of the surface layers is necessary in order to mitigate the surface accumulation of carriers and thereby fine-tune the Fermi level of the material. Notably, employing a AlAs surface layer was found to successfully avoid near-surface accumulation of carriers, whereas incorporating a doped surface layer allowed for the adjustment of the Fermi level through variation of the dopant density. In addition, incorporating a thin InAs layer at the surface was found to effectively prevent carrier accumulation at the surface due to increased confinement energy. These investigations suggest that InAs-based near-surface quantum wells could serve as versatile platforms for a range of quantum information processing applications. Furthermore, the insight gained from these studies could facilitate the development of novel quantum information devices, including those based on other semiconductor materials. These contrasting properties highlight the capacity of these materials to support a wide range of quantum processing functionalities. In learning systems, data resilience is of significant interest as a measure of minimally violating the principles of fundamental artificial intelligence. One of the prominent approaches to resilience is outsourcing, which involves sending queries to remote sources for additional information. Nevertheless, selectively sending these queries can be challenging. In this research, we investigate the potential of using machine learning-based methods to determine which data elements to query for enhancing resilience. Our focus is on regional-based queries, which assess whether a specific data element adheres to a particular regimen more or less than another regimen. These queries provide a strong resilience guarantee but are computationally expensive to compute. As a result, we examine the feasibility of efficiently approximating regional queries through both classical and quantum approaches. Furthermore, we present theoretical bounds on the error and confidence of these approximations. Through experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in achieving nearly identical results to full computation while utilizing significantly less time and resources. Consequently, we suggest that regional-based queries be used to guide an adaptation in multigoal reinforcement learning scenarios. Our research reveals that application of regional queries can result in improved on-the-fly goal switching compared to unconditional sampling of the same dataset. As a result, we anticipate that the theoretical connection between query-based computation and AI fundamental principles will lead to further breakthroughs in AI research. Our second significant breakthrough reveals the hidden potential of triangular matrices with specific eigenvalues to accelerate the exact computation of optimal transport. By taking advantage of a novel, rapidly computable formula for the stochastic matrix's entries, we develop a pioneering, time-efficient method that computes optimal transport while maintaining precise pairwise distances. This innovative technique enables the computation of optimal transport in $O(n)$ time and $O(n j^2)$ space, showcasing substantial improvements over existing algorithms. Furthermore, we derive the derived linear time formula for the term involving the vector $j$, closing a long-standing gap in the literature and resolving a question initially posed by Chakrabarti in 1981. The discovered properties of collinear triangular matrices also find additional applications in the domains of multivariate statistics and graph theory. The developed code is made publicly available on GitHub, featuring the function 'phi_Q22' and demo files. We have successfully captured the various physical mechanisms driving charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting terminal using radio-frequency sensing of the quantum dot's gate. Our results show that in addition to conventional Coulomb blockade, the data exhibits unexpected crossover behavior and three distinct crossover transitions. Through in-depth analysis, the distinct tunneling mechanisms driving these transitions have been pinpointed, incorporating the influence of environmental spin and Majorana modes. Furthermore, our research marks the first instance where radio-frequency sensing of the quantum dot's gate has directly detected crossover behavior and identified charge tunneling mechanisms in the context of superconductivity. Our findings are expected to facilitate the clear identification of charge tunneling mechanisms in future hybrid devices, encompassing topological or unconventional superconducting quantum circuits. The radio-frequency sensing technique could be particularly valuable for detecting charge signals in systems lacking well-defined charge states, such as Majorana or topological qubit signals. The technique may also be applied to other quantum control systems, potentially enabling the direct measurement of their local magnetic fields. The study's innovative technique is set to be a crucial contributor to the development of topological quantum computers. The research further delves into the quantum noise affecting the quantum dot's electrical signal and reveals the distinct characteristics of the two tunneling mechanisms via spectroscopic analysis. Our ability to distinguish between these two behaviors and identify their underlying causes serves as a model for interpreting quantum behavior in hybrid devices, a crucial skill in the field of quantum computing. The study's experimental data and the underlying analysis provide valuable insights and theories for the quantum scanning community, particularly in the context of superconducting quantum circuits. The research could potentially be expanded to the broader quantum scanning of hybrid devices, enabling the global understanding of quantum mechanics that is a primary goal of the quantum computing community. The technique is set to be a key tool in the development of quantum computers, allowing for the direct observation of quantum mechanics in complex systems, a requirement for quantum computer development. The study is consistent with established theories and contributes to the development of quantum computing by expanding the available techniques into the superconducting quantum computing sector. The associated data is available through the NIST Science Data Repository for the benefit of the quantum computing community. The technique has potential for growth in the quantum computing and quantum information field, utilizing sensing to measure quantum mechanics in new and unseen ways. Research on the contractor of entropic discontinuities in conservation law frameworks is presented in this paper. Through in-depth analysis, existence and standards of entropic discontinuities in the framework of weakly continuous solutions for conservation laws with multiple components were demonstrated. A unique standard of entropic discontinuities at vanishing discontinuity levels was established, utilising a carefully designed contraction technique on the L1 space. This innovative approach has broadened applications to diverse conservation law systems, encompassing partial differential equations, scalar conservation laws, compressible Euler equations, and others. Furthermore, existence theorems for entropic shocks and vanishing discontinuities were proven without employing small initial data constraints. Lastly, theoretical findings were validated with numerical examples in various frameworks. Here, existence of entropic shocks in scalar conservation laws was numerically demonstrated from the initial conditions featuring a single singularity, rather than requiring the necessity of smooth initial data. Additionally, numerical examples of vanishing discontinuities in the Euler equations for a polytropic gas, featuring a diverse range of Eulertypes and initial data, were presented and demonstrated to converge to the corresponding exact entropic shock states at vanishing discontinuity levels. At present, the method of obtaining standard entropic shocks at vanishing discontinuity levels is unparalleled in the existing literature. Moreover, existence theorems for vanishing discontinuities were proven without employing the constraint of small initial data, thereby expanding the existing standards in conservation law research to various systems, (Mihaila-Vinnikov, 2014, Wang-Yu, 2019). We introduce a novel task known as chronic vision generation, which involves extending a limited sequence of images into an infinite progression, while maintaining consistency in the individual frames and overall dynamics. To achieve this, we develop a model, the DiffDreamer, based on a conditional diffusion model, where the model's conditioning signal is comprised of both the previous image and a temporal representation extracted from the sequence of inputs. The DiffDreamer learns to generate synthetic, plausibly authentic images by leveraging its internal temporal representation of the sequence, allowing it to capture and accurately model the inherent long-term patterns present in the training data. As a result, the DiffDreamer demonstrates exceptional spatial and temporal coherence in its generated images, while also approximating state-of-the-art performance in single-view chronic vision generation. The efficacy of the DiffDreamer is further demonstrated through both subjective and objective human vision tests. The implementation of the DiffDreamer can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/Ashe1996/Conditional_Diffusion_Model_for_CV. Additionally, a user-friendly web interface for interacting with the DiffDreamer is provided at http://diffdreamer.com. Through the integration of the DiffDreamer and a user interface, we enable the creation of realistic synthetic images, while also exploring its potential applications in image manipulation, specifically instance segmentation and object removal. Importantly, the generated images produced by the DiffDreamer can be used as high-quality training data for a variety of down-stream vision tasks, while also potentially being exploited in image editing applications such as automatic removal of obtrusive objects or people. Moreover, the DiffDreamer demonstrates a unique capacity for realistic image synthesis in scenarios involving extreme zooms and exposure variations, thereby surpassing prior state-of-the-art models. Ultimately, the generated images produced by the DiffDreamer exhibit a level of spatial and temporal coherence comparable to that of the recently developed Imaganeration model, while differing in that the former is based on a more realistic assumption involving a fixed, single-view perspective. Subsequent work has involved extending the DiffDreamer to enable the generation of multi-view sequences in a newly published paper, while a complementary research study has concentrated on developing a model for multi-view sequence generation. Currently, additional investigations led by the research group are focused on expanding the capabilities of the DiffDreamer to enable the detection and removal of unwanted entities in multi-view sequences. The purpose of this study was to assess the reliability of using robotic ultrasound scanning assistance for evaluating scoliosis, compared to traditional manual scanning techniques. Two physical therapists with limited experience in spinal ultrasound were randomly assigned to either perform ultrasound scans manually or utilize a robotic scanning assistance. Scoliosis was simulated by placing a flexible rod under a participant's back. Ultrasound images were taken from five key spinal levels and the degrees of curvature were measured using the Cobb angle method. Results showed that both manual and robotic scanning groups demonstrated high reliability, with the robotic scanning assistance group exhibiting reliability similar to the manual scanning group. This novel application of robotic scanning assistance was well-received by the therapists, offering a potential non-radiological method for scoliosis detection and allowing for real-time measurements of spinal deformities. It has potential for use in various fields such as physical therapy, sports medicine, and orthopedic surgery. Further research is needed to explore its clinical applications and potential pitfalls. This research proposes a novel, length-driven approach to artificial speech generation,
where task implementation is straightforward within existing statistical speech synthesis
techniques. We've identified three key challenges associated with the length-constrained
task: finding an acceptable median point, constructing the length space, and determining
neighborship. Our proposed algorithm addresses these issues, utilizing a median-driven
approach to navigate the length space and establish neighboring references. We've tested
this method and found that length variability is reduced, yet nearly all produced utterances
exhibit distinct lengths. Furthermore, listener comprehension of this approach exceeds that of
existing reduced-fidelity datasets. We've also demonstrated that the generated data meets
the essential characteristics of synthetic datasets, including balanced length and gap
distribution and random word/phrase exchange. Our results indicate that the proposed
algorithm is a feasible length-driven artificial speech generation method. Its implementation
is presented in an open-source Jupyter notebook for public use, and data collected from
human subjects can be accessed through our website. The research aims to enhance the end-
user experience in length-driven artificial speech generation. A paper supporting this
research is available on arXiv. Please contact us at share@csuchico.edu for further details.

The prevalence of hate speech on social media transpires to inflict grave harm on individuals, including mental health issues, as exemplified by hate-based attacks against a user named Jessica Benners. Our study highlights the critical role of characteristic extraction in text classification tasks. To illustrate this concept, we present a novel approach to classifying hate speech, which utilizes a supervised method with a trained neural network. Our results indicate that character-based models are well-suited to overcome data scarcity issues. We analyzed a 10% sample of 1.6 million Twitter posts, achieving a 77.2% accuracy in predicting the network's classification of the full dataset. Moreover, our approach demonstrated a 53.1% accuracy in identifying hate speech through a reverse prediction process. Our study contributes to the hate speech detection task by providing new benchmarks for the Twitter HATE17 dataset of 20,419 labeled posts, as well as the IMDB dataset of 28,601 WASHINGTON datasets. Our approach's efficacy has also been validated in less resource-intensive settings, such as low-end GPUs and mobile devices. The research demonstrates the capacity of characteristic extraction models to overcome the inherent complexities of text classification tasks. The current model represents one of the most advanced characteristic extraction models, having surpassed the state-of-the-art models in hate speech detection tasks. The study aims to inspire researchers to explore text classification methods based on characteristic extraction, as well as make the model accessible for practical applications through a deployed Web API. Multi-input multi-output neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, yet their internal workings - where multiple parallel pathways in the output layer calculate tasks based on shared input and parameters - raise a critical question: What exactly is being shared? This paper argues that in most current applications of MIMO networks, features are being shared, rather than parameters, and provides the first systematic analysis of how feature sharing impacts learning and application performance. In an effort to optimize feature sharing in MIMO networks for task multiple instances, the authors introduce a novel MIMO architecture called Shared-MIMO, and compare its effectiveness to conventional MIMO networks through extensive experiments conducted on multiple datasets. Results indicate that Shared-MIMO outperforms the conventional version and delivers comparable performance to the best available models for task instances, and also improves inference efficiency by reducing model size and computations by 50%. Moreover, Shared-MIMO's benefits extend to model transfer learning, with accelerated learning rates for new tasks and enhanced generalization. This representation change is data-independent and requires zero pre-training, making it a practical solution for the growing multi-task challenge. Deciphering undeciphered historical languages is a persistently challenging task for researchers. One innovative approach to this challenge is the application of machine learning algorithms to analyze and interpret undeciphered inscriptions in low-resolution bitmap images. However, the success of this approach relies heavily on the accumulation of substantial datasets containing both the inscriptions and their corresponding translations. This paper aims to consolidate a comprehensive collection of publicly accessible datasets that have been utilized in similar research endeavors. A detailed description of each dataset, encompassing its characteristics and data origin, as well as the corresponding benchmark task and evaluation metrics, is provided. Additionally, the paper identifies shortcomings within existing datasets and proposes necessary improvements through the design of a standardized format for optimal data exchange. A comparative analysis of the datasets is also included to highlight both their similarities and differences, followed by possible paths for future expansion and development. Ultimately, this paper serves as a reference point for researchers tackling the intricate issue of deciphering historical languages. Dataset repositories and associated codes are accessible via the links https://github.com/Pointedhead/HRI_Datasets and https://github.com/Pointedhead/HRI_Code. These links also contain experimental outcomes from our studies, along with the codes employed in the research. In the proposed solution, a mathematical model describes the position movement, incorporating both the primary and additional encoder measurements. An optimized control strategy is then designed, using only incremental measurements from the encoders, but not requiring any calibration with the position sensors. The algorithm induces a smoothness constraint on the movement velocity, ensuring that at the end of the movement, the position error is corrected. The effectiveness of this method was tested in a numerical simulation and a real-world experiment, demonstrating improved position accuracy, specifically with regards to reaching the target position and drawing straight lines. The results showed that this method surpasses traditional PID control. Overall, this method provides a cost-effective, straightforward solution for enhancing the position accuracy of industrial robots with position measurement only from the encoders. Traditional statistical models are inadequate in capturing the intricate relationships between these conditions, particularly how they impact individuals' future health trajectories. A new mathematical framework attempts to address this gap by providing a unified approach to studying multiple event histories in relation to a person's overall health path. This framework is applied to data on patients who had a heart attack between 2003 and 2008 to examine how the progression of their diseases affected their ultimate health outcomes after ten years. To facilitate this analysis, a new statistical model is developed to describe the relationships between the diseases and a person's health status over time. Additionally, a new method of estimating these relationships is proposed, which takes into account the unique progression of each individual's diseases. Results from modeling and estimation indicate that certain factors such as age, sex, and whether the individual smoked or had a high blood pressure, are significantly correlated with the diseases' progression. Moreover, a person's health status in the past is strongly linked to their future health trajectory, and that long-term health outcomes can be accurately forecasted based on this information. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the utility of the new framework and its potential in informing clinical decisions, particularly in identifying target groups for preventive measures and promoting early detection of complications when they are still manageable. A practical implementation of the proposed method is also presented with a view to informing clinical interventions. The application of the new approach highlights its capacity to break new ground in research on the interconnectedness of health conditions and how they shape a person's overall life course health path. The study data used for analysis in the paper are drawn from the Spanish National Health System, providing a comprehensive insight into the interplay between heart attacks, other cardiovascular events, and lab results over a person's lifetime. To facilitate replication of the findings presented in the study, the related data and a detailed methodology of the proposed method's implementation has been made publicly available for future reference. The study's results are the first to demonstrate the link between a person's earlier health states and their long-term health status in a homogeneous population, providing key information for healthcare planners to guide decision-making. A novel numerical technique, the Multi-Site Quadrature Method (MSQ), has been developed to solve the Schrödinger equation for a molecule. This approach employs a finite element discretization on a grid with an adapted mesh size, coupled with a weighted non-uniform quadrature formula accounting for near-neighbor interactions. Analyzing the method's convergence, we found that the error decreases at a rate of $O(h^2)$ in the $l^2$ norm and $O(h^2)$ in the weighted $l^2$ norm, where $h$ is the grid spacing. Additionally, we validated the method by computing eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the hydrogen molecule ion and the water molecule. Comparing our results to established methods, we found that the MSQ method offers a reliable alternative due to its simple implementation and efficient computation. However, we observed that the method's error is slightly higher than the theoretical estimate. Therefore, to improve the method's accuracy, we proposed a post-processing procedure, which can achieve a maximum error of $O(h^2)$. Implementing this process with a refined mesh, we were able to reduce the error to the specified limit. This study's contributions are threefold: Firstly, we introduced a new method for approximating molecular eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Secondly, I compared it to existing techniques such as the Finite Element Method and the Quadrature Finite Element Method and discovered that it produces results with fewer errors. Thirdly, I proposed a strategy using a relatively simple procedure to further reduce the method's initial error, which in turn makes the method even more accurate. As a result, the MSQ method has been proven to be a viable option for computing molecular eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in the future. Furthermore, due to its stability, the method can easily be extended to more complex problems such as solving partial differential equations describing interacting systems within external fields. This research has significant potential for applying theoretical methods from mathematics to solve practical problems in science and engineering. Specifically, the method can be utilized not only for modeling molecular interactions but also for computing eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of much more complicated systems such as the Helium-4 molecule and the Diatomic molecule, thereby pushing the theoretical methods further into more complex problems in science and engineering. A substantial body of evidence exists to support the usefulness of timed definition in
developing real-time software as seen in numerous academic and industrial projects. 
The basic usage and enhancements of timed definition in HOL are discussed, along
with an investigation into potential drawbacks including difficulty in understanding,
inefficiency in computation, and potential conflicts with type checking. 
Furthermore, we highlight how timed definition in HOL can facilitate the
implementation of advanced techniques such as real-time synthesis and timed model checking. 
Ultimately, we offer advice on the most effective approaches to utilizing timed definition in
HOL based on the outcomes of our study. 
An extension of timed definition to support multi-dimensional integer-based timing is
presented along with a practical application in verifying the time-sensitive properties of
scheduler algorithms. 
The utility of timed definition in enabling step-by-step reasoning in time-sensitive systems is
emphasized through a detailed example illustrating its application in validating a system
equipped with a timer that forces periodic activity from its components. 
Through these example use cases, we showcase the practical value of timed definition in the
development of real-time software.

HOL, including its formal definition, fundamental properties, and theoretical justification. 
The code and documentation for timed definition in HOL, including any custom library tools
and configuration, are explicitly presented to facilitate easy adoption by others.

use of timed definition in HOL.

Recommendations for future research are provided at the conclusion of this study.

Mechanical screening within granular matter results in an accelerated exchange of momentum between particles due to external forces, leading to a phenomenon where particles respond in a manner typically associated with solid matter rather than typical granular behavior. This unusual screening effect is attributed to the external driving force, which in previously studied cases, was shown to result in novel mechanical responses and potentially unprecedented screening behaviors. Nonetheless, all existing research on this screening effect has been focused on systems with a relatively simple structure and a limited range of external excitations. The present study investigates a more intricate model of granular material, specifically a hexagonal lattice of particles subjected to periodic pumping, preserving the material's overall volume. Initial experiments were conducted to observe the system's stress responses over multiple periods of pumping. The resulting data revealed distinct periodic and quasi-periodic patterns in stress responses. To grasp the underlying screening dynamics, researchers employed force-coupling method-based simulations, while incorporating the effects of inherent noise that arises in real-world granular systems. The results of simulations successfully replicated the observed stress responses from experiments and revealed that accelerated screening is linked to the complex interactions between particles and the system's chaotic dynamics that emerge at a specific threshold of pumping amplitude. Furthermore, researchers found that stress responses exhibit a characteristic characteristic characteristic time that corresponds to the period of pumping; this specific time frame dictates when screening effect and stress responses reach a steady state. These study's results validate the anomalous screening theory and provide quantitative connections between pumping amplitude and characteristic screening times. The present work's findings also underscore the crucial impact of lattice geometry on screening dynamics, implying that certain material structures may impede the screening effect. Ultimately, researchers propose that granular materials exhibiting intricate stress responses and associated anomalous screening dynamics may serve as novel forms of non-equilibrium fluids, characterized by complex and variable properties that can be adjusted via external driving forces. These study's results may potentially open up a new research area at the intersection of and materials science, inspiring a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between mechanical forces, material structure, and screening dynamics. Recent breakthroughs in growing hexagonal boron nitride films have provided an ideal platform for supporting two-dimensional materials. This research examines the electronic properties of a single layer of silicene decorated with manganese in the presence of a boron nitride substrate. Through self-consistent density functional theory, our findings reveal that the manganese atom experiences a significant environmental shift in its electronic levels when in contact with the substrate and phosphorus dopants. Notably, the presence of these dopants triggers distinct unpaired electronic states in manganese, and our results also indicate that silicene and manganese states are coupled with a boron nitride substrate. Furthermore, our data highlight that manganese's electronic properties are heavily influenced by its position within the substrate and highlight the inherent ferromagnetic nature of systems containing this element. Overall, our findings suggest that manganese-adorned silicene exhibits ferromagnetic properties on a boron nitride substrate. In contrast, the presence of dopants has a substantial effect on system interactions, and our data show that systems containing manganese and phosphorus exhibit antiferromagnetic properties. In stark contrast, the system lacking this element exhibits a lack of magnetic properties. The need for data classification is widespread, with text categorization being a prominent example.  The imbalanced nature of many such datasets has long been a subject of research, particularly regarding the application of oversampling methods.  While previous studies such as Szummer and Skumeika (2005) focused onoversampling in the context of two-class systems, we investigate its application in multi-class text categorization.  In doing so, we compare the effectiveness of artificial examples created through different methods - including selection, modification, and duplication - as well as the techniques for integrating these examples into the training dataset.  Our research demonstrates that artificial examples must be carefully tailored not only to the majority class but also to the specific characteristics of the datasets in question.  Ultimately, we recommend a novel method for generating and incorporating these examples, and our findings show that this approach surpasses current methodologies in terms of accuracy and complementarity.  Our results were obtained through experiments using various classification algorithms, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of the impact of oversampling in multi-class text categorization. The Rapid Multipole Method effectively simulates the long-term effects of many N-body interactions in a compact, time-efficient manner. However, there has been limited clarification on how this approximation affects the preservation of key physical properties, such as energy and angular momentum, especially in situations involving non-axisymmetric, rapid-rotation systems. Our study introduces a sequence of strong and weak multipole corrections that consistently conserve energy and angular momentum in such complex systems, with a particular focus on the conservation of angular momentum by our method. Our results are verified through direct comparisons with exact N-body simulations of a few crucial tests: stabilizing planetary orbits around a rotating star, solving the Provenzale problem, and modeling a rapidly rotating, non-symmetrical galaxy. In these scenarios, the time it takes for the energy or angular momentum to deviate from their initial values by a factor of 10 is measured and compared with the corresponding values obtained by the methods of Laskar and CERES, as well as with the energy preservation capabilities of the symplectic integrator used in the ALEHELE project. Our new algorithm demonstrates its ability to provide accurate results with minimal computational overhead, and its code will be made open-source for the benefit of the N-body dynamics research community. Specifically, the integration time for the non-axisymmetric, rapidly-rotating galaxy model is measured as 38 million years with our method versus a mere 229 years by the ALEHELE project, yet at a computational cost that is only 2.5 times greater. This exceptional performance underscores the open-source Rapid Multipole code's suitability for a wide range of applications in astrophysics and orbital mechanics. Furthermore, the insight gained from this research indicates that there is likely no general algorithm that can simultaneously preserve energy and angular momentum when these quantities are initially conserved, and that the preservation of angular momentum by the Rapid Multipole method, and similarly by the methods of Laskar and CERES, should be considered a remarkable outcome rather than an expected one. With a few minor adjustments, the methods analyzed in this study could collectively achieve an overall error that is orders of magnitude lower than what was previously considered acceptable in the N-body dynamics community, and this breakthrough has the potential to significantly impact a broad range of scientific fields from astro dynamics and planetary science to stellar astrophysics and star cluster dynamics. Ultimately, the findings of this study are a testament to how accurately and efficiently the Rapid Multipole method can capture the intricacies of complex, high-dimensional Hamiltonian systems.

Our research focuses on finding an optimal decision tree to make accurate predictions on a target dataset Z, based on a trained neural network's output. This network was previously fed classified training data X, along with corresponding labels Y, processed through an information-enhancing step. A subsequent optimization procedure calculates the neural network's output for each possible decision tree, and a loss function is minimized to find the best fit. In this way, the value of sigma in a signal enhancement process plays a crucial role in achieving accurate predictions on the target dataset Z. By analyzing the distribution of sigma's optimized parameter h_0, we find that a larger sigma leads to a more well-defined peak at the mean value. Consequently, a higher sigma enables the system to achieve lower generalization errors near the mean, while pushing predictions for Z away from the mean. By comparing Gaussian and Laplace distributions for sigma, we find that the Laplace distribution yields better results and proposes a semi-supervised approach to obtain a larger sigma. Finally, our theoretical findings are verified through experiments using generated and real datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/kim-hyegwang/data_amplification. This research aims to examine the application of artificial neural networks in identifying hate-speech from complex linguistic patterns, specifically focusing on languages such as Hindi and Bengali. We observe that previous studies on hate-speech classification predominantly centered on English, leaving other major languages underrepresented in the field. Our investigation seeks to address this disparity by analyzing hate-speech in two prominent South Asian languages using a similar approach. We initially applies a sequence-labeling technique, hidden Markov models, to the task, followed by a comparison with a transfer learning method utilizing a pre-trained recurrent neural network. Our analysis extends to an evaluation of the intercoder agreement between human assessors, as well as a sensitivity study involving the impact of training data size on hate-speech classification performance. Ultimately, we compare our findings with those of other relevant studies. The research is available in its entirety, complete with code and data, at https://github.com/aararirar/Hate-Speech-Identification. Our results indicate a significant 8% difference in performance between the two languages, with a Hindi model exhibiting the greater accuracy. Our work highlights how neural networks can effectively identify hate-speech in less commonly studied languages, driven by an increasing need to address this issue online in order to mitigate its harm. Additionally, our research demonstrates the value of a transfer learning approach, especially in cases where limited data is available for model training. Lastly, our work underscores the importance of incorporating a measure of intercoder agreement between human assessors into the evaluation of hate-speech identification models, especially in cases where the data itself is not publicly accessible. Relevant APIs were utilized in data collection, authorized for non-commercial use. Our research assumes that the data will not be used to discriminate against individuals or groups. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to detect the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable with time projection chambers (TPCs), offers opportunities for sole detection of nuclear recoils or simultaneous tracking of charged particles generated by weak interactions or dark matter. Nevertheless, identifying directionality with high precision while maintaining low capacities for energy discrimination poses a challenge to conventional TPCs. Our study proposes a new approach that utilizes specialized readout technology to record and analyze low-count, high-resolution TPC data, allowing for the efficient recovery of recoil direction information. This method was applied using data from an electron ionization detector, based on a 1 cm^2 sector of a 300 micron-thick TPC. Our analysis indicates that directionality information with high precision (5.8 mrad residual angle at 1 keV i.e. 175 photon-electron conversion) can be obtained at very low counts (mean 1.5 per readout frame). These high precision angles are achieved at a signal energy corresponding to 1 keV for electrons, which translates to ~ 50 keV for nuclear recoils of mass similar to that of a nucleon. Our findings also suggest that in situations where the rates are much higher, this method could potentially allow for energy discrimination as sharp as 10% at 1 keV. When combined with an understanding of the rates of ionization, this technique provides a means to distinguish between electrons and nuclei, making it potentially suitable for use in detectors such as XENON1T-like xenon detectors that have a significant amount of ionization. Our research offers possibilities for optimizing this method, including reducing the amount of readout noise and utilizing data from multiple projection directions. These possibilities could result in substantial gains in precision, potentially reaching the level required for the direct detection of dark matter. Our study delves into the underlying physics of recoil identification and provides quantitative assessments of precision that can be achieved based on counts rate and energy. These calculations, in conjunction with the experimental findings, delves into the factors that influence the capacity of direct detection to identify directionality. This new detection approach at low counts offers the potential to significantly expand the possibilities for detecting directional direct dark matter signals, and could be applied more broadly in fields such as nuclear and particle physics. In commercial vehicle operations, effective driving behaviors are crucial for delivering superior customer service and reducing costs. Various companies use driving scorecards to measure quality of service and driving behaviors, with automatic processing of telematics data to produce machine-readable scores. However, scores are often unreliable and may bias certain drivers. To address these issues, we propose a new approach: expert oversight of commercial driving scores. An algorithm is first generated using telematics data and then reviewed by experts, with adjustments made as needed. To complicate things, we don't have access to pure expert scores, just their thoughts on the original scores and individual driving histories. So, we built on previous studies to develop a new supervised learning method. Utilizing a combination of self-supervised methods and operator feedback, our approach significantly improves over previous results in fixed-time score evaluation. Moreover, our approach also achieves a more fair and through evaluation in commercial driving metrics by considering multiple scoring objectives and using expert feedback to refine diverse model outputs. Through experimentation, we showed that our approach accurately predicts expert scores and improves upon the reliability and fairness of traditional evaluation methods. To promote broader societal and environmental benefits, we also believe that effective driving behaviors lead to reduced emissions and improved air quality. Therefore, we are making our code available in order to facilitate replicating our study in other domains where machine and expert collaboration is crucial for making informed decisions. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates that effective collaboration between machines and experts leads to enhanced model evaluation and driving behaviors. Thus, our research advances the study of human-machine collaboration in order to generate useful automated decision-making systems for a variety of applications. In the event of a lack of solutions, the algorithm either converges towards a measure that diverges from the initial conditions or stagnates indefinitely. This study explores the dynamic behavior of the Sinkhorn algorithm when the Schrodinger equation has no solution, primarily for distance coupling. It demonstrates that the algorithm either converges towards a distinct, stationary distribution or oscillates indefinitely. This research provides mathematical proofs as well as illustrative real-world examples that underpin the theoretical findings. Furthermore, the examples highlight the importance of initial conditions in determining the algorithm's course of convergence. To complement the theoretical analysis, the accompanying code is provided for reproducibility of the results presented. Despite its efficiency, the algorithm's capacity to handle critical circumstances such as bistability or the lack of solutions poses significant hurdles, particularly when dealing with complex data. The distinct characteristics of localization in an interaction-ramped Fermi gas with an intermediate spin value of $s=1$ are examined through exact mathematical analysis for both the $s=1$ spin and charge degrees of freedom. It is discovered that the critical interaction beyond which localization occurs is lower for spin localization than for charge localization. An underlying reason for this distinction is found to be the differing nature of spin and charge imbalances in the system. When spin imbalances are relatively small, multiple particle-hole pair excitations result in the loss of spin coherence, whereas when interactions are substantial, total spin imbalances cause complete spin polarization, leading to the loss of spin coherence. In contrast, charge localization is determined by critical interactions that result in the loss of spatial coherence of the particles as a whole. Notably, this disparity emerged at the lower end of the income spectrum, suggesting that individuals with lower incomes were more affected by the pandemic than those with higher incomes. Furthermore, our study indicates that the pandemic disrupted the spatial patterns of human behavior, with individuals who lost their social connections to other people during the pandemic (such as service sector workers) experiencing a more significant shift in their interaction patterns than those who did not (such as university professors). Overall, our analysis suggests that the pandemic exacerbated income disparity and that understanding human behavior through complex networks is essential for addressing societal challenges like the current pandemic. The findings presented here could inform research on the social and economic impacts of the pandemic and provide a basis for developing policies to mitigate these impacts. A novel preconditioning technique for Navier-Stokes equations in complex two-phase flow situations has been developed to expedite finite volume-based Newton iterations when dealing with uneven porous media. This approach, known as Field-Split Preconditioning, simultaneously solves for conservative equations related to each phase and their interaction, presenting multiple preconditioning matrices to achieve consistency between equations. Although the original method succeeds in achieving optimal performance with a high-condition number, it fails to account for discrepancies in the permeability of the porous material, resulting in divergent iterations in extreme cases. To address this limitation, a modified approach, called Nonlinear Field-Split Preconditioning, uses a sequence of linear rather than nonlinear solves for each field, achieving significant improvement in cases with substantial differences in permeability, with an even further enhanced variant incorporating an additional compression step. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of this advanced technique in reducing the total time of computation and decreasing the total number of linear iterations in realistic scenarios. Moreover, NFSP has been found to maintain the stability that is characteristic of the original method, despite its modification, with an added benefit of decreased total compression time. This method has been made accessible through the open-source library, OpenSIFL. Research has been focused on the technique's performance in scenarios based on realistic data, including cases with substantial disparities in permeability and spatially varying velocity. Results indicate that this method holds promise for expanding its application to a broader range of complex problems in the study of two-phase flow. As robots increasingly share the space with humans, the possibility of a physical collision between them becomes a pressing safety concern. To avoid accidents, these agents must be able to convey their intentions to each other, allowing them to cooperate and stay safe in shared environments. In order to examine the way humans and robotic colleagues communicate to avoid collisions, we designed a task where humans and robots work together to move objects into defined zones, and these interactions are replicated outside of a controlled environment setting. Our study found that, in the absence of explicit instruction, human-robot collaborations tend to adopt a standardised structure that reflects the robot's ability to convey its intentions through predictable and consistent behaviour. Furthermore, when this behavior is nuanced and influenced by various factors such as the available path and the proximity of other objects, humans are more likely to intervene and take control, indicating an ability to share autonomy on a collaborative task. Observations from our experiments revealed that, in response to a potential collision, humans who shared the environment with the robot tended to anticipate the robot's intentions based on the observed patterns of action leading up to the incident, rather than relying solely on explicit safety measures like collision detection. These findings have significant implications for the way robotic systems and their human counterparts convey intentions and anticipate each other's actions in shared environments. They also emphasize the importance of understanding the role of attention and variability in communication between cooperative agents, and highlight the significance of developing systems that can convey their intentions through multiple channels of information. Lastly, our study offers valuable insights into the design of cooperative tasks and environments that are tailored to the capabilities of multiple agents and highlight the benefits of shared autonomy in facilitating efficient and safe goal-oriented behaviour. Given that conventional regularization methods often fail to accurately model low-rank structural patterns in polyenergetic CT, we introduce a novel weighted Poisson model with rank-constrained priors for both bright and dark data. By converting the model into its variational form with various penalty parameters, and employing an alternating minimization algorithm with a novel data-independent smoothing technique, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our algorithm's convergence is substantiated through theoretical analysis, and its practical applicability is validated by both numerical simulations and real-world experiments. Furthermore, our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of performance, as shown in the experimental results. Specifically, our method enhances image quality by reducing artifacts and noise to a greater extent than previous approaches, particularly in regions with material boundaries, artifactual regions, and noisy areas. Additionally, our method accurately decomposes materials into their physical characteristics. Finally, the source code of our method is provided for research purposes. Software development begins with clear goals: developers describe what the software needs to do and then design it to behave that way. Unfortunately, crucial specifications often get lost or, if recorded, are inaccessible for later use. This paper demonstrates how specifications can be automatically extracted from non-structured text and then cross-checked against the actual software behavior, highlighting any discrepancies between what is coded and what is intended. We showcase our method's effectiveness on two large projects and highlight promising areas for future improvement. Our research aims to resolve a major challenge in software engineering: helping developers and maintainers align their expectations and what the software genuinely implements. This effort is facilitated through the SpecUse project (specuse.com). We use natural language processing and fine-grained semantic analysis to collect and structure software requirements, accompanied by a novel visualisation tool to compare them with code. We have developed a unique metric to assess text similarity and quality, and demonstrated its applicability across various domains. Our current implementation employs static analysis to identify differences between specified and actual behavior, and we plan to adapt dynamic analysis for just-in-time applications. Successful experiments on over 200 projects validate our approach and open up further opportunities for innovation. We intend to release our software under an open-source license to empower users to try it out and provide valuable feedback. Additionally, we have established a GitHub repository for the SpecUse project, where you can find related content and collaborate with us and others. You can also access videos illustrating our results and leverage the software using our easy-to-use interfaced at specuse.com. Our work has generated significant interest from the software engineering community, and multiple universities, industry leaders (e.g. Microsoft, Google), and researchers have expressed interest in integrating SpecUse into their tools. One such example is our integration with the Copernicus tool, developed by the University of Novi Sad. We're also exploring a partnership with a prominent Italian IT company to complement their existing tools with SpecUse. Following an initial meeting with Leanpub, the leading publisher of software-related books and documentation, we're discussing a partnership to incorporate SpecUse within their platform. Finally, the SpecUse project has received a non-profit grant from the Google Summer of Code program, enabling us to develop the project further. Our vision for the future is to enhance SpecUse to become a one-stop tool for software developers, engineers, and researchers, helping them streamline their workflows and find relevant software for various tasks. A comprehensive mathematical framework for the electronic structure of magnetic impurities integrated within a density functional theory (DFT) description of host materials has been developed for systems governed by the Dirac equation. This model distinguishes between two types of electronic states, including localized magnetic impurity states (Yamada--Shiba--Rusinov states) and host--impurity hybrid states. Utilizing an relativistic, spin--orbit compatible implementation of DFT, this framework evaluated the unpaired electronic states of a single Mn atom and Mn heteroatoms attached to the Nb(110) surface. Results indicate strong magnetic exchange effects between these atoms at near room temperature. Moreover, this framework's findings for Mn heteroatoms are in line with experimental data and recent DFT computations with non-relativistic methods. This new model is considered versatile and can be applied to various magnetic atoms or dimers attached to metals with a body--like (100) surface orientation. This model is available as an open--source, Python--based code called 'YSR--DFT'. The openness of this framework encourages users to extend its capabilities to accommodate novel initial principles or physical phenomena to analyze their impact on calculations. Furthermore, YSR--DFT source code can be utilized to investigate various magnetic impurities attached to the surface of metals with a body--like (111) surface orientation by simply modifying the computational lattice basis without requiring new code. This flexibility in YSR--DFT can lead to diverse applications such as investigations of Kondo hole formation, magnetic impurity state splitting driven by spin--orbit coupling, magnetic exchange effects between impurities, and visible magnetic ordering between impurities on the surface of metals through first--principles calculations. These findings can be further validated or refuted by performing experiments such as low--temperature quantum tunneling spectroscopy with scanning tunneling microscopy. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of a combination of DFT and Yamada--Shiba--Rusinov theory in describing the electronic structure of magnetic impurities attached to metals, which is particularly valuable for systems with significant spin--orbit coupling. YSR--DFT represents a significant advancement over existing DFT computations of Yamada--Shiba--Rusinov states by incorporating spin--orbit coupling through a reliable, systematic, and comprehensive mathematical framework. Recent research has focused on improving pose estimation accuracy, but concerns about prejudice against underrepresented data remain largely unaddressed. This issue is particularly critical in robot mapping and slam as errors can have catastrophic consequences. In our study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of using deep learning-based filters to remove prejudice from data generated by robot motion simulations. Simulation results show that a well-trained neural network filter can substantially mitigate prejudice in individual distribution models, but achieving this requires training the filter on diverse data, including the robot's field of view. Furthermore, we found that using a filter trained on simulated data does not guarantee prejudice reduction in real-world distributed datasets. This contradiction highlights the need for further research on prejudice mitigation in distributed systems. Ultimately, we recommend incorporating a dataset filter to remove prejudice and make significant improvements to resulting distribution-to-distribution systems. We derive a large N limit formula for the radial distance-dependent thermal entropy of a 2d scalar field, applicable to any interaction strength, within a spatially-finite box, using random matrix theory. We apply the Gopakumar-SR formula to the double-scaled target CFT, then computes the adjacent Minkowski CFT's radial thermal entropy using the previously established Knafelbach-SEM formula. We demonstrate that the thermal and entanglement entropies converge at large N, and that their ratios do not depend on the interaction, verifying large N limit agreements between the two theories. This research marks the first time the Knafelbach-SEM formula has been applied to non-hermitian CFTs, and it sheds light on the underlying physical cause of the previously-observed equivalence between entanglement and thermal entropies in large N limit, which holds true for holomorphic QFTs but had a notable exception in the case of non-holomorphic QFT. We also outline open problems and potential future works in this area. The research reveals that the large N limit of the radial thermal entropy can be used to test the underlying thermofield double state description of CFTs, and it provides experimental criteria to verify the proposed Knafelbach-SEM formula. Additionally, the study indicates that the large N limit of the radial thermal entropy can be applied torenormalization group flows, and it provides criteria for validating the approximation that the CFT stress tensor corresponds to a semi-classical description of the Klein-Gordon field. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal representations for both text and video modalities increasing representation accuracy. Current state-of-the-art methods have made significant progress by employing pre-trained transformer models to aggregate complex features from diverse time and spatial dimensions. Nevertheless, these approaches face challenges in handling 3D pre-trained models, and also, the uniform aggregation of features from different temporal or spatial dimensions may mix up confusing information. To address these limitations, we introduce TS$^2$-Net, a lightweight neural architecture composed of multiple alternating layers of token movement and selection and cross-attention blocks. The token shifting operation dynamically aggregates features from different temporal dimensions into a single temporal dimension, whereas the token selection component aggregates features from diverse spatial-temporal positions into a single semantic space. Furthermore, we propose an innovative training method for enhancing our framework's cross-attention block, using a dynamically selected sample from the video and text pools for each video-text instance during backpropagation. In this paper, we explore the concept of graph degradation within the context of Cayley graphs and hypercubes. A graph degradation, conceptualized by Alberts, Hopfield, and Sulewski, is a transformation that maps stronger connections to weaker ones. We prove that any graph degradations on finite hypercubes are automorphically similar to standard hypercube mutations. Moreover, we demonstrate that graph degradations with a finite group of order 'n' as its vertex set have an automorphism that preserves the graph structure, thereby making every graph degradation equivalent to its corresponding hypercube mutation. This equivalence also applies to graphs represented by finite abelian groups, leading to the conclusion that all graph degradations are equivalent to mutations, as proven by Bollobas and Sell. Our findings generalize and expand on the outstanding problem proposed by Bollobas and Sell. Additionally, we establish a connection between graph degradation and the basis of a matroid, as well as prove that any graph degradation 'n' possesses a clique covering and independent set properties similar to a standard hypercube mutation 'n'. Furthermore, we present examples that illustrate graph degradation and its associated problems with varying numerical values. The study's key contributions lie in the proof of essential theorems and verification of conjectures regarding graph degradation, particularly in the context of hypercubes and finite abelian groups. Along the way, we also identify unsolved problems for future research. The study is presented in a manner accessible to both graduate students and non-experts in the field, with supplementary materials available for further reading. The primary tool employed in this study is the concept of group actions and automorphisms. The study's mathematical content was verified using the theoretical computer systems Isabelle and Mathematica. The latter's functionality was explored in a related paper titled 'Mathematica: 3-dimensional Linear Group Action Determination.' The study's last page contains an abstract of our associated PhD dissertation, which delves deeper into the topic, along with a related study on hypercubes that employs the fast matrix exponentiation technique. Traditional vector-based neural networks assume signals follow a continuous and smooth pattern, but this is often inefficient when dealing with sparse signals. A sparse signal, with many zeros, poses challenges to network responsiveness and can result in the wrong interpretation by the network. Motivated by applications in computer vision and NLP, we've developed Spartan, a differentiable function that enables the use of zero-filled signals in neural networks. Spartan applies a controllable level of "discomfort" to input values, gradually replacing them with a smooth transition value, such as a Gaussian noise pattern, to form a distinct signal that captures sparseness. This approach introduces an optional regularizer to enhance sparseness retention. Spartan achieves superior performance in tasks including image classification on Graphene, a platform specializing in edge computing for vision tasks. When compared to existing methods, Spartan demonstrates improved performance on various benchmarks, indicating its applicability in promoting sparseness within neural networks. Furthermore, we've published accompanying code at https://github.com/GraphenePlatform/spartan. A live demo is accessible through the Graphene platform at https.//graphene.io/spartan/demo. A related video demonstration can be found at https://youtu.ub/6o7Iu7tUuUk. A pre-trained model generated using Spartan is available for download at https://models.graphene.io/spartan/0.1.0. Spartan has been approved for use in production environments due to its permissive licenses, with combinations of BSD-2 and MIT licenses. Our work highlights the use of Spartan as a "signal enhancer" that can be used in a variety of applications. Unlike existing sparsity methods, Spartan can be combined with existing differentiable functions, allowing it to be easily integrated into existing neural networks. A critical factor contributing to Spartan's success is its "fill value," which must accurately represent the pattern of zeros in the signal. Various experimental findings illustrate the significance of the fill value in achieving sparseness. Additionally, we demonstrate that Spartan's regularizer can be used to improve the structure of task features by applying it to the last batch norm layer of the network. This approach enables the production of more accurate and generalizable features. Finally, we've investigated the use of Spartan in conjunction with existing explanation methods, resulting in substantial improvements to Explanation Performance.
