The study of frustrated quantum transport often reveals valuable insights about
the nature of quantum matter. In this paper, we investigate the influence of
interactions on quantum many-body systems by using the density matrix
representation on a two-dimensional torus lattice. We demonstrate that a weak
interaction in a correlated Bose gas leads to an emergent Pauli obstruction,
which is the origin of a quantum geometric phase captured by the second Chern
number defined by the linear spectrum of edge states. Moreover, we verify that
this phenomenon is also present in a Bose-Mott-Jarlov-Sokal model through both
analytical and numerical calculations. Our results suggest that a similar
mechanism can be applied to various bosonic systems, thus potentially guiding
experimental efforts in directly detecting the emergent Pauli obstruction. It
is estimated that, in a dilute gas with Bose-Einstein condensation, the second
Chern number would be approximately 10^(-10), which poses significant
challenges to detecting this phenomenon through current quantum metrology
methods. Therefore, theoretical validation of this effect in various models
motivates future research on a potential realization in experimental
settings. Additionally, the second Chern number defined by the linear spectrum
of edge states may be useful in differentiating topological phases of non-
topological phases of Bose-Einstein condensation. Finally, the second Chern number
defined by the linear spectrum of edge states may facilitate the replication
of theoretical predictions from topological codes in realistic bosonic systems.

When working on software projects, developers often smell code in their daily routine, either to identify critical issues or to gain better understanding. A recent study discovered that code odours are quite prevalent, with more than half of the surveyed projects experiencing issues related to them. However, the developer community's perspective on these problems seems understudied. To gain insights, a research paper was published in 2020, which aimed to understand the community's perspective on the prevalence and impact of code odours. The researchers conducted a empirical study by creating a Google Forms survey with eight closed-ended questions and three free-text questions, which was disseminated via social media and relevant email lists, garnering 226 valid responses from active open-source developers. The results indicated that nearly 80% of the developers had encountered code odours, with the majority indicating that they found the odours either mildly or moderately annoying. Interestingly, despite the odours' frequency, very few developers attempted to address the issues, with the main obstacles being a lack of clear instructions and the developers' own competence. When asked about the usefulness of specific tools in resolving odour-related problems, the results showed that code reviews, diff tools, and version control were preferred. A follow-up free-text question also provided valuable recommendations from developers on how to effectively deal with code odours. The researchers aimed to make a positive impact by raising awareness and obtaining developer feedback to aid in the development of tools to aid in identifying and resolving code odour-related issues. The researchers aimed to obtain more precise and detailed requirements by actively collaborating with developers to build more useful tools. The final section of the paper discusses how its findings align with relevant theoretical foundations in software engineering. The researchers acknowledge that the surveyed population is likely a minority representation, and they intend to conduct further research in the topic. This work introduces a novel framework, known as the sweeping procedure, to tackle sets that are moved at varying rates, differing from traditional scenarios where rates are constant or naturally dependent on state variables. We establish mathematical proofs for the existence and uniqueness of solutions, along with their stability properties, in a measure-valued solution context. Markov processes and their relation to jump processes are used to derive a significant result showing that local solutions unique to these processes are also unique under Lipschitz conditions. Our study encompasses instances of its application, such as a scenario involving parallel pipes with dynamic set velocities and a model of pedestrian traffic using individual characteristics to define set velocities. Additionally, an illustrative numerical example is provided to validate our theoretical findings. The contributions of this research lie in addressing a long-standing open question regarding the application of the sweeping procedure to Fokker-Planck equations, where previously methods only ensured entropy solutions, but our work presents a counterexample for a specific class of completely dissipative systems, where we demonstrate the existence and stability of classical solutions. Furthermore, our findings have the potential to enhance the analysis of measure-valued solutions in parallel systems and other areas. The work's originality is recognized through the first explicit example of a nonconvex integral-differential sweeping procedure in the context of Lagrangian systems. The text is supplemented by three appendices, covering various complementary results, including an abstract existence theorem for differential inclusions with monotone operators, the application of the sweeping procedure to interpolate Fokker-Planck-Langevin equations with dissipation, and a general property of measure-valued solutions to Lagrangian systems exhibiting dissipation. These results are considered novel and useful in their own right. The work's contribution is best characterized as being part of the theory of measure-valued solutions to Lagrangian systems, with a focus on the development of distinct areas: dissipative integro-differential systems, parallel systems, and Fokker-Planck-Langevin equations with dissipation. The work's primary thread revolves around the application of the sweeping procedure, with the first two examples centered around the integro-differential equation, while the last example focuses on the integro-differential equation itself. The work's originality, with the nonconvex integral-differential sweeping procedure as its centerpiece, differentiates it from other contributions. Evaluating a person's cardiovascular health through electrocardiogram (ECG) readings is an essential part of health monitoring. In particular, determining the time between heartbeats, known as the inter-beat interval (IBI), is significant in diagnosing conditions such as cardiovascular diseases. While machine learning has been successfully used to analyze IBI from ECG signals, existing models have significant room for improvement in terms of accuracy and efficiency. A novel, open-source deep learning model, known as Tiramisu, has recently emerged as a highly effective tool for extracting IBI features from ECG signals. In this research, we modify the Tiramisu model by fine-tuning its architecture and processing parameters to achieve better results on existing cardiovascular datasets. Additionally, we establish a new repository of error-corrected labels to facilitate more accurate model training. By using this updated model with corrected labels, our experiments demonstrate that it outperforms existing approaches with significantly reduced error rates on multiple datasets. Notably, our model achieves top-notch results on the NCAP dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art models by setting a new record with an average classification error rate of $2.04$ from $7.35$. A critical assessment of our model's performance, along with an extensive experimental methodology and source code, has been made available on GitHub to support further research in cardiovascular disease detection. This study has the potential to expand our understanding of machine learning application in cardiovascular health, ultimately leading to the development of more accurate and efficient models. Additionally, we discuss how the general architecture of our model could be applied in other biomedical fields where machine learning has not been widely adopted. Notably, our model's success has inspired similar improvements in a related study that achieved state-of-the-art results in larynx lesion detection. A useful resource that allows users to easily replicate our study is available through a corresponding GitHub repository. A significant breakthrough in tensor decomposition is the multilinear singular value decomposition (mSVD), which is analogous to the singular value decomposition for matrices. This decomposition has numerous applications across various fields including chemistry, physics, and data analysis. Given a third-order tensor, the mSVD involves tensor decompositions that are equivalent to multilinear transformations followed by matrix singular value decompositions. Our research presents PTTTSVD, a non-iterative stochastic method for mSVD that is capable of providing an approximate solution. We provide an algorithm that determines the approximate solution and specify the number of passes required to achieve a target error probability. Additionally, we provide theoretical justifications for the method, discussing why a stochastic approach can be beneficial in mSVD. Finally, we include experimental results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. Although our method does not always produce the exact solution, it offers the advantage of reducing memory usage by utilizing an optional specified number of passes beyond just terminating at an error probability. This allows users to evaluate the trade-off between memory cost and computational time. Our method achieves linear scalability in hardware terms, including the use of cores and bytes, and is proven to be reliable with no occurrence of NaN in our experiments. Moreover, we found that the majority of decompositions happen within the first few passes, thus the method can be viewed as a form of early termination. Our experimental findings also show that the method performs best on sparse and semi-definite tensors. Overall, the method presents an appealing alternative to existing numerical mSVD methods. As an example of its usage, the method can be viewed at https://github.com/akosiak/ptttSVD/tree/v1.0.0-rc.1 (in the 'Usage and Examples' section). To the best of our knowledge, this method for mSVD is an innovative technique and a first of its kind stochastic approach. We believe that the method can be applied and extended to various multilinear transformations such as matrix products and Kronecker products. A potential area of improvement could be to adapt the method for computing the multilinear singular value decomposition of a set of tensors. This area of study may lead to new advancements in tensor-based AI applications. Our findings also reveal that highly correlated output modes of a tensor lead to a slower method, thus the use of intermediate random formats in our approach helps to mitigate this issue. Real-world applications such as social media, infrastructure, and transportation networks evolve rapidly with the arrival of new nodes and edges over time. This research paper focuses on the task of embedding dynamic networks, which represents their temporal nature, by combining the information from individual snapshots with the overall network structure. We examine the characteristics of Twitter social media platform, which is a prime example of an evolving network, and evaluate three existing embedding methods - NodeR-GAN, GraphSAGE, and R-GAN -- for handling growth patterns of their subgraphs. Furthermore, we propose a metric to measure the temporal properties of networks and find that Twitter is primarily influenced by local factors. As a result, we discover that NodeR-GAN, which uses temporal information from node-level networks, yields the highest performance across various node classification experiments. Our findings also reveal that the effectiveness of network embedding models is greatly affected by the network's evolution rate. When handling such tasks becomes challenging, we can leverage our developed framework to swiftly and effectively derive a network's initial and final state representations from the evolving graph. This approach is then applied to solve node classification problems in social media networks. You can find the related code at https://github.com/kinneru/Temporal_Graph_Embedding. Experimental results demonstrate that the primary driver of node embedding is the network's evolution rate, which significantly impacts both the quality of node embeddings and the performance of corresponding classification tasks. This research makes two key contributions: (i) a framework to represent a network's initial and final state from an evolving graph; and (ii) a method to determine an optimal embedding rate for a node from a network. Our findings reveal that there is an inverse relationship between the network's growth rate and the quality of node embeddings. This requires developers to carefully select an appropriate threshold for the growth rate of networks, which significantly influences the performance of classification tasks. On the other hand, the quality of node embedding is affected by the network's structure rather than its size, which indicates that embedding different nodes with varying degrees has distinct implications for the performance of classification tasks. This highlights the importance of considering the role of central nodes in the network and accordingly, adapt and refine your algorithm accordingly. Moreover, the local connectivity and intermediate node roles of central nodes significantly impact the performance of classification tasks, which can be improved simply by focusing on these nodes and their properties. This research has the potential to impact a variety of fields including information representation, graph learning, and recommendation systems. You can find the related code at https://github.com/kinneru

The ground-state properties of $^7$H have been calculated using the ab initio neutron-removal method, combined with theoretical Hartree-Fock calculations for $^3$H. By considering four neutrons to be dynamically involved, the accuracy of this method was verified through a comparison with experimental data on $^7$H's binding energy and spectroscopic factors. Our study not only explains how these spectroscopic factors behave as the number of involved neutrons changes, but also reveals their individual structures as being composed of both high and low-lying states. These analyses contribute to a deeper comprehension of the $^7$H ground state's collective excitations, which arise from a $^3$H core that is perturbed by the separate excitations of four individual neutrons. Two distinct particle-removal channels, namely 0+ and 2+, were considered to analyze these collective excitations. Our calculations demonstrate that a $^7$H ground state, which is often described as a 0+ state, can also be interpreted as the result of both a $^3$H+4n process and two 2+ particle-removal channels. This finding has significant implications for the theoretical calculation of electromagnetic transitions within odd-odd nuclei. Our study sets a precedent for utilizing a more collective neutron-removal model, which combines the theoretical Hartree-Fock calculations for the $^3$H core with the density matrix mixing method, to investigate nuclei in which the neutron-removal mechanism is particularly important. This collective neutron-removal model could potentially be applied not just to $^7$H, but to a broader range of nuclei in the A=7 system and beyond. By doing so, the theoretical limitations associated with separate-neutron-removal model are addressed and the role of zero-point collective correlations is more deeply understood. Our study concludes by highlighting how a more collective neutron-removal model, which is capable of generating a wide range of collective states with significant collective correlations, could be developed. This research paper investigates a set of Nirenberg equations on half-spheres with non-positive curvature in high dimensions via blow-up techniques from minimal solutions. These equations can be expressed as $-\Delta_g U +aU = f(x) \cosh(U)$ in a standard half-sphere $(S^N, g)$ with its metric determined by a constant and an arbitrary real number $a \in \mathbb{R}$. Considering U a function that minimizes energy in $\Omega = S^N \times \{x^1 \leq 0\}$ with boundary $\partial \Omega$, the study shows that if $a<0$, with f being a function with a specific exponential decay in $\Omega$, then any minimal solution U that stays in $L^q(\Omega, x^1)$ with $q < 2$ will experience a blow-up. Moreover, this research also demonstrates that by employing a Lorentz-Korn on a half-sphere with boundary $\partial \Omega$, the function U will experience a different type of blow-up that is non-trivial and translation invariant, with its blow-up occurring within a region in $\Omega$. This non-trivial and translation-invariant blow-up was previously observed by Kim and Schoen in a Nirenberg equation on a sphere. With an alternative approach using Lorentz-Korn energy, this research derives a useful inequality with Lorentz exponents. A distance metric called sinkhorn distance offers a useful analysis tool for measuring the difference between two probability distributions that have been transformed through a specific, often complex function. Notably, this distance is inherently resistant to variations in data input order and possesses uniform Lipschitz continuity, which provides an ideal basis for training a deep neural network capable of approximating optimal solutions for various geometric optimization problems. These problems, characterized by the requirement to find an optimal transformation preserving a target distribution's structural integrity, have practical applications in multiple fields. It has been demonstrated that a sinkhorn distance function can be approximated through the use of two convolutional networks, trained in conjunction with a minimax loss function, to the point of achieving zero training error on a dataset comprising various umbrella step geodesic trajectories, spread across multiple dimensions. Furthermore, examples illustrating the capacity of the learned representation to tackle more complex problems effectively have been provided. These problems include training a self-similar transformer for handling symmetric bidirectional signals, filling in missing values within a signal, and carrying out image denoising tasks. It has been observed that the learned representation successfully supports a wide range of applications. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that a sinkhorn distance-based model can serve as an effective discriminator in the process of generating synthetic samples, especially in the case of pairwise geometric transformations. Moreover, it has been shown that the model displays impressive performance in the task of solving the problem of matching geodesically displaced objects, an application area where the problem is characterized by the requirement to find the best pairwise transformation preserving structural integrity, given a pair of input images. Notably, it has been provided with examples illustrating the model's capability to perform highly accurate object matching in the case of tasks involving complex, densely rotating objects. Finally, it has been demonstrated that the learned representation can effectively support a wide range of problems requiring variable-order data rearrangement. Such problems include the task of image segmentation, carrying out the problem of learning a self-similar transformer for handling symmetric bidirectional signals that may exhibit repeating structural elements, and the problem of filling in repeating structural elements within a signal. Notably, it has been observed that the model's performance in these tasks exhibits uniform Lipschitz continuity, a desirable property in its own right. These examples serve to illustrate the breadth of applications that a sinkhorn distance-based representation can effectively support. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that through the learning of a universal sinkhorn distance function, a wide range of problems requiring structural-preserving data transformation can be effectively formulated and solved. In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, numerous voluntary local tracing efforts were initiated to supplement the official tracing program conducted by Public Health England.  Due to a lack of existing research on the activities of these groups, we conducted a nationwide study to evaluate their influence.  Through a standardized online survey, we gathered detailed information on the operations of 164 local tracing groups, as well as broader insights into their broader impacts.  Our key findings include that these groups were highly active, processing nearly 4000 cases per day at their peak, and greatly increased the official tracing service's (TS) case finding capabilities, with the TS being unable to isolate a substantial proportion of its own previously reported targets.  Additionally, we discovered that the actions of the local tracing groups led to a significant reduction in hospital admissions and deaths.  While our data did not enable us to calculate the precise reduction in hospitalizations and deaths avoided, it indicated that the local tracing groups may have been instrumental in preventing a substantial number, potentially in the hundreds of thousands.  Finally, we explored the reasons behind volunteers' participation in local tracing efforts and provided recommendations for enhancing the effectiveness of the TS by exploring potential avenues for further research.  Specifically, we suggested that future research could be conducted to assess the effectiveness of augmenting the TS with complementary local tracing groups.  Such an exploration may offer valuable lessons in how to augment the capabilities of other public health systems globally.  Furthermore, we could discover the optimal circumstances for the collaborative model of the local tracing groups and scale up the volunteer-powered model to other public health campaigns both during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.  In doing so, we could help to maximize the resources available to the TS and contribute to the enhancement of the public health response in other contexts.  Ultimately, our research provides significant policy relevance and insight that could be applied not only to the COVID-19 response but also to future public health crises.  Specifically, the lessons learned from the local tracing groups may be adapted to other pressing issues such as the recent measles outbreaks in London and other parts of the United Kingdom, where the services of the local health authorities have been overwhelmed, and the swine flu pandemic of 2009, and could be supplemented by the efforts of private initiatives, such as the Hannah Charity Project, to contribute to the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals related to health, specifically SDG3. As Graph Neural Networks increasingly gain attention for their robustness in handling data with minor inaccuracies, they are still susceptible to attacks that alter seed nodes. To address this limitation, we develop an attack method utilizing a reinforcement learning agent that selects contaminated nodes. Our agent's reward function prioritizes accuracy degradation over minimal alteration of network structures. Through experiments, we demonstrate that the reinforcement learning agent outperforms a method that contaminates nodes at random, achieving more significant reductions in accuracy. Interestingly, the reinforcement learning agent tends to target nodes with high centrality in the semantic attention graph. Our findings show that these nodes hold critical information and effective attacks can be launched by disabling them. Additionally, through analysis within the fairmind framework, we discover that the underlying reason for success of the reinforcement learning agent lies in its focus on nodes with high centrality, resulting in biased outcomes for certain groups. Consequently, employing the reinforcement learning agent on datasets with significant group-imbalanced characteristics leads to detrimental consequences, making it a significant consideration for organizations operating in environments where fairness is a top priority. To address this concern, we present an alternative that combines contamination with concepts from adversarial training. The process of matching astronomical source catalogs involves identifying individual sources within each catalog and linking them to their counterparts across all available lists of sources. This study explores how using more photometric data can improve source matching by increasing the amount of information used to identify sources, specifically by incorporating a statistical model that accounts for sources having different brightness levels. A novel approach is presented, combining astrometric data (position information) with a statistical model of photometric measurements to estimate source properties, and then using these estimates for matching purposes. This new method is based on a statistical model of photometric measurements, which allows for uncertainties to be calculated for source brightness levels. These uncertainties can then be used in a Bayesian algorithm to determine the most likely match between sources within different catalogs based on their brightness levels. The proposed technique is demonstrated to have several benefits, including increased resistance to errors due to instrumental problems and the removal of errors caused by incorrect measurements of source positions. When applied to catalogs of galaxies and stars within the Milky Way, the method was found to be more accurate than traditional source matching techniques, improving matching rates for the most detailed catalog by 30%, and also correcting errors in the process that were causing some sources to be mismatched in the first place. Overall, the approach presents an efficient new way to utilize photometric data for matching purposes, and it was found to be more accurate than expected when applied to analysis of the brightness variations in stars that are thought to be caused by irregular objects within their vicinity known as exoplanets. Future plans are to use the technique to analyze two-way communication data from ground-based observatories and space-based satellites, and then utilize the derived source properties for a variety of scientific studies. Domain-specific data sets consisting of numerous entities and describing their associations are extensively employed, frequently in the form of conceptual diagrams. As these graph structures are comprised of entities and edges, visualizations focusing on entities often overlook the importance of edges or fail to illustrate relationship distribution. In order to address this shortcoming, a new visualization approach called OntoPlot is presented, enabling users to gain comprehensive understanding of entity and edge interrelations by simultaneously displaying network structures through color-coded entities and gradient-colored nodes representing edges. The implementation of OntoPlot is made accessible via an online tool utilizing the Apache Jena framework, allowing for simplicity and user-friendliness through straightforward input methods. In order to evaluate its effectiveness, OntoPlot is put through a comparative analysis with Prot\u08B8é, showcasing its applicability on real-world data sets comprising biomedical and educational ontologies. Results indicate that OntoPlot possesses superior grasp of complex network characteristics such as scale-free distribution, clustering coefficient and communalities, particularly in data sets characterized by non-hierarchical structures. In addition, OntoPlot is found to be quicker in communalities computation compared to Prot\u08B8é. Furthermore, studies have also demonstrated the practical applications of OntoPlot in data mining and educational settings, such as discovering frequent sequences of concepts. The present research underscores the importance of edge-centric visualization in visualizations of large-scale data sets. Moreover, OntoPlot's source code is made available through a public repository on GitHub, while the online demo is hosted at https://onto-plot.herokuapp-remote.com. The dashboard for Prot\u08B8é is accessible at https://prot\u08B8é.ontovirt.org. The data sets employed in the research can be retrieved at https://github.com/educational-ontologies. The educational ontology data set is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ontovirt/ontology-plot-2022. The related paper is found at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-07751-4_25. We introduce an innovative technique that addresses the challenge of limited labeled data in model training for speech recognition, combining an end-to-end automatic speech recognition model with a CycleGAN-based speech enhancement component and a specially designed inter-domain penalty. Our approach involves leveraging inter-domain penalties to align the speech enhancement and recognition tasks and ensuring that speech features produced after correction are consistent with ground truth annotations. Experimental validation on the Librispeech and WSJ datasets reveals that this method significantly boosts word error rates when using a minimal amount of transcribed data, and also produces high-quality speech enhancement outcomes, with improvements of up to 8.2% and 2.5% in the Librispeech corpus and 3.2% and 1.5% in the WSJ corpus, respectively, in terms of character error rates and word error rates across various data richness conditions. Our research further demonstrates that our method is adaptable to different end-to-end model architectures and can be successfully applied to other tasks involving transfer learning. Our study shows that utilizing this method results in WER reductions of over 10% when training our model on unlabeled data derived from crowdsourced sources, when compared with a simple inter-domain penalty. Additionally, when utilizing standard Librispeech evaluation conditions, model fine-tuning using distillation enables us to attain the state-of-the-art for speech recognition models, without the need for extensive data annotation processes. With a small set of perfect transcriptions, we managed to reduce the WER5 score to 2.17 and 0.76, outperforming existing methods. Our method is publicly available at https://github.com/ashish760/speech-enhancement-inter-domain-penalty.

A theoretical model called Active Inference provides the mental representations and processing mechanisms for perceived environments and expected outcomes.  Through internal molar drives and predictive error, this framework manages curiosity and motivates goal-oriented behavior.  We propose that training this model more deeply can improve the autonomy of robots navigating their surroundings.  Our results indicate that training Active Inference models yields better state estimates and target reaching performance in a self-guided learning setup, and we discuss the benefits and limitations of this approach.  Although our method achieves more efficient movement, it increases the risk of colliding with objects in the environment.  To minimize this risk, we suggest incorporating an additional module that uses experience to identify dangerous actions and adjust the movement strategy accordingly.  Our research presents a practical method for creating sophisticated active inference models and developing more robust algorithms using these models.  A demonstration robot can navigate and explore its environment using these algorithms, even when its perception is impaired.  A demonstration video is available at https://bit.ly/robot-AI.  Our code is available at https://github.com/pskel612/torchactiveinference and https://github.com/pskel612/profound-ai-robot. In the realm of music composition, the notion of evaluation spans a wide range of opinions, encompassing varied perspectives that are often difficult to quantify. This diverse array of viewpoints, encompassing both expert and layperson views, necessitates multiple evaluation methodologies to be developed to capture their individual nuances. In this paper, we introduce a groundbreaking evaluation framework for assessing algorithmically generated musical compositions by leveraging the collective wisdom of both experts and non-experts in the field of music composition. By employing a qualitative approach using textual feedback and a quantitative method using pairwise comparisons of compositions, we demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing a masked language-model architecture to provide a comprehensive evaluation framework. This approach enables us to surpass current state-of-the-art performance levels by leveraging the pairwise evaluation method with the masked transformer model. Furthermore, through qualitative analysis of the collected expert and non-expert feedback, we gain valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of our proposed composition evaluation framework. Our primary objective is to investigate the impact of incorrect throwing mechanics on movement patterns. To accomplish this, a simulation of virtual objects was employed, where participants had to replicate throws either with or without considering the forces of gravity and rotation. The results showed that even though participants claimed to follow standard throwing mechanics, the actual motion captured by sensors deviated from expected patterns. Notably, when these sensors were used to calculate the point at which the ball left the user's hand, it became apparent that some participants did not accurately apply the standard release point. The combination of both accurate and inaccurate throwing mechanics, along with considering and neglecting the forces of gravity and rotation, resulted in a total of 8 possible throwing styles. To better understand the quality of the simulated movements, a machine learning algorithm was trained to classify the different throwing styles based on the motion patterns, where the models achieved a high level of accuracy in classifying the various throwing styles. Moreover, when the algorithms were trained to classify only the correct or incorrect throwing styles, it achieved a high accuracy in classifying the standard (correct) throwing style but struggled with the non-standard (incorrect) styles. Our work provides valuable insights for the development of machine learning models in motion capture applications, especially where there may be variations in how an action is performed, rather than strictly adhering to a single standard method. Ultimately, this research has significant implications for our understanding of how non-standard behavior is generated in both artificial and human decision-making processes. The current research is presented in a virtual reality setting but could be expanded to other fields such as game design and controlled movements. Furthermore, this approach can also be applied to syntactic parsing by utilizing the predicted syntactic dependencies derived from the training data.
Experimental outcomes on the English-to-German and English-to-Russian datasets seem to validate the method's effectiveness.
Detailed analysis and qualitative assessments also highlight the need for future optimizations based on language pairs used in the study.

The conventional viewpoint holds that abstract concepts must be learned early in life, 
but then become fixed and unchanging. Yet, at our age of vast digital storage, 
people are now learning new skills throughout their lifetime, contradicting this idea. 
Despite this, researchers have made little effort to develop methods for confirming and 
accelerating knowledge acquisition throughout a person's life. To address this, we're 
pioneering a novel framework for visual understanding that not only allows for one-shot 
learning but also proves that new concepts can be linked to existing knowledge. 
Our 'Prime-Learn' framework focuses on learning the underlying linear associations 
between objects' appearances and their essential qualities. To validate its utility, 
we created a set of straightforward educational lessons in basic skills like 'color 
coherence' and 'counting,' enabling us to verify that humans can indeed learn these 
conceptually, and that our model effectively emulates this ability. Our experiments 
show that Prime-Learn achieves impressive results across various self-guided learning 
experiments, including learning to recognize natural language, generating synthetic 
images, and enhancing knowledge through lifetime self-study. Our code and data are now 
available for public access at https://github.com/alexseydan/Prime-Learn. With this 
research, we're one step closer to developing a versatile AI model that mimics 
human learning and can be applied in educational settings to expand a person's 
knowledge throughout their lifetime. Additionally, the underlying framework of 
Prime-Learn has potential uses in various fields, such as educational platforms, 
autonomous vehicles, and other multi-modal systems where identifying the 
interconnections between disparate data types may be necessary. Ultimately, this 
research lays the groundwork for an AI that genuinely understands and interprets 
the world around it, just like a human does. As such, it may lead to a breakthrough 
in creating AI systems that keep learning and evolving throughout their own 
'lifetimes.' A related demonstration video can be accessed at https://youtu.be/NRgQx9p9y50.

Using multilingual language models has become increasingly common in low-resource machine translation scenarios. In order to deploy such models in resource-constrained environments, they need to be reduced in size without sacrificing their performance. This can be achieved through quantization, which reduces number sizes, and word dropping, which decreases vocabulary sizes. While both methods are well-established in NLP, their long-term effects on model performance have not been thoroughly investigated. This leads to a significant question: which method is more stable and less prone to degradation in small MT systems. Our study aims to answer this question by comparing the effects of quantization and word dropping on the performance of small low-resource machine translation models. We discovered that word dropping is more stable and produces fewer drops in performance than quantization. This is likely due to the fact that quantization causes performance drops in proportion to the number of tokens processed. On the other hand, word dropping's decline is typically minimal and within a range of a few PERs. This study marks the first time that the effects of word dropping on the performance of small MT models have been investigated. Our findings have significant implications for model downsizing which could lead to a surge in the development of lightweight, low-resource machine translation models. We have released all of our code and data on GitHub. Future studies could delve into the causes for the differing levels of stability between quantization and word dropping. It is also possible that the results of this study could be extended to other areas such as text generation and language modeling. Finally, we propose additional methods for decreasing model size while maintaining performance, which would represent an advancement in this field. Our suggestions are supported by the results of a word dropping experiment involving six distinct models and text datasets. This study was completed as part of a series of initiatives aimed at reducing the size of low-resource machine translation models launched by the TUL3MT project. As a result, the techniques and the study's outcomes could have a significant impact on the advancement of resource-constrained machine translation. The findings of this research may also motivate the machine translation community to develop smaller, yet efficient MT models that save valuable resources while maintaining their performance. This study was completed without support from a funding agency. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to an overwhelming number of patients worldwide who need to be treated, highlighting the significance of deep learning-based medical image analysis. Nevertheless, extensive annotated image datasets are required to train such models, a resource constraint particularly evident in the medical field. In response, we investigate the potential of data augmentation and image upscaling techniques to facilitate the creation of high-quality segmentation models utilizing fewer labeled resources. By employing a combined approach of pre-training, transfer learning, and image upscaling, we demonstrate that our proposed solution can generate enhanced radiographic images leading to significantly better model performance even when trained with greatly reduced labeled data. Experimental evaluations were conducted across various combinations of data augmentation, image upscaling methods, and depth models, ultimately revealing that the use of sophisticated upscaling algorithms and certain depth models can yield superior results. Moreover, our findings illustrate that the proposed technique is compatible with other segmentation approaches and datasets, thus possessing a high potential for widespread adoption in the medical imaging community. Ultimately, our experiments demonstrate that effective segmentation can be achieved even with as few as $100$ labeled annotations per class. To address this, we developed a novel image description task that requires accurate, detailed, and aesthetically-pleasing descriptions. Our task incorporates three distinct constraints: image quality assessment, where descriptions should not be overly detailed; aesthetic evaluation, where descriptions should be aesthetically pleasing; and content and aesthetic coherence, where both should be consistent. Our findings demonstrate that by utilizing a prompt-based system, it is possible to achieve high levels of accuracy in isolating various attributes of a model's image captioning style. Notably, our results highlight the significance of leveraging multi-modal datasets in enhancing the aesthetic quality of image captioning outputs. Different fields, including physics and biology, use the concept of damage to describe systems that can be affected or harmed. In this study, we apply causal analysis to the phenomenon of damage. It is demonstrated that damage is the direct consequence of a system's ability to absorb disturbances and its inability to repair the effects of those disturbances. Any given system is characterized by a distinct shape of its damage processes, which is determined by the ratio of its capacity to absorb disturbances and its repair rate. Conversely, the damage process of a system can also be predicted based on the characteristics of its individual components and various disturbances. It is shown that the damage pattern of a system can transition from one stage to another as the ratio of its repair rate to the disturbance ratio changes, regardless of the specific damage system model. Essentially, the damage process of a system can be divided into distinct stages, which can be represented on a phase diagram. The study not only offers a universal definition of damage but also a universal method for classifying the damage process of any system, providing valuable insights and strategies for enhancing system resilience. It is shown that the repair rate of a system or its components can be regulated through specific internal and external mechanisms, such as developing the ability to adapt to new situations or employing a memory network that facilitates repair. It is also shown that the damage process of a system can be influenced by external factors, such as introducing a particular molecule or changing the surrounding environment, and that the damage process of a system can be reversed or advanced for tactical purposes. It is hoped that the information presented in this study can benefit researchers and clinicians in various fields. Moreover, the study offers a universal set of strategies for enhancing system resilience, which can be broadly classified into three stages: preventing disturbances, improving repair rate, and reducing the extent of disturbance propagation. Such strategies are applicable not only to biological systems but also to physical systems and even human societies. Finally, the study introduces a simple statistical model for describing the damage process of a system following a sudden event, which is similar to well-known models used to describe the spreading process of diseases. Although the model proposed in this study has not been tested statistically, it is hoped that it can be used for predicting the stage of system damage in advance of actual events and for comparing the effectiveness of different strategies for enhancing system resilience. Such predictions can be challenging given that the study not only examines damage but also the processes of disturbance propagation and repair. This research introduces a new challenge, zero-shot voice translation, where speech-based input in a source language is translated into written output in a target language. Differentiating it from other voice translation approaches, where voice recordings are translated into spoken versions of another language, zero-shot voice translation requires no parallel speech-data and relies solely on unpaired speech from the target language and text from the source language. To tackle this challenge, we developed a voice translation model combining two transformer models: one for speech-to-text and another for text-to-text. This hybrid approach outperformed comparable methods, achieving notable improvements in translation accuracy. Notably, when the model was fine-tuned with a small amount of zero-shot training data, there was minimal decline in translation accuracy. This hybrid method achieved superior results on a range of languages, demonstrating its translation accuracy with languages such as English, Spanish, German, and Mandarin Chinese. Nonetheless, further enhancements are needed to address translation inaccuracies for languages with complex syntax and those that are morphologically rich. Future research could explore incorporating additional modality transformations to expand the scope of zero-shot voice translation models. The full paper can be found at a publicly available GitHub repository, complete with supplementary materials and videos demonstrating the translation process. This work introduces a novel extension of the Coleman-Gurtin equations, which incorporates dynamic boundary constraints, to model thermodynamic behavior. The model accounts for spatially distributed phase transitions and occurs within a domain with its own unique thermodynamic properties, along with the boundaries that are separate from the domain but still evolve over time. The model's behavior is governed by a linear relation between the boundary flux and the difference between the boundary temperature and an equilibrium temperature, along with non-algebraic boundary constraints that are influenced by the temperature and its time derivative, calibrated using laboratory measurements of a heated plate. The well-posedness of this highly nonlinear problem is demonstrated in a limited-time setting, with the help of the theory of monotone operators and the existence of weak solutions, under very strict constraints such as constant boundary constraints and no phase transitions occurring either in the domain or across the boundaries, for a limited period of time. Furthermore, our analysis explores the long-term behavior of this system when it reaches a steady state, showing the uniqueness of the equilibrium state, along with the convergence of the system towards this equilibrium, without the need for boundary constraints, provided that the boundary constraints are non-degenerate. Lastly, our approach allows for the integration of the theory to a broader range of phase transitions, encompassing more complex scenarios such as surface diffusion, volume-surface diffusion, and complex systems with multiple phase transitions. However, this extension is only explored in a linear framework and does not depend on the theory of thermodynamics, as it would in a nonlinear setting. Special recognition and gratitude are offered to Dr. Peter Knabner for his selfless contribution and invaluable feedback. The model's behavior is also explored through numerical simulations, with the purpose of better understanding the theoretical findings and their practical implications. Precise and continuous forecasting of energy consumption is essential for the effective management of low voltage distribution networks. This study compares four load forecasting models that combine weather data and historical consumption patterns, all of which utilize a Bayesian approach. By examining the interactions between weather and consumption, these models can identify the relationships that are crucial for low voltage distribution. The proposed methods successfully incorporate the effects of seasonal changes and incorporate predictions of daily peak consumption, which is crucial for optimizing network operations. The research demonstrates the benefits and limitations of probabilistic load forecasts, rather than definitive predictions. Furthermore, it highlights how probabilistic forecasts can be used in conjunction to enhance accuracy and provide a level of network operators with the representation of prediction uncertainty. The models were trained using consumption and weather data from the entire UK, as well as from specific regions with distinct climatic characteristics, such as Scotland and the southwest of England. The findings of this research were validated by comparing them with actual consumption values, demonstrating that the proposed methods were effective. The generation of the models' uncertainty through the use of the auto directional noise algorithm was found to provide a accurate representation of actual consumption variability. The models' ability to predict consumption was found to degrade over a period of 24 hours, with peak consumption accuracy occurring at the level of individual households and lower consumption accuracy occurring at the level of aggregation. The disparity in accuracy was found to be substantial, with models such as ARD and ARD-RNN achieving 8% and 12% accuracy in relation to daily peak consumption, but only 2% and 3% accuracy in relation to total daily consumption. The findings of the research were found to be consistent with the physical properties of consumption data and it demonstrates the significance of incorporating the effects of seasonal changes in the analysis. The models' ability to utilize the autoencoder's latent space to distinguish between typical and unusual consumption patterns was found to provide a valuable insight into the relationships between consumption and weather. The research was found to be relevant not only to the specific context in which it was developed but also to a broader range of applications. For instance, the methodologies employed in the research could be adapted for analysis of consumption data from other regions with distinct climatic characteristics. The research could also be applied to the analysis of other types of temporal data by modifying the models to accommodate the specific data at hand. The research provides insights into the value of incorporating the effects of seasonal variations, which is crucial for the effective management of consumption data. Recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning have led to a surge in automated model creation, but the integration of domain expertise still poses a significant challenge. From a practical perspective, this issue often results in the problem domain being unclear, with unclear or no performance metrics, and uncertain sampling methods. To mitigate this, our proposed research approach, "domain fusion," aims to synchronize domain expertise with machine learning outcomes. A general framework for domain expertise integration is introduced, with specific attention to data and performance customization. We outline certain domain knowledge elements that can be incorporated into machine learning and provide a general performance evaluation method. Additionally, we discuss common research dataset characteristics and specify corresponding data preparation procedures. Samples from the dataset can be selected using established and customizable methods. Performance metrics can be chosen from a range of existing metrics or introduced directly. Based on this framework, we develop a tool to assist researchers in integrating domain expertise, which is applied to the "Wildlife Audio Classification" problem. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of domain fusion in achieving superior performance with limited resources, using a reasonable amount of domain-specific data. The proposed approach, domain fusion, is published under the BSD-3 license. An implementation of this framework, including the framework and models, is available at https://github.com/fharsha222/domains_first. Furthermore, the pre-trained models, dataset, and performance evaluation results can be found at https://www.github.com/fharsha222/blueprint. An interactive website at https://blueprint-DFI.gitea.io/ provides a simplified user experience. The blueprint website offers detailed guidance on domain fusion. Our efforts have received awards in multiple competitions, notably the Data Science Bowl 2017 and Audio Census 2019. More information on our success can be found at https://dsb.berkleyharvard.org/ and https://www.audioquantum.ai/competition. In the medical imaging field, combining computer-aided detection and segmentation capabilities can facilitate accurate diagnosis of COVID-19 and normal controls (NCs), thereby assisting in the identification of individuals at risk. Nevertheless, the traditional supervised learning approach is problematic due to its bias and limitation in generalizing to unseen data. To address these shortfalls, we propose a novel methodology, comprising two stages: (i) semi-supervised segmentation of chest CT scans from individuals with COVID-19, utilizing atmospheric correction functions; and (ii) a segmentation-and-rereprojection feedback loop that refines the model's performance using normaled and pseudo-labeled data obtained through segmentation and reversal of the images. Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits considerable potential for data augmentation by accounting for numerous confounding factors such as radiation dose, noise, positioning, and breathing. Ultimately, the proposed approach is suitable for both diagnostic settings, allowing for accurate detection and differentiation of COVID-19 and NCs from chest imaging. With the continued spread of the virus worldwide, the proposed methodology is invaluable in informing the clinical community and public about the unique characteristics and dangers associated with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. A novel vertebral body localization and recognition framework is introduced, 
comprising unique characteristics such as vertebrae identification, 
segmentation, and alignment. This framework is distinguished from others 
by its ability to work with complex spinal curvatures and the absence of 
pre-defined landmarks. The framework's initial stage involves rectifying and 
normalising the spinal column, followed by the detection and labelling of 
vertebrae. Anatomically-guided optimization ensures accurate vertebral 
body alignment. Evaluations conducted on large, diverse CT image sets 
confirm the superior performance of the proposed framework compared to 
existing methods. Additionally, the impact of vertebral recognition and 
segmentation is explored in the context of image-based quantification. 
The new approach will primarily facilitate vertebral quantification and 
quantitative analysis based on CT scans. The method is open-source and 
can be easily integrated with existing workflow systems. An accompanying 
dataset consisting of 580 CT scans is also available for public use. 
The related code can be found at https://github.com/rtkdc/spine_alignment. 
The dataset can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/spine-dc.

found at https://dx.qinjiani.org/quantify-spine.

Researchers are highly intrigued by the ultrastrong light-material coupling regime because of its unique properties.  In this highly-coupled regime,  predictions yield an unexpected implosion of energy in a negative parabola -  a phenomenon often referred to as the "death spiral of light and matter".  Our team has discovered a different story:  in this highly-coupled regime,  a stable electron trajectory emerges when the radiation pressure's frequency matches the natural oscillation frequency of the electron in the cavity.  This stable path arises from a previously unexplored dynamics where the electron's motion is simultaneously steered by both radiation forces and the conservation of phase - a concept known as Bohr-Sommerfeld conditions.  This stable trajectory can be accessed by resonantly scattering electrons within the cavity at the specific matching frequency.  This resonance also results in an enhanced light-matter coupling that surpasses previous limits and is complemented by an exceptional sensitivity to changes in the electron's initial conditions, making this process highly suitable for applications in quantum sensing.  Our theoretical findings are accompanied by a set of numerical examples that illustrate the novel concepts and solutions that arise in this highly-coupled regime.  Ultimately,  the findings reveal that the highly-coupled regime is not just a "death spiral" but also a path that holds many opportunities for creating stable and novel quantum states -  a promise that is particularly significant in the context of quantum sensing applications.  This new theoretical discovery is believed to open up even more avenues for research in the field of quantum optics and will likely have a significant impact on future technologies in quantum sensing and other related areas.  Our study is available in the published journal, Physical Review Research.  Researchers anticipate that their findings will not only shed new light on quantum optics but will also inspire cutting-edge applications in the future.  The work is already sparking a new line of inquiry into exploring quantum states in the ultrastrong light-matter coupling regime,  and researchers are confident that it will lead to a significant breakthrough in quantum sensing and related technologies.  The theory is currently being tested in the laboratory for the ultrastrong light-matter coupling regime and is being promoted through an associated experiment as part of a new approach to understanding quantum mechanics.  The project demonstrates how even seemingly unstable quantum states can be stabilized by dynamics and predicts that the resulting findings will have a significant impact on quantum physics and the development of quantum technologies in the future.  The project is expected to lead to numerous applications in quantum sensing and related fields and researchers

This research explores the capabilities of reinforcement learning to control a quadruped robot equipped with ideal elastic actuators. In simulations, various RL methods were applied and evaluated in tandem with a dynamics-based movement policy. A key goal of fashion image retrieval involves pinpointing a target item's style characteristics, despite limited labeled data being available for various attributes. To address this, a semi-supervised method for modifying fashion images at the feature level has been proposed, using a siamese network to tackle the shortage of labeled data. This method involves two approaches for retrieving similar items after feature-level manipulation, ranked-hamming distance and centroid distance, to enhance the model's retrieval performance. Additionally, the proposed method significantly outperformed baselines in accuracy and recall for the Stylized Fashion Semantic Editing Challenge 2022. In the past decade, smartphone and WiFi network technology has experienced a rapid increase in popularity. According to a recent survey, an astonishing number of 5.22 billion people, which constitutes more than 68% of the world's population, use smartphones. Additionally, it is estimated that the average person spends approximately 4 hours per day using their smartphone, adding up to a total of 30 billion hours, equivalent to one million years in a single day. Furthermore, a significant number of people rely on their smartphones to access the internet, indicating that the network will only become increasingly congested in the future. In order to prove this, a study conducted by OpenDNS found that as of 2016, the average smartphone generated 1 GB of internet data in just 5 days. Given these remarkable statistics, it is clear that the deployment of a large number of WiFi access points and extenders within homes and public spaces can help alleviate the congestion by segmenting the network into smaller, more manageable sections, thereby preventing a total network collapse. However, proper configuration of these devices is crucial to avoid any potential interference or congestion caused by unnecessary overlap in coverage areas. Otherwise, it may lead to a suboptimal network performance and a frustrating user experience. In light of these challenges, this research paper proposes an innovative solution that utilizes the IEEE 802.11k/v standards to optimize network performance by strategically placing WiFi access points and extenders within homes and public spaces. The goal of this approach is to minimize WiFi interference, ensure seamless coverage, and provide high-speed WiFi connectivity to a maximum number of devices.
